20987-story-of-the-war-in-south-africa-1:
Cape Horn and the Cape of Good Hope owed their fame to trade routes, this history notes. For centuries, only those wild capes linked Europe to Pacific and Indian shores. The Story of the War in South Africa opens with that wide, lone frame.

Alfred Thomas Story tells the Boer War of 1899-1900 as it unfolded. Sieges, commandos, and British columns clash across veld and town. The war shook the British Empire and taught it harsh new lessons. This early account, written close to the events, keeps the shock and scale of a war that proved far harder than London had dreamed.
22620-researches-on-cellulose-1895-1900:
Researches on Cellulose, 1895–1900 is a scientific review gathering five years of work on the chemistry of cellulose, the fiber that builds plant cell walls. The catalog record names no author. Paper, cotton, and wood industries all rested on this substance, and chemists raced to learn its true makeup.

The sample weighs a claim about silica in the plant skeleton. Does it play a special structural role beside the cellulosic parts? Or does it merely sit among the ash left after burning? Notes and references crowd the discussion, as the review tests rival findings against each other. The volume shows industrial chemistry in its careful, cumulative mode. Historians of materials science can watch a field sorting signal from noise.
22807-a-difficult-problem-1900:
A Difficult Problem is a mystery story dated 1900, in which a widow reads a name and wonders whether she is dreaming. The catalog record names no author. Its problem begins with paper: a slip, a letter, and a name that cannot be what it seems.

My husband, the narrator says, was James Forsythe De Witt Holmes. His last letter, lying beside the cushion at that very moment, came dated from the Colonnade. Was I dreaming, she asks? Or had some frightful hallucination made me misread the name on the slip before me? A dead husband's name, alive in the wrong place, sets the inquiry moving. The tale belongs to the turn-of-the-century school of lady detectives and drawing-room puzzles.
a-phrenological-chart-of-character-with-: A Phrenological Chart of Character, 1900. The character chart. This book preserves that chart. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
abramelin-book-3-mathers-1900:
The Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage claims to record the system Abraham of Worms learned from an Egyptian mage. S. L. MacGregor Mathers translated the French manuscript, and his edition appeared in 1900. Book Three, given here, is the book of magic squares, and it completes the three-book Mathers Abramelin in the library.

After the long holy operation of the earlier books, the magician receives word squares for many purposes. Each square of letters serves a stated end, from finding treasure to raising storms. The squares are the working tools the whole rite exists to deliver. Mathers's Abramelin shaped modern ceremonial magic deeply. Book Three is its toolbox, page after page of lettered power.
abramelin-sacred-magic-book-3-mathers-19:
Abraham of Worms was a Jewish traveler of the late 1300s. He wrote down a system of ritual magic that he said he learned in Egypt from a mage named Abramelin. S. L. MacGregor Mathers turned the French manuscript into English, and his edition appeared in 1900. The third book holds the working tools of the system.

Inside are grids of letters called magic squares, each square tied to a spirit and a stated aim, from finding lost goods to raising storms. After months of prayer and strict living, the mage was to call on these spirits and direct them through the squares. Later occult groups treated these pages as the heart of the whole Abramelin operation.
alchemical-treatises-by-christophorus-pa: Christophorus of Paris left treatises and letters around 1500. The correspondence with fellow adepts survives. The late-medieval alchemy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This book preserves that collection. Kept for readers. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
alphonsus-uniformity-gods-will-1900: Uniformity with God's Will by St. Alphonsus Liguori, in a 1900 translation. The saint teaches accepting all things as from God's hand. This book preserves that beloved devotional treatise. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
arxiv-2512-00400:
Embedded systems must do more every year while staying strictly predictable in time. Yifan Zhang and co-authors present TenonOS in 2025, a self-generating framework that stacks one library operating system on another. Monolithic designs and rigid layers bring resource bloat and unpredictable scheduling.

The framework targets time-critical embedded operating systems, where temporal determinism is as important as raw function. Generating the system in layers aims to keep functionality rich but timing behavior controlled. Such work matters for vehicles, medical devices, and industrial controllers, where a late answer can be as bad as a wrong one. A library operating system assembles system services like building blocks, per application. For folks who write code for cars, pumps, or plant gear, the gain is a base that can grow step by step. All the while, the clocks in the gear stay true.
arxiv-2512-00600:
Xinyuan Dou, Ming Jin, Guangbin Ren, and Irene Sabadini study pure math in a 2025 paper on sedenionic power series. Sedenions are a sixteen-part number system that extends the better known quaternions and octonions. The authors ask where a certain kind of series, built from star powers, settles down and converges.

Their work sits inside slice regular function theory. That field extends complex analysis, the study of functions of complex numbers, to larger number systems. It has already been pushed to Clifford algebras, octonions, and other settings. Mapping the convergence domains helps show how far the theory can safely reach.
arxiv-2512-00800:
Shawan Jha, Makoto Tsubota, and Pankaj Mishra study two-dimensional quantum turbulence in a 2025 paper. A quantum fluid can swirl through vortices, whirlpools whose spin comes in fixed steps. How a tangle of vortices settles down over time is a basic question about such fluids.

The team follows four starting patterns: dipole, plasma, cluster, and lattice arrangements of vortices. They evolve each with the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, the standard model for these fluids. The cluster pattern reaches equilibrium fastest, they find. The other three stay out of balance and drift toward non-thermal fixed points instead.
arxiv-2512-01100:
Fatemeh Khashami examines quantum features in nuclear magnetic resonance systems in a 2025 paper. NMR systems use the spins of atomic nuclei, and a pair of spin one-half nuclei is a clean test bed for quantum effects. At thermal equilibrium under strong magnetic fields, such systems hold subtle quantum correlations.

Using suitable quantifiers, Khashami analyzes quantum coherence, mixedness, and entanglement in these two-spin systems. She also examines witnessing tests, which certify that such links are present without a full rebuilding of the state. The results clarify how much genuine quantumness survives in warm, everyday NMR settings used by chemists.
arxiv-2512-01200:
Chang-geun Oh, Haruki Watanabe, and Naoto Tsuji study a light-based probe of superconductors in a 2025 paper. Superconductors host collective modes, shared vibrations of the whole condensate, such as the Higgs mode. That mode is named for its likeness to the Higgs particle's role in its own field.

Third-harmonic generation, where a material emits light at triple the input frequency, is a primary tool for probing the Higgs mode. Its signal competes with quasiparticle excitations, and impurity scattering rates decide which dominates. The authors examine the role of quantum geometry in that competition, clarifying when the Higgs signal can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-01400:
Paula Harder and co-authors test if rain models trained in one place work in others. Deep learning can sharpen coarse rain forecasts to fine detail. That skill is called downscaling. Most models are built for one region only.

Whether they hold up in new terrain and climate is not clear. The team checks broad models across many regions. They score how well fine rain patterns move to unseen places. The results show where one global model can serve and where local training is still needed for safe flood and farm plans.
arxiv-2512-01500:
Alfredo Reichlin, Miguel Vasco, and Danica Kragic offer a simpler way to gauge doubt in neural nets. Bayesian nets model doubt by a spread over weights. Exact sums for that spread cannot be done. Common shortcuts scale poorly and miss the true spread in big nets.

Their method walks along a fiber, a curved path in weight space. That walk gives a geometric guess of the spread. A simpler path could make doubt scores cheap for large models. Cheap, sound doubt scores matter for safe use in robots, clinics, and self-driving cars.
arxiv-2512-01800:
Zhe Chen gives conservative forms for the Standard Enskog and Povzner equations. Both extend the Boltzmann equation by adding particle volume in collisions. Dense gases need that volume term. Non-conservative forms can break mass or energy bookkeeping in simulations.

Chen's main result writes each collision integral as a divergence in velocity space. That form makes conservation manifest. Manifest conservation steadies numeric solvers for dense gases. It also clarifies how the two classic extensions relate to each other. Divergence form also aids boundary treatment in codes, since fluxes at cell faces can be balanced exactly in the new variables.
arxiv-2512-02100:
Watching a quantum system changes it, and frequent local measurements can tip a spin chain between very different behaviors. Yicheng Tang and four co-authors study this measurement-induced phase transition in 2025, in spin chains burdened by strong disorder.

They examine the transverse-field Ising model with a random field at each site, alongside a many-body localized Hamiltonian written in localized bits. Their finding is stark: both the prethermal and the localized regimes fall apart under local measurements, whichever direction the measurements point. The result limits how well disorder can protect quantum order once an observer keeps looking.
arxiv-2512-02200:
The Doughnut framework pictures a safe economy: a social floor below which no one should fall, and planetary boundaries that must not be crossed. Stefano Vrizzi and Daniel O'Neill show in 2025 how frugal machine learning can be applied to a simple macroeconomic model of that Doughnut.

Their analysis is a proof of concept, deliberately small, testing whether learning methods can track many social and environmental indicators at once. Frugal methods matter here because sustainability modeling must stay transparent and cheap enough for wide use. If the approach scales, it could help policymakers see which economies sit inside the Doughnut and which spill outside it.
arxiv-2512-02400:
A robot told to find an object it has never seen, in a building it has never entered, must reason openly about language and space. Wentao Xiang and a large team present Nav-R2 in 2025, a navigation system built on dual-relation reasoning for open-vocabulary object-goal navigation.

Existing approaches suffered from opaque decision-making and low success at locating novel objects in unseen environments. Reasoning over two kinds of relations aims to make the agent's choices both better and more legible. Robots that can hunt for arbitrary named objects are a step toward household and warehouse helpers that take instructions in plain words.
arxiv-2512-03100:
Adding outside knowledge to language models brings a privacy risk. Haowei Fu, Kunpeng Liu, Dan Lin, and Tyler Derr study that risk in this 2025 work. Two common ways to add knowledge are search-based retrieval and fine-tuning on new data.

Attackers can probe a model to guess if a given item was in its training data. Such membership attacks threaten trust in fields with private records. The authors propose a team-based defense that guards the model. Strong guards matter as firms add client files and records to their AI tools. The defense focus fits real deployments, where private files sit close to the model's core knowledge.
arxiv-2512-03500:
Long videos hide key moments in hours of footage. Te Yang and co-authors present an exploration-exploitation agent for that task in this 2025 work. Current methods either preprocess densely at high cost or balance search poorly.

Dense methods waste compute, while weak search misses sparse but critical information. Their agent, EEA, navigates long visual data more efficiently. It balances exploring new segments with exploiting promising ones. Better long video understanding helps surveillance review, sports analysis, and meeting archives. Exploration choices decide coverage, since a fixed scan of long footage wastes most frames.
arxiv-2512-03800:
Exotic particles made of four quarks, rather than the usual two or three, are a live frontier in particle physics. Bing-Dong Wan and colleagues compute the masses of such tetraquarks in a 2025 preprint. These states hide a charm or bottom quark pair inside. They carry spin and parity labels that ordinary mesons cannot have.

The calculations use QCD sum rules, a standard technique that connects quark-level theory to particle masses through an expansion including condensates up to dimension eight. The method predicts four hidden-charm states with masses just under five gigaelectronvolts. Their hidden-bottom partners come out near eleven gigaelectronvolts. Wan and colleagues also map the likely decay routes for these states. Those maps tell experimenters at BESIII, Belle II, and LHCb where to look, turning theory into a concrete search target.
arxiv-2512-03900:
Lasers that must hold an exact frequency, for clocks and precision spectroscopy, are commonly steadied with the Pound-Drever-Hall technique. Roame Hildebrand and colleagues expose a routinely underestimated error in that method in a 2025 optics preprint. The trouble starts when leftover optical sidebands meet higher-order spatial modes inside a slightly misaligned cavity.

In offset locking, that interaction shifts the lock point away from the intended frequency. The shift can reach half the cavity linewidth when the offset comes from a sinusoidally driven modulator. The team measures the deviation in the laboratory and matches it with a simple model. Swapping in a spectrally pure frequency offset shrinks the error by about tenfold. Their warning matters for optical clocks, precision spectroscopy, and quantum information experiments, where a silent frequency shift of this size can corrupt results.
arxiv-2512-04000:
Asking a multimodal model about a long video is expensive, because it can only swallow so many frames at once. Jialuo Li, Bin Li, Jiahao Li, and Yan Lu show in a 2025 preprint that the right frame selection strategy depends on the question. Global questions about a whole video behave differently from localised ones about one moment.

For global queries, plain uniform sampling already works well and cheaply, and elaborate search adds little. Localised queries genuinely need frames chosen with the query in mind. Their framework, DIG, routes each question accordingly: uniform sampling for global queries, and a specialised grounding pipeline for localised ones, all without training. On three long-video benchmarks, DIG beat existing baselines and kept improving performance as frame counts scaled into the hundreds. The lesson is restraint: spend computation only where the query demands it.
arxiv-2512-04100:
Sharing radio spectrum fairly requires a map: which frequencies are busy, where, and how strongly. Mukaram Shahid and colleagues build such maps with a physics-informed neural network in a 2025 preprint. Their system, ReVeal-MT, extends an earlier single-transmitter design to the messy case where many transmitters overlap and interfere.

The authors first write a partial differential equation for received signal strength from multiple sources. They fold its residual into the network's loss, so physics disciplines the fit to sparse sensor readings. Validation uses real measurements from the ARA living lab, a wireless testbed spanning rural and suburban terrain. Against standard channel models and their own single-transmitter baseline, ReVeal-MT reconstructed hundreds of square kilometres from fewer than fifty samples, with errors of a few decibels. The authors aim the tool at fine-grained spectrum management between primary and secondary users.
arxiv-2512-04200:
The Magellanic Clouds are an interacting galaxy pair close to the Milky Way, yet their three-dimensional geometry is still poorly pinned down. Slater J. Oden and a large team map them in a 2025 galactic astronomy preprint. Their rulers are red clump stars, standard candles once age and metal content are corrected for.

The sample combines about two million stars from Gaia's third data release. Median distances come out near fifty-one kiloparsecs for the Large Cloud and sixty-one for the Small. The maps refresh structures from the northern arm and southern hooks to the Magellanic Bridge and outlying overdensities. Fitting the disk yields its tilt and orientation. The striking find is a U-shaped warp around the periphery, reaching seven kiloparsecs vertically. The authors read it as a tidal scar from the Small Cloud's close passage three hundred million years ago.
arxiv-2601-06700:
Zhiyao Zhang, Yazan Mash'Al, and Yuhan Wu characterize toxicity in generative models in 2026. Their paper explores linguistic factors that might cause toxic output. Models can produce harmful text even from ordinary-looking prompts.

They aim to identify how prone large language models are to toxicity. They also study lexical and syntactic structures that trigger toxic generation. Certain words and sentence shapes may reliably provoke bad outputs. Knowing the triggers helps builders filter and steer models better. The work treats toxicity as a linguistic phenomenon with structure. Safety researchers get factors they can measure, not just examples. Findings could guide training data curation and prompt design alike. It adds precision to a debate often run on anecdotes.
arxiv-2601-06900:
Issey Sukeda and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers minimum information markov model. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. The analysis of high-dimensional time series data has become increasingly important across a wide range of fields.

Recently, a method for constructing the minimum information Markov kernel on finite state spaces was established. The authors propose a statistical model based on a parametrization of its dependence function, which we call the Minimum Information Markov Model . The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07300:
R. Arun and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers self-oscillations induced by self-induced torque in magnetic double tunnel junction. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Self-oscillations of the magnetization due to self-induced torque (SIT) in a magnetic double tunnel junction that consists of perpendicularly polarized.

Pinned and free layers is investigated along with the field-like torque (FLT). The associated Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski equation is numerically analysed to exhibit the oscillations of magnetization driven by the current. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07600:
Juan José Martín, José Flich, and Carles Hernández test how well modern NVIDIA GPUs can isolate competing inference jobs. Safety-critical systems need predictable inference times, even when several deep learning models share one chip. The authors compare three isolation tools: MPS, MIG, and the newer Green Contexts. Their 2026 preprint reports performance tests on two platforms.

Experiments run on both the NVIDIA A100 and the Jetson Orin, covering data center and edge hardware. The team measures how partitioning affects speed and how strong the time isolation between processes really is. Weak isolation means one job can slow another without warning. The results speak to engineers placing AI models in cars, robots, and medical devices, where late answers can be unsafe.
arxiv-2601-08000:
Can Jin and colleagues strengthen language model safety by reasoning over legal precedents as well as rules. Ensuring models follow safety principles without refusing harmless requests is a standing challenge. Deliberative alignment teaches models to reason over detailed, code-like safety rules. Its success in open-source models, which usually reason less strongly, is understudied. Their 2026 preprint adds case augmentation to the approach. Precedents sit alongside statutes in the model's deliberation.

Lawyers reason from both written rules and past cases. The authors borrow that habit for model safety. Cases show how abstract principles land on concrete situations. That grounding may help smaller open models apply rules more faithfully. The paper serves AI alignment scholars. It tests whether richer deliberation material closes the gap with proprietary systems.
arxiv-2601-08100: Xinping Yi, Gaojie Jin, Xiaowei Huang, and Shi Jin work toward one PAC-Bayesian framework for norm-based generalization bounds. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that why deep networks generalize remains a core open question. PAC-Bayesian norm-based bounds stand out because they depend on the data at hand. They can also capture properties of both the algorithm and the geometry of learned models. A unified framework could replace scattered bounds with one clear account. That would help theorists compare methods and guide safer model design.
arxiv-2601-08400:
E. Rodriguez and G. Plunk wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a large bank of magnetic field forms for fusion. A stellarator is a ring-shaped device that holds hot plasma with magnets. A good field form for it is quasi-isodynamic, a trait that keeps the plasma held in well. The authors work close to the axis of the ring. There, the field can be summed by a short-cut rule called the near-axis expansion.

With that rule, the team built a bank of more than 800,000 field forms. Each form is stable and close to quasi-isodynamic, in a vacuum with no plasma yet. The forms span a range of field period counts and shape controls. Those controls cover the shape of the magnetic axis and how stretched the plasma is. Teams can mine the bank for strong designs, which beats shaping each one from scratch.
arxiv-2601-08500: Cristian Santini, Marieke van Erp, and Mehwish Alam wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on linking names in old texts to who they mean. The task is called entity linking. It stays hard for old texts, in spite of gains from large language models. Old texts vary in tongue, hold noisy input, and use words in ways that shift over time. Past tools need much training data, or field-bound rules that cap their scale. The authors set out a way with no training phase, based on trust in each link.
arxiv-2601-08600: Rodrigo de Medeiros and Francisco Queiroz wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on models for data that can not go below zero. Such data is nonnegative continuous data. The team works with Box-Cox symmetric distributions, a broad class for data above zero. The class can bend to fit skew and tail weight. Its values can be read by quantiles, which helps when the model is used in regression. Few members of the class had been used in regression work. The team adds a zero-adjusted form, for data with true zeros.
arxiv-2601-08700: Nam Van Tran studies a class of hard math tasks where one must find a point that meets a set of mixed rules. Such tasks show up in game play, traffic flow, and price balance work. The rules mix a map, a cost term, and a set that the answer must stay in. Plain step by step methods can be slow to settle.
arxiv-2601-08900:
Anush Lakshman S, Adam Haroon, and Beiwen Li build a test set for a 3D scan method that uses striped light. The method shines stripe lines on a thing and reads how they bend to get its shape. Learn tools for it lack large, rich train sets. Real scans are slow to make, so progress has limped.

The team makes a fake set with true to life light and shade in a sim tool. It holds a vast set of stripe shots and depth maps for scores of things. They also give a full test plan so labs can grade tools the same way. A reader in 3D sight gets both data and a scale. New tools can now be trained and ranked with less guess work.
arxiv-2601-09000:
Annalisa Belloni, Lorenzo Noci, and Antonio Orvieto ask if a fav train pace plan works past chat models. The plan warms up, holds a flat pace, then drops the pace late. It trains large chat models well, and it bends with ease to new run lengths. But is its gain a quirk of that one model type, or a broad law of train work.

The team tests the plan on more than one model form and task. They track how loss falls in each phase of the plan. A broad gain would hint at a deep rule in how nets learn. A narrow gain would tie it to chat nets. A reader who trains nets gets a test that can guide pace picks for new work.
arxiv-2601-09200:
SK Telecom gives a tech report on a vast tongue model called A.X K1. The model has a huge count of set values, split by a mix of experts plan. In that plan, just a few experts wake for each word, so run cost stays far below full size. It was trained from scratch, not tuned from a past model.

Train used a vast text set, near ten trillion tokens, sifted in more than one stage. Scale laws set the train shape and word list size for a fixed power bill. The aim is step thought skill at a lean run cost. A reader gets the build facts for a top tier model from a phone firm.
arxiv-2601-09400:
Olgierd Unold and Stanisław Franczyk test a learning system that builds maps of its world from experience. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins the Anticipatory Classifier System, ACS2, with Hindsight Experience Replay, known as HER. ACS2 learns by anticipating what each action will do next.

That style of learning, called latent learning, makes ACS2 strong at building cognitive maps. Its weakness shows in sparse-reward settings, where success signals are rare and progress stalls. HER replays past attempts, treating reached states as if they were the goal. The authors report preliminary tests of whether the pairing lifts the stall.
arxiv-2601-09500:
Yichen Wang and five co-authors study when a hypergraph is forced to contain a forbidden pattern. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at graphs appearing as traces inside uniform hypergraphs. A trace arises when the edges of a hypergraph, cut down to a chosen vertex set, reproduce the graph.

The forbidden graphs here are edge-critical ones, graphs where removing any edge drops the chromatic number. Asking which hypergraphs avoid them as traces is an extremal problem. Results of this type extend classic Turán-style questions from graphs to hypergraphs. They show how much structure a hypergraph can have before a sharp pattern must appear.
arxiv-2601-10600:
Joshua Caiata, Carter Blair, and Kate Larson study fairness in multi-agent bandit problems. In these problems, several agents learn by trial and error which option pays off best. Fairness is often judged by outcomes alone, such as total welfare or equal shares. The authors argue that this view is too narrow.

Work in psychology, economics, and Rawlsian theory shows that process matters too. People care about who gets a say in the choices made. The paper brings that idea of procedural fairness into bandit models. It asks how learning rules should share voice, not just rewards. The shift matters for systems that split tasks or goods among many users.
arxiv-2601-10800:
John D. Roberts, Marc H. Pinsonneault, Jennifer A. Johnson, and Madeline Howell use two mass measures to study red giant stars. Red giants shed mass as they age, but the mechanism is poorly understood. The surface carbon-to-nitrogen ratio tracks a star's birth mass and is not directly changed by mass loss. Asteroseismology, reading a star's quakes, gives its current mass.

By comparing giants with the same carbon-to-nitrogen ratio but different evolutionary states, the team can spot mass lost or gained along the way. Transfer between companion stars also leaves a trace. The method turns two routine measures into a diagnostic of a star's hidden history. It sharpens the story of how Sun-like stars end their lives.
arxiv-2601-11000:
Zhongxiang Sun and co-authors study hallucinations in personalized language models. Personalized models adapt to each user to raise satisfaction. That adaptation can distort factual reasoning: a model may bend facts toward what a user seems to believe. The authors work to understand this failure and to mitigate it.

Personalization is spreading into assistants, tutors, and search. If it quietly trades truth for agreement, users get flattered and misled at once. The study maps when the distortion appears and what fuels it. Fixes that keep the personal touch while guarding facts would help every product that tailors a model to its user.
arxiv-2601-11100:
Zhezheng Hao and co-authors present ReCreate, a system that builds domain agents from experience. Language model agents are reshaping industry. Yet most working agents are still designed by hand, because tasks differ so widely. Building each one is labor-intensive. The authors ask the central question directly: can agents be created and adapted automatically in the wild?

ReCreate drives both reasoning and creation with accumulated experience. Past runs become the material for better agents. If the loop holds, agent design shifts from craft to cultivation. The work speaks to teams that deploy agents across many niches and cannot hand-tune each one.
arxiv-2601-11400:
Shuai Yuan and nine coauthors map wetlands from sparse labels in this work. Their 2026 preprint joins satellite time series with a SAM variant. Wetland maps are vital for ecosystem tracking and care. Dense pixel labels for training are too costly to make.

In practice, only sparse point labels are at hand. Deep models trained on so little tend to struggle. Wetlands also shift with seasons and across years. One date of imagery misses much of that change. Errors of omission and commission then pile up. The team adds a temporal-aware segment anything model. Time series plus that model aim at maps from few labels. The goal is sound wetland maps at a sane labeling cost.
arxiv-2601-11800:
Huy Q. Nguyen and Noah Stevenson study large waves that travel on a fluid in a porous layer. The fluid is two dimensional and sits at a set depth. Gravity holds it to a flat, hard base, and air at fixed pressure sits on top.

The top is a free surface with no surface tension in their setup. Flow in the layer obeys Darcy's law, used for flow through stone and soil. Large waves are hard to treat, since small wave maths fail. Their work adds proof on how such big surface waves behave in this porous case.
arxiv-2601-11900:
Shiheng Zhang and Jingwei Hu present a fast method for a hard flow system that mixes free flight, fields, and crashes. The system is the Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck set. It models charged parts in plasma and gas.

Their low-rank method splits the crash term into parts that act on speed alone and space alone. That split makes the low-rank steps cheap. Their time steps also cope with stiff crash terms. Fast, sound tools for this system aid fusion and plasma design.  Plain forms help users test code for this flow case.  Such forms also aid tests of disk and flow code.
arxiv-2601-12200:
Mingyang Gong, Adiesha Liyanage, Braeden Sopp, and Binhai Zhu start the study of maximal repeating patterns in a single string. A maximal pattern is one that cannot be grown, though it may not be the longest. Like tasks on two or more strings were studied from 2019 by Hirota and Sakai.

The one-string case is new ground in their work. Repeating patterns help compress text and find motifs in bio data. Algorithms for the maximal case can be faster than for the maximum. The team set out the problem and its first results.
arxiv-2601-12700:
Haolin Chen works on audio question answering, where a model hears a sound clip and answers questions about it. He uses a method from statistics called variational inference. It treats the weights of a model as ranges, not fixed points. That way, the model can show how sure it is as it trains.

Chen applies a recent tool for this task, called IVON. He fine tunes a large model that works with both sound and text. A model that knows its own doubt gives answers users can trust more. Its stated trust in an answer is more likely to match how often it is right. The study tests if this gain holds for hard tasks that mix sound with words.
arxiv-2601-13300:
Yow-Fu Liou, Yu-Chien Tang, Yu-Hsiang Liu, and An-Zi Yen test how extra choices sway large language models. Test sets for such models are key to map skill, caps, and calm. Past work showed that cues past the core task can sway a model's pick. Social cues, frame, and stray orders all count.

Their bench is called OI-Bench, for option injection. It adds a directive laden choice to a task and checks if the model takes the bait. A model that flips for a stray choice is weak where it counts. For teams that grade models, the bench adds a test of nerve that plain skill tests miss.
arxiv-2601-13400:
Nhat Thanh Tran, Kevin Bui, and Jack Xin smooth pics with a deep prior plus a sharp edge guard. Pic smoothing keeps big forms, such as strong edges and rims, and wipes fine grain and texture. Old tools use local stats or solve an opt task. New deep tools score well but need a hand picked train set.

Their tool needs no train set. It uses a deep image prior, the bias of a net's own plan toward true pic forms. It adds an L0 gradient guard, a term that counts edge jumps and keeps the count low. That guard holds strong edges while grain is wiped. For pic teams, a train free smoother that keeps edges is a handy base tool.
arxiv-2601-13500:
Ashwani Anand and co-authors grant plan templates that let two foes move at once in graph games. Two player games on graphs are a firm base to model a system next to its world. In concurrent play both sides pick a move at the same step. That form fits the sync acts of cyber physical systems.

Yet such games see thin use in real system design. One block is how plans are stated. A plan template states a class of good plans in brief form. The team treats permissive templates, which keep all moves that stay in the class. Such templates may make concurrent games apt for design teams to use.
arxiv-2601-13600:
Paul He, Elke Kirschbaum, and Shiva Kasiviswanathan study how to check if a large set of facts fits together in 2026. Tasks like fact checks, short summaries, and knowledge bases all need facts that do not clash. Large language models can judge small groups of facts for clashes. But their calls are noisy, and pair-by-pair checks can miss clashes that span the whole set.

The team lays the base math for global checks with such flawed judges. They ask what can still be known when each small check may err. The work maps the limits of trust in model-based checks. It also points to where extra care or proof is a must.
arxiv-2601-13800:
Mukul Dwivedi, Ruben Gutendorf, and Andreas Rupp build a numeric method for a nonlocal wave equation in 2026. The equation blends Camassa-Holm and Kadomtsev-Petviashvili models in two dimensions. It holds a nonlocal operator that links far points, which is hard to compute. Their method is a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme.

Cartesian meshes with tensor-product polynomial spaces split x and y work apart. An auxiliary variable turns the nonlocal term into a local one. That trick allows efficient element-by-element computation. Fast solvers help model shallow water waves and plasma flows. The method keeps the hard part of the work in small local steps. Teams that model waves can use it to cut cost and time in their codes.
arxiv-2601-13900:
Michal Parnas surveys two rank measures for matrices and their link to a classic one in 2026. Binary rank and Boolean rank count how a matrix splits into simple parts. Real rank is the standard version taught in linear algebra. The survey covers both the math and the computational sides of the topic.

Parnas reviews the basic definitions and main alternative formulations. Computational complexity of these ranks gets full treatment. Their deep connection to communication complexity is also covered. Such ranks matter for data compression, logic, and network coding. The text is a good first stop for new students of these ranks. It pulls math and code views into one clear map.
arxiv-2601-14100:
Guilherme Inacio and co-authors propose a light-based probe for a subtle break in relativity in 2026. Some materials lack a center of symmetry, and their optical response can reveal hidden effects. The team targets emergent Lorentz symmetry violation in such noncentrosymmetric materials. Lorentz symmetry is a core pillar of modern physics.

Their protocol is electrically controlled and uses the second-order shift photocurrent. In a spinful Rice-Mele model, a stationary violating background changes the Bloch Hamiltonian. That change adds an odd-in-field term to the shift current. A tabletop probe could test physics once thought to need huge machines. The test uses light that a lab can make and read with care. A clear odd-in-field mark would be hard to fake with plain effects.
arxiv-2601-14900: A French text in the file states the theorem long known as Catalan's conjecture. It says that no two whole numbers next to each other, apart from 8 and 9, can both be exact powers. The entry is credited to the theorem proved by Mihăilescu. The text gives the claim in its classic short form, with a note that the words come from a letter by E. Catalan.
arxiv-2601-15000:
Christos Petridis and Konstantinos Pelechrinis rate basketball lineups, the groups of five players who share the court. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a stat called adjusted plus-minus. It tries to credit each lineup for how the team scores while it plays.

The hard part is sparse data. Players swap in and out all game long. Many lineups share the court for only a few plays. The authors add informed priors, prior beliefs built from known facts, to steady the ratings. Their method is named Lineup Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus, or L-RAPM for short.
arxiv-2601-15100:
Yanwei Huang and Arpit Narechania design help for people who make decisions on the web. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with web AI agents such as ChatGPT Agent and GenSpark. People use them for routine tasks, but the agents wait for typed prompts.

They also miss chances to act first, and they give no support for hands-on data study. The authors present WebSeek, a design probe. It aims to guide users in two modes: proactive hints before they ask, and reactive help once they do. The probe tests how such guidance could feel in use.
arxiv-2601-15300:
Weiwei Wang, Jiyong Min, and Weijie Zou find the point where long inputs start to break a language model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with intelligence degradation: performance falls off a cliff as context nears a critical length. The drop exceeds thirty percent on a composite of tasks.

The fall happens even when the long input stays relevant. That limits real uses that need long-context understanding. The authors pin down the critical threshold. They use the natural length distribution of texts to find where the break begins, rather than testing at round numbers alone.
arxiv-2601-15500:
Saptarshi Roy, Alessandro Rinaldo, and Purnamrita Sarkar study a popular image-generation method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The method is rectified flow, prized for fast, high-quality sampling. Real data often lie near a low-dimensional structure inside a large space. A good sampler should exploit that fact to run faster. The authors ask how well rectified flow does so on its own.

Their lens joins two viewpoints, per the title. One comes from diffusion methods. The other comes from stochastic localization, a tool from probability theory. Together they frame how the method adapts to low-dimensional support. The question matters for practice, not just theory. If adaptation is automatic, users get speed without extra tuning. If not, the paper points to where help is needed.
arxiv-2601-15700:
Anthony Lee classifies subgroups of the Bianchi group in a 2026 arXiv paper. The group in view is PSL(2, Z[sqrt(-2)]), built from matrices over a ring of algebraic integers. Inside it sit Fuchsian subgroups, which act on the hyperbolic plane. Lee describes the maximal nonelementary ones. Maximal means they cannot be enlarged within the class. Nonelementary marks the rich, non-degenerate cases.

His description is explicit, per the abstract. Each conjugacy class of such subgroups appears as integral orders of certain quaternion algebras. Those algebras are indefinite and defined over the rationals. Classification results like this give a complete map of a group's large pieces. Geometers and number theorists both use Bianchi groups, so the map serves two audiences.
arxiv-2601-16000:
Hao-Hsuan Chen and Ching-Ming Lee reframe the theory of a spin-based device in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their devices are non-collinear antiferromagnetic spin-torque oscillators. Such oscillators could serve as fast, compact signal sources. The authors unify spin dynamics under the Poisson bracket formalism. They move away from the usual torque-based accounts. Their new view rests on continuous operational symmetry. Two linked viewpoints follow from it.

A vector view reveals special states of the system. Infinitely many degenerate rigid body precession states arise. The exchange energy depends only on the rotational change involved, they note. The title adds hysteretic excitation and a terminal velocity view of the motion. A symmetry-first account can simplify how engineers think about these oscillators and their switching.
arxiv-2601-16100:
Rogelio Orozco-Duarte and coauthors model hot bubbles blown by dying stars. Their 2026 preprint is the third in a chain on such nebulae. A hot bubble forms when a fast wind hits slow gas shed by the star. The glow in X rays tells of the heat and mix in the bubble. This part adds winds of the Wolf Rayet type.

The team runs wind and glow models with the new wind type. They ask how the strong wind shifts bubble shape and X ray glow. Clear shifts would help read real nebulae with such stars at heart. The work links wind force to what space scopes see. It builds on the past two parts of the chain.
arxiv-2601-16200:
Song Xia and four coauthors give proof bounds for attacks on models that join sight and words. Their 2026 preprint deals with large models that take pics and text. Small tweaks to a pic can bend the deep code of the model. Bent code then leads to wrong picks by the model. Past guards oft lack firm proof that they hold.

The team smooths the deep code space to gain such proof. Smooth code gives a zone where no tweak can flip the pick. Proof zones tell users when a pick can be trusted. That trust counts for high stakes use of such models. The work adds a guard with maths to back it.
arxiv-2601-16300:
Alexander Savin shows that graphene bubbles can hold in more than one firm state. His 2026 preprint deals with tiny bubbles of graphene on flat bases. Gas atoms sit in the bubble, drawn from argon, krypton and xenon. Each bubble can rest in a set of firm states. Each state has its own count of atom layers in the clump.

More than one rest state makes the bubble a multi firm system. The state in use rests on how the bubble was formed. Such traits could serve in tiny stores or sense gear. They also warn that one bubble need not act the same twice. The work maps the states for three gases.
arxiv-2601-16600:
T. M. Shneidman and R. G. Nazmitdinov study a strange form of atomic nucleus. In their picture, two heavy nuclei join like parts of one molecule. The pair spins and shakes as a linked pair. Their 2026 preprint builds the math for this pair. They call the joined form a nuclear molecule.

The authors first write the energy rules for the two-part system. They then solve those rules with a set of round math tools. From that work they get clear formulas. The formulas tell how the joined nucleus can be stirred up. Such states are stretched far from a round shape. The study aids our grasp of how heavy nuclei fuse and split.
arxiv-2601-16700:
Ludwig Felder, Tobias Eisenreich, Mahsa Fischer, Stefan Wagner, and Chunyang Chen survey German software firms. Their 2026 preprint asks how deep AI tools have spread in that trade. Such tools now write, test, and fix code in many shops. Use rates climb month by month. Yet raw rates hide how well the tools are used.

The team probes what drives firm, deep use of the tools. They weigh skill, firm rules, and years on the job. Their poll shows where use is broad but thin. It also shows where use is deep and sound. Firms can use these facts to train staff. They can also set rules that help, not block, good use.
arxiv-2601-16800:
Gaurav Negi, M. A. Waskow, and Paul Buitelaar test if chatbots can tag fine views in text. Fine tags mark who a view aims at, not just its tone. Such tags take long hours of human work. Crowds must tag each view by hand. Their 2026 preprint asks if big models can take that load.

The team tries models as the first tag hands. They also try models as judges when hands clash. Sound tags would cut the cost of view polls. Brands and states track views to shape their acts. The tests show where bots help and where they slip.
arxiv-2601-16900:
Madeline Lisaius, Srinivasan Keshav, Andrew Blake, and Clement Atzberger map crops in Senegal from space shots. Crop maps back food plans and aid for small farms. Yet most space-based maps fail on small farm plots. Plots there are tiny, mixed, and shift oft. Their 2026 preprint works in the Groundnut Basin of Senegal. It builds maps from learned shot codes, called embeddings.

Codes pack each shot's traits in a compact form. The team tests how well codes sort crop types. Small farm zones need maps that fit their scale. Sound maps can guide seed, water, and aid plans. They also track how rains shift farm health.
arxiv-2601-17000:
Jie Gao, Shasha Li, Jianhua Zhang, Shan Li, and Tingting Wang track how students pace their own study with AI tutors. AI tutors now guide study in many schools. Self-paced study skill drives gains in such halls. That skill shifts step by step as students work. Their 2026 preprint reads those shift chains in tutor logs.

Chains show which study moves tend to follow which. Some chains end in deep work, some in drift. The team reads chains from a GenAI tutor's logs. Clear chain maps can help tutors nudge good moves. They can also flag students who drift to poor chains.
arxiv-2601-17100:
Arash Azizi shows how a split path can mute or wake a heat sense in quantum bits. A lone sense bit, flown on sped paths, feels heat from its rush. That feel is called the Unruh response. His 2026 preprint puts the bit's core in two sped paths at once. The paths stay apart in space the whole way.

At read-out, the path mark is wiped by the read choice. That wipe can mute the heat feel to nil. Or it can bring the feel back in full. Such tricks test deep links of heat, speed, and chance. They may aid fine sensors in years ahead.
arxiv-2601-17400:
Zhe Li, Mélanie Prague, Rodolphe Thiébaut, and Quentin Clairon present a new way to fit drug and disease models. Their models are nonlinear mixed-effects models built on ordinary differential equations. Data come from many subjects over time. The standard fit tool is likelihood-based and leans on Monte Carlo steps. It can be slow and fragile in mid-size problems.

The team uses a variational autoencoder instead. Their design is identifiability-aware, so it flags traits the data cannot pin down. That honesty matters in health research. Wrong certainty can mislead dose and care choices. A faster, aware fit tool could widen use of rich models in clinics and trials.
arxiv-2601-17500:
Emmanouil Georgios Lionis and five co-authors ask a small question with big search effects. Should learned sparse retrieval use cased or uncased models? Sparse methods build word-based vectors for queries and texts. Inverted indexes then search them fast. Past work used uncased backbones near by default. Uncased text drops case marks, which cuts word mismatch.

New top language models, though, keep case. The team tests the choice in learned sparse search. Case can split names and terms that lowercasing merges. It can also split one word into rare shards. Their study gives builders proof for a base choice. Search quality can hinge on such quiet details.
arxiv-2601-17600:
Mikheil Amaglobeli and Alexey Myasnikov study tensor completions of nilpotent groups. The groups are finitely generated, torsion-free, and of class two. Completions are taken in a quasivariety of R-exponential groups. R is a binomial integral domain. Tensor completion extends a group's scalars in a controlled way. It is a base step in model theory of groups.

Such completions let algebraists move groups into richer settings. Results here pin down the class-two case in full. Nilpotent groups model systems with layered commutators. Their theory feeds cryptography and geometry as well. A firm completion theory makes those uses safer. The work closes a clear gap in the theory.
arxiv-2601-17800:
Thanawat Sornwanee argues that a recent claim in optimization rests on a math error. His 2026 preprint examines a 2025 paper on differentiable integer linear programming. Integer programs choose whole-number values, and making them smooth enough for gradient methods is a prized trick. The earlier paper claimed such a method in its fifth theorem. Sornwanee shows that the proof of that claim is wrong.

The stakes go past one paper. Later work has already built on the same flawed step, so the error spreads. A clear notice of the fault helps others avoid building on sand. Work of this kind is part of how a field keeps its results sound. Readers get a warning plus a close look at where the proof fails.
arxiv-2601-18400:
Andrei Lebedev and Vincent Gramoli ask a plain question that had not been put to a test: how much net traffic does each blockchain plan burn? New plans for shared ledgers have grown fast in the past few years. Each plan asks home nodes to swap notes with peers, and that swap has a cost in data flow.

No past study had set the plans side by side on that cost. The pair run the first such test, with the same yard stick for each plan. Home users who host a node pay for the flow in time and in fees, so the count counts for them. A clear chart of flow cost could help teams pick a ledger that small hosts can still afford to run.
arxiv-2601-18500:
Chen Liang and eleven colleagues tackle a kind of missing data that breaks the usual fix. In most sets, a blank cell can be filled by a guess from the rest. Here some cells are blank by rule: the value cannot exist at all, given the facts of the case. A child with no job has no wage to fill in. The blank can also hinge on facts that are hid or on blanks in the next cells.

Plain fill-in tools treat such blanks as if the value were just lost. That misread can bend all that comes from the set. The team build a way to learn from such sets that is close to the best one could do. Their work serves fields like health and law, where blanks by rule are the norm. Sound tools for such sets could stop false claims built on bad fills.
arxiv-2601-18800:
Yoontae Hwang and six colleagues build NavFormer, a tool that reads where a craft points from the Earth's field while the craft turns. A cheap chip feels the field on three lines. As the craft turns, the read on each line shifts, though the full strength of the field stays the same. Tools that chase the line reads chase that turn noise. The true mark to chase is the full strength, set by a world chart of the field.

NavFormer chases that full mark. It builds its traits so that turns can't shift them, and it firms the spread of each batch of reads. A firm read of the field could guide craft with no need for sky marks. That serves subs, drones, and craft deep in mines or seas. The work ties a world chart to a learn tool in a new way.
arxiv-2601-19100:
Md Rayhanul Masud and three co-authors survey how to pay software agents for good work. Reinforcement learning now trains models for coding tasks: writing, fixing, testing, and speeding up code. In many classic settings the reward is one clear number, but software quality is not one number.

A reward that is easy to count may miss what makes code good, like clarity or safety. The team reviews how rewards for software tasks are built and where they mislead. Sound reward design is the hinge of the whole field, since agents grow into whatever the reward truly measures.
arxiv-2601-20300:
Jing Xu and four colleagues extend self-supervised speech models to new languages without losing the old ones. Such models learn strong speech representations, but they are limited to the languages seen in pretraining. Retraining from scratch for new languages is costly, while training in sequence often erases earlier skill, a failure called catastrophic forgetting.

Their method, MiLorE-SSL, scales multilingual ability while guarding past languages. The balance matters for speech tools in regions whose languages were absent from the first training run. Adding a language without breaking others makes voice technology fairer across the world.
arxiv-2601-20600:
Junmin An, Ji-Hoon Hong, Jon-Lark Kim, and Haeun Lim study the shortest embeddings of linear codes into LCD codes. LCD codes, whose hull is trivial, are counterparts of self-orthogonal codes and are prized in coding theory. Recent work on self-orthogonal embeddings produced some optimal codes, which raises the natural question for LCD codes.

The authors ask how short an LCD code can be while still containing a given binary, ternary, or quaternary linear code. Short embeddings matter because code length is cost: every extra symbol is bandwidth. Optimal LCD embeddings would extend a fruitful line of code design.
arxiv-2601-20800:
Kaito Baba, Yoshihiko Ozaki, and Shuhei Watanabe tackle a bookkeeping problem in machine learning tuning. Their 2026 paper concerns hyperparameter importance: which settings of a model matter most. Tools like PED-ANOVA estimate that importance fast, inside the best regions of the search space. But they assume every setting is always present. Real search spaces are conditional.

In a conditional space, one setting can switch another on or off. It can also change the range a setting may take. The original tool cannot handle such cases in a sound way. The authors propose conditional PED-ANOVA to fill that gap. It estimates importance while respecting which settings are active. The work helps tuners spend effort on the knobs that truly drive results.
arxiv-2601-20900:
Sergio Burdisso and a large team of co-authors adapt speech recognition using text alone. Their 2026 paper studies LLM-based automatic speech recognition in new domains. Text-only adaptation is a significant yet underexplored challenge. New domains offer plenty of text but little transcribed speech. Standard fine-tuning trains the language model on that target text. The risk is real, though.

Such tuning can disrupt the alignment between speech and text. That alignment is learned by the projector that joins the two. Once it degrades, recognition gets worse, not better. The authors turn to text denoising as the adaptation signal. Denoising teaches domain language while respecting the speech link. The method promises domain gains without new audio data. It suits call centers and clinics where text is plentiful but recordings are scarce.
arxiv-2601-21000:
Muhammad Ali Shafique and four co-authors build a reasoning test for a language with few such tools. Their 2026 paper introduces UrduBench. Large language models now reason well in English. Evaluating them in low-resource languages remains challenging. Urdu reasoning tests have been limited by fragile machine translation. They also favored general language tasks over true reasoning. UrduBench aims to fix both flaws.

The team built contextually ensembled translations. Multiple translation passes are combined for fidelity. A human-in-the-loop step checks the results. The benchmark then probes reasoning, not just fluency. Such tools matter for the hundreds of millions who speak low-resource languages. UrduBench gives model builders a fair scoreboard for Urdu. It also offers a recipe other languages can copy.
arxiv-2601-21500:
Tim Tomov, Dominik Fuchsgruber, and Stephan Günnemann make language model answers respect the hidden structure of the task. Many replies carry an inner form, such as a label, a number, or a graph. Standard decoding and uncertainty tools work only on the text and ignore that form.

The authors model outputs directly in a latent space shaped by the task. Knowing the task in advance improves both the answers and the model's sense of its own doubt. A model that knows it is choosing a label can weigh options more sanely. The gain is better calibration where answers feed real decisions.
arxiv-2601-21600:
Kshitij Mishra, Mirat Aubakirov, Martin Takac, Nils Lukas, and Salem Lahlou let language models teach each other during training. Models make different reasoning mistakes: on one problem, one model's split of the task works while another's fails. That spread is usually wasted.

Their framework, CoRe, turns a peer's success into a learning signal through cross teaching. When one model solves a case, its path becomes a lesson for the others. arxiv-2601-21800:

arxiv-2601-21900:

Harmful meanings, the author contends, act as distributed circuits spread across layers, not as single switches. Interventions aimed at one spot are therefore brittle, and they tend to damage the model's usefulness as well. A defense that respects how meaning is actually spread through a network would need to work at the level of those circuits. arxiv-2601-22500:

arxiv-2601-22600:

Their loop, MulFeRL, feeds verbal feedback back into training over several turns. Detailed comments can point at the exact step that went astray. arxiv-2603-01900:

arxiv-2603-02100:

arxiv-2603-02200:

The Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act passed the British Parliament in 1900, joining six far-flung colonies into one nation. Unlike most founding charters, this one was first approved by the settlers themselves, in referendums held colony by colony. Westminster then gave the people's choice the force of law, and the Commonwealth began on the first day of 1901.

The act creates a federal parliament of two houses, modeled on both Westminster and Washington, with a Senate guarding the states. It splits powers between the Commonwealth and the states and sets up a High Court to judge between them. Queen Victoria's assent closed the act's long road from colonial conventions. The founding law of modern Australia is still in force today, little amended, and its federal design still shapes the continent's politics.
