conrad-lord-jim-1900:
Joseph Conrad published Lord Jim in 1900, a novel about a young British officer at sea. Jim jumps from a ship he thinks is sinking and leaves hundreds of pilgrims behind. The ship survives, and Jim faces a public inquiry. Shame follows him from port to port in the East.

Jim later finds work and respect in a remote trading post. There he hopes to prove his courage at last. A final act of violence tests that hope. Told in large part by Marlow, the novel asks whether one bad act must define a whole life. It is a deep study of guilt and honor.
dannunzio-flame-1900:
Dora Knowlton Ranous translated The Flame, D'Annunzio's Venetian novel of 1900. Venice itself glows on nearly every page of the lush tale. The poet Stelio Effrena loves the great actress called La Foscarina.

Their stormy affair plays out amid art, music, and fading grandeur. Readers have long seen Foscarina as a portrait of Eleonora Duse. Duse was the famed actress D'Annunzio loved in real life. Passion pushes toward its limits in scene after glowing scene. Gorgeous and excessive, the book catches decadence at high tide, a style and a shining moment that could not last very long at all.
darrell-true-narration-1600:
John Darrell, a Puritan minister, published A True Narration of the Strange Vexation by the Devil in 1600. Darrell had prayed and fasted with people said to be possessed, most famously seven persons in Lancashire. Church leaders doubted his work and later banned such exorcisms.

Darrell described fits, voices, and strange acts he took as signs of demons, and the relief that followed prayer. He wrote to defend himself against charges of fraud and to prove that possession was real. His case book sits inside a fierce fight over exorcism in Elizabethan England. It records both the suffering of the afflicted and the doubts of his enemies.
davy-researches-chemical-and-philosophic:
Humphry Davy published Researches, Chemical and Philosophical in 1800, when he was still a young chemist in Bristol. The book reports his tests on gases, above all nitrous oxide, the gas later called laughing gas. Davy breathed the gases himself and recorded what he felt.

Careful accounts describe how each gas was made, tested on animals, and tried on Davy and his friends. He noted the glee and strange calm nitrous oxide produced, and he even hinted it might ease pain in surgery. That hint waited decades for others to use. The book made Davy's name and shows a bold, hands-on style of early gas chemistry.
deniker-races-of-man-1900:
Joseph Deniker, a French scholar of the races of man, wrote this survey in English in 1900. He worked from a vast store of notes on the peoples of all lands. His aim was to sort mankind in a scheme more true than the old five race frame.

Deniker sorts mankind into twenty nine races, by hair, skull, nose, and skin. His scheme pushed Blumenbach's old five to one side and set the terms for the next age. Books of the 20th century on the races of man all start from his work, or fight it.
detection-against-harsnett-darrell-engli:
John Darrell, a Puritan minister, won fame by casting devils out of possessed people. Samuel Harsnett attacked his cures as fraud, and this anonymous Detection of 1600 answers Harsnett in Darrell's defense. It is the other half of England's great possession controversy, fought in pamphlets as fiercely as in sickrooms.

The writer charges Harsnett with lies and ridicule unfit for the subject. Case by case, the dispossessions are defended as true deliverances. Exorcism itself stands on trial here, with both sides pleading hard. The pamphlet shows a religious culture arguing over evidence for the devil. Few documents catch that quarrel at full heat.
dhammasangani-rhys-davids-1900:
C. A. F. Rhys Davids translated the Dhammasangani into English in 1900. She titled it A Buddhist Manual of Psychological Ethics. The Dhammasangani opens the Abhidhamma Pitaka, the third basket of the Pali canon.

The text takes consciousness apart piece by piece with methodical care. Every mind-state gets sorted as good, bad, or morally neutral. Lists and matrices organize feelings, thoughts, and mental factors exhaustively. Later Theravada philosophy built its psychology on this foundation. Rhys Davids made the formidable analysis readable for Western students. Her translation treated Buddhist thought as serious philosophy from the start. Ancient mind-science is the fair label for the Dhammasangani's project.
doe-osti-2584724-swelling-of-fk800: FK800's swelling got its DOE study, and this text measures the material's expansion. The pages detail the findings. The materials scientists get their numbers. The material was FK800. The expansion was measured. The study was DOE's. The numbers were material.
doe-osti-2589193-high-fidelity-digital-t: BWRX-300 got its digital twins, and this DOE report covers high-fidelity critical systems. The pages detail the virtual reactors. The reactor engineers get their models. The twins were high fidelity. The systems were critical. The engineers got models. The reactors were virtual.
doe-osti-3009655-development-of-hydrogen: FT4000 hydrogen burners got developed, and this DOE final covers the aeroderivative engine. The pages detail the findings. The turbine folks get their closeout. The engine was FT4000 aeroderivative. The closeout was turbine. The burner was hydrogen. The report was final.
doe-osti-3030867-filtration-performance-: 200 West feeds got filtration-performed, and this DOE text simulates waste feeds. The pages detail the area findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The feeds were waste. The data were nuclear. The West were 200. The area were waste. The feeds were waste.
douais-documents-inquisition-languedoc-1:
Célestin Douais printed the raw archive of the medieval Inquisition in his Documents of 1900, drawn from the Doat collection. Sentences, depositions, and acts from the Languedoc fill the volume in their original forms. The target of the machine these papers built was the Cathar heresy of southern France.

Names, villages, questions, and answers pass in dry legal order, which makes the human cost hit harder. Douais, a bishop and historian, edited the records so scholars could work from the sources themselves. Anyone studying how heresy was hunted in the thirteenth century starts with collections like this one.
dreiser-sister-carrie-1900:
Theodore Dreiser published Sister Carrie in 1900, a novel about a young woman who comes to Chicago to seek her fortune. Carrie Meeber works in a shoe factory for low pay and falls ill. A salesman helps her, and she trades respectability for comfort and the stage. In New York she rises as an actress.

Her lover Hurstwood falls as Carrie rises, losing job, family, and hope. Dreiser shows city life as a force that lifts some and crushes others. Publishers at the time found the book too frank and gave it little support. It is now seen as a founding work of American naturalism.
ellis-studies-sex-vol-2-1900:
Havelock Ellis published Studies in the Psychology of Sex, Volume 2, in 1900, subtitled Sexual Inversion. The book was written with the poet John Addington Symonds. It is the first sympathetic scientific study of homosexuality in English. Ellis gathers case histories of men and women and reports from history and anthropology.

He argues that inversion is inborn for many and not a vice to be cured or punished. Symonds died before publication, and legal threats shadowed the volume. Ellis's calm case for tolerance was bold for its time. The book influenced law reform debates for decades. It remains a landmark in the history of sexuality studies.
europmc-pmc10064400:
Sweet and a panel of European experts present the 2022 update of guidelines for respiratory distress syndrome in newborns, in a 2023 paper. The syndrome strikes mainly babies born early, whose lungs lack a coating that keeps air sacs open. Care has improved over decades, and guidance must keep pace with the evidence.

Now in its sixth version, the guideline reviews what works at each step of care. It covers breathing support, the use of lung coating treatment, and feeding and pain care. Neonatal teams across Europe use this consensus text to align practice in intensive care units.
europmc-pmc10319900:
Zhang and co-authors gave a 2023 review of the TRP family of ion channels. An ion channel is a pore in a cell wall that lets charged atoms pass. Mammals have 28 TRP proteins, split into seven groups. These channels sense heat, cold, pain, stress, and taste.

Zhang sums up how each group is built and what it does in the body. Many TRP channels sit on the cell surface and link to key signals inside cells. That makes them strong targets for new drugs. The review covers drugs in progress for diseases tied to these channels. It also flags limits that slow the use of such drugs in clinics.
europmc-pmc10482700:
Bravo González-Blas and co-authors built SCENIC+ in 2023, a method to map gene control in single cells. Two data types meet in each cell: which genes are on, and which DNA stretches lie open. Open stretches hold enhancers, switches that boost a gene. The method links each switch to its gene and to the factors that bind it.

The team stocked a library of over 30,000 binding patterns to name those factors. Tests spanned human blood cells, cancer cells, and fruit fly eye growth. Bravo González-Blas then compared gene nets between human and mouse brain cells. Shared switches and factors stood out. The tool also tracks how control shifts as cells mature.
europmc-pmc1151600:
Vonderheit and Helenius track how a forest virus rides the cell's sorting stations to its replication site in this 2005 study. Semliki Forest virus enters cells through a coated-pit route and travels through early endosomes, then late endosomes, and on to lysosomes. Endosomes are sorting compartments that route incoming cargo. The team followed single fluorescently labelled virus particles in living cells.

Viruses moved from early endosomes marked by Rab5 into a subset, about 10 percent, that held both Rab5 and Rab7, they found. Rab proteins are molecular tags that define each compartment. Viruses were sequestered in the Rab7 domains. Those domains then detached as carriers free of early-endosome markers, ferrying the virus onward. The sorting was independent of acid levels and of one partner protein. Blocking Rab7 trapped viruses in early endosomes.
europmc-pmc1479700:
One mosquito gene can yield more than 31,000 unlike immune sensors. Dong, Taylor, and Dimopoulos reported that in 2006 for the malaria mosquito. The gene, AgDscam, has 101 parts that can be shuffled as the RNA is cut and rejoined. Each mix gives a sensor with a unlike grip.

Infection prompted the mosquito to make sensor mixes matched to the germ at hand. Silencing the gene weakened defense against bacteria and the malaria parasite. The sensors also helped immune cells engulf bacteria. Dong calls AgDscam a shape-shifting guard that lets one gene cover a vast range of foes.
europmc-pmc1829400:
Kulterer, Trajanoski and co-authors tracked gene activity in human bone marrow stem cells in 2007. These mesenchymal stem cells can become bone-forming osteoblasts, which makes them promising for healing large bone defects. They are rare in marrow, so clinics must grow them outside the body first, raising fears the cells drift.

The team built custom gene chips with 30,000 elements to profile the cells during long growth and bone differentiation. Expanded cells kept their bone-forming ability, their surface marker pattern, and stable expression profiles. During differentiation they passed through three phases: growth, matrix maturation, and mineralization. Three genes stood out for follow-up work: ID4, CRYAB, and SORT1. The profile offers a check that lab-grown cells stay true to type.
europmc-pmc2124500: A medical paper contributing to the pathological anatomy of malarial fever. The fever's damage. This article preserves that pathology study. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125000: A medical paper on studies in ferment action and immunization with proteolytic products. The enzyme immunity. This article preserves that biochemistry. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128100: A medical paper on the erythropoietic action of germanium dioxide. The blood-making mineral. This article preserves that pharmacology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2128200: Another medical paper on experimental rabbit syphilis, bone and tendon affections. The rabbit bones again. This article preserves that venereology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131000: A medical paper on effects of obscure lesions on organ weights of normal rabbits. The hidden lesions. This article preserves that pathology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140300: A biology paper on amphoteric colloids, volumetric analysis of ion-protein compounds. The charged proteins. This article preserves that biochemistry. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2180200: Doctors once learned pneumonia by giving it to lab animals, and this opening study generated true lobar pneumonia with pneumococcus. The team documented each stage of the induced disease. The manufactured lung infection, recorded. The article preserves that early medical research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2254600:
Djikeng and colleagues adapted a random priming method in 2008 for sequencing whole viral genomes. Most emerging health threats are RNA viruses from animals, including influenza, SARS and Ebola. Understanding global viral diversity needs fast, flexible sequencing that works without prior sequence knowledge. The team adapted the SISPA approach, which amplifies DNA using a single tagged primer, for both RNA and DNA viruses from many sources.

The method produced near-complete genomes for viruses sized from 3,000 to 15,000 bases. Median coverage depth reached 14.33 across those genomes. It worked despite host contamination in samples from cell culture fluid, egg fluid and faeces. It can recover viral genomes even from messy real-world material. The authors recommend it for uncharacterised viruses, divergent families and mixed infections. Standard targeted sequencing would fail to capture the full genome there.
europmc-pmc2265800:
Tellinghuisen, Foss and Treadaway pinpointed in 2008 a single amino acid switch controlling hepatitis C virus particle production. The virus infects some 170 million people and often causes cirrhosis and liver cancer. Its NS5A protein was long suspected of regulating the viral life cycle. Domain III of NS5A is not needed for RNA replication, and its role was unknown. The team deleted a small stretch of domain III and mapped the effect genetically.

The deletion blocked production of infectious virus without slowing RNA replication. No intracellular virus formed, and no viral RNA or capsid protein was released. One serine residue inside the deletion proved responsible. It sits in a recognition motif for the enzyme casein kinase II. Mutations mimicking phosphorylation restored production, and blocking that kinase stopped it. Phosphorylation of NS5A thus gates the switch from replication to assembly.
europmc-pmc2323700: A biology paper on the brightness of the light of the West Indian elaterid beetle. The glowing beetle. This article preserves that entomology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2443200:
Degenhardt and a large team compared alcohol, tobacco, and drug use across 17 countries in 2008. The data came from the World Health Organization's World Mental Health Surveys, household interviews with 85,052 people using one standard diagnostic interview. Most drug statistics were national, so this gave a rare like-for-like global picture.

Alcohol use was near-universal in Japan, New Zealand, Europe, and the Americas, and far lower across China, Africa, and the Middle East. Cannabis use peaked in the United States and New Zealand, both at 42% lifetime use, well above every other country. The US also stood out for cocaine, at 16% lifetime use. Men used more than women everywhere, but the gap is closing in younger generations, who also start later into adulthood than older cohorts did. Strict drug laws did not map onto lower use.
europmc-pmc2481500:
Grimshaw and colleagues grew metastatic breast cancer cells as floating balls to enrich tumor-starting cells in 2008. The cells came from pleural effusions, fluid around the lungs where spread breast cancer collects. Grown without serum on non-stick dishes, such cells form spheres called mammospheres, a trick proposed to concentrate cancer stem cells.

Most effusions, 20 of 27, produced spheres that could be regrown repeatedly. Sphere cells could also mature when given serum and a surface, switching on mature breast markers. The stem-marker pattern on the starting cells varied hugely and did not predict sphere size. The decisive test was in mice with no immune system. Four of eight sphere cultures grew tumors from 5,000 cells or fewer. The same number of uncultured cells grew none. One highly tumor-forming sample carried neither marker at all, complicating the marker story.
europmc-pmc2571100:
Taylor, Agho, Stevens, and Raphael surveyed the psychological toll of Australia's first equine influenza outbreak in 2008. When the horse disease appeared in 2007, authorities imposed movement bans and property quarantines. The team ran an online survey of the affected horse community, measuring distress with the Kessler 10 scale and collecting 2,760 responses.

Distress was strikingly high: 34 percent of respondents scored in the high range, against about 12 percent in the general Australian population. People in the highest-risk red zones had twice the odds of high distress of those in uninfected zones, and buffer zones also showed elevated risk. Those earning their living from horses had 2.23 times the odds of high distress. Younger people and those with fewer qualifications were also more vulnerable.
europmc-pmc2702100:
Adeyemo and colleagues ran in 2009 the first genome-wide hunt for blood pressure genes in African Americans, a group hit hardest by hypertension. Earlier gene evidence was weak and came almost entirely from European samples. Their discovery group held 1,017 African American adults recruited around Washington, D.C. Each was typed at over 800,000 variants.

Several variants cleared the strict genome-wide bar for systolic pressure. They sat in or near five genes, including PMS1 and SLC24A4. Two are biologically appetizing: SLC24A4 moves sodium, potassium, and calcium, and CACNA1H is a calcium channel, the target of a major class of pressure drugs. No variant cleared the bar for diastolic pressure or for hypertension as a yes-no trait. Some signals repeated in West Africans. Pathway analysis showed the top genes cluster in pressure-relevant networks.
europmc-pmc2705500:
Chang surveyed in 2009 new blockers of tyrosinase, an enzyme that starts melanin making in skin and browning in cut fruit. Melanin is the dark pigment that shields skin from sun, but too much in patches can be unwanted. Browning after harvest also lowers the value of fruit and mushrooms.

The survey gathers blockers found in natural sources and made in labs, and weighs their strength against kojic acid, a standard blocker. It also sets out how each blocker works, such as by binding copper in the enzyme. The aim is practical: safer, stronger options for skin products and for food handling and storage.
europmc-pmc2710500:
Diawara and co-authors reported in 2009 the first proof that river blindness can be eliminated in parts of Africa with the drug ivermectin alone. The disease is also called onchocerciasis. Mass dosing had controlled the worm disease as a public health problem. But no one knew if it could stop spread for good. Biting blackflies pass the parasite very well in those areas.

After fifteen to seventeen years of dosing in three intense foci in Mali and Senegal, surveys found infection rates below one percent. Dosing was yearly or twice yearly in those foci. Dosing then stopped in test villages. Checks well over a year later found no infected people there. They also found no infected flies there. Elimination, at least in such foci, was shown to be feasible.
europmc-pmc2719800:
Silkworth and co-authors traced in 2009 how cancer cells with unstable chromosomes keep mis-sorting chromosomes at each division. Such cells often build spindles, the machines that pull chromosomes apart, with many poles in early division. Yet almost all still divide with two poles, which left the source of their errors unclear.

In colorectal cancer cells, they found faulty attachments were far more common after multi-pole stages than after normal ones. Extra chromosome anchors, called centrosomes, often merged at one pole when poles coalesced. Attachments made in the multi-pole stage then survived and caused lagging chromosomes in final division. Pole merging is thus a major source of mis-sorting.
europmc-pmc2758600:
Wojtasz and co-authors studied in 2009 two mouse proteins, HORMAD1 and HORMAD2, that sit on chromosome axes during meiosis, the cell division that makes sperm and eggs. HORMA-domain proteins in many organisms steer repair of programmed DNA breaks toward the homologous partner chromosome, which is needed for crossovers and correct segregation. The two mouse proteins were previously uncharacterized.

Both proteins clung to unsynapsed axes, the parts not yet paired, and vanished from paired regions as the synaptonemal complex, the pairing scaffold, formed. Where they piled up, checkpoint kinase activity seemed high. An enzyme called TRIP13 was required to clear them from paired axes. Mutants lacking the scaffold kept the proteins, while break repair faults alone did not block their removal.
europmc-pmc2791200:
Harrison and colleagues tested whether snakebite deaths track with poverty, in a 2009 study covering one hundred thirty-eight countries. Most earlier reports covered a single country and noted that rural farming areas faced the greatest risk, but hard proof of a link with wealth was missing.

The team plotted snakebite death rates against four measures for each country, covering development level, health spending, farm work share, and income per person. Every comparison pointed the same way: poorer countries lost far more people to snakebite. The regions carrying the highest burden are also those least able to buy effective antivenom. Deaths also rose as government health spending fell, showing the heaviest burden sits where care is hardest to afford.
europmc-pmc2847200:
Borlee and colleagues characterized in 2010 a glue protein that stiffens the biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the bacterium that chronically infects cystic fibrosis lungs. Biofilms are cities of bacteria embedded in a self-made matrix that resists antibiotics. A chemical messenger inside the cell, cyclic-di-GMP, promotes matrix building, and the team hunted proteins switched on when that messenger runs high.

One hit, CdrA, is a large rod-shaped sticky protein cut to size before export through its partner transporter. It appears mainly in biofilms, not free-swimming cultures, and it binds directly to Psl, a sugar polymer in the matrix, cross-linking it to cells. Bacteria missing CdrA built thinner, weaker biofilms that fell apart more easily.
europmc-pmc2910600:
Holt-Lunstad, Smith, and Layton pooled in 2010 the evidence that social relationships predict how long people live, and sized the effect against famous risks. Their meta-analysis gathered one hundred forty-eight studies following hundreds of thousands of participants for mortality. People with stronger social ties, whether measured as marriage, friendships, or community involvement, survived at markedly higher rates.

The survival advantage of strong ties came to roughly fifty percent higher odds of being alive at follow-up. That magnitude rivals the harm of smoking and alcohol use and exceeds the protection from exercise or losing weight in the same comparisons. The effect held across age, sex, and cause of death. Medicine should treat social connection as a genuine risk factor, the authors argue, not a soft extra.
europmc-pmc2928800:
Schwarz and co-authors examined the five type VI secretion systems of the soil bacterium Burkholderia thailandensis in a 2010 study. Such systems let bacteria attack host cells or rival microbes, and the team tested each system in both kinds of encounter.

One system, T6SS-5, proved vital for harming mice in a melioidosis model, while losing the other four left virulence intact. A different system, T6SS-1, mattered against other bacteria: mutants lacking it lost heavily to Pseudomonas and Serratia rivals in contact contests. Biofilm tests suggested these contests also shape life outside the lab.
europmc-pmc2948500:
Skrzypczak and co-authors mapped signalling changes as bowel growths progress from normal lining to benign polyps to cancer, in a 2010 study combining several analysis routes. Single-method gene studies often disagree, so the team sought a more reliable consensus.

Samples from surgery and colonoscopy covered more than a hundred whole-tissue specimens plus micro-dissected subsets. Running two normalisation methods and several sorting rules in parallel, they kept only signals that survived every route. The consensus flagged sets of known pathway groups differing along the progression and between tissue layers, giving cleaner targets for follow-up work.
europmc-pmc3004000:
Jung, Hugot, and Barreau reviewed Peyer's patches, the gut's immune sensor stations, in a 2010 article. These clusters of lymph tissue sit in the intestinal wall and sample whatever passes through the gut.

Special surface cells ferry antigens and bacteria across to the immune cells beneath, whose interplay decides between tolerance and defence. A sensing protein called Nod2 tunes patch size, number, and cell mix in response to gut flora, while resident helper T cells adjust how leaky the gut wall is. Faulty NOD2 and patch behaviour feature in Crohn's disease and in graft-versus-host disease.
europmc-pmc3043000:
Rey and colleagues mapped in 2011 how a master clock protein in mouse liver binds DNA across the day and night cycle. The protein, called BMAL1 in short, switches genes on and off in a daily rhythm that times liver jobs such as clearing toxins and handling sugar and fats. The team sampled liver tissue every few hours and read out where the protein sat across the genome.

They found roughly two thousand binding sites, and most of the strongest ones rose and fell with the daily cycle. Known clock genes were among the most tightly bound. Binding peaks clustered in the early hours of the light phase. Many sites sat in pairs that seem to work together to set output timing. The map shows daily control reaches far beyond the clock genes themselves, into wide metabolic programs.
europmc-pmc3186800:
Asiri Wijenayaka and colleagues showed that a bone-brake protein also orders bone destruction in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The protein, made by mature bone-embedded cells, was known for blocking bone building. Whether it also had a demolition role was untested, so the team dosed human and mouse bone-cell cultures with it and watched the signals controlling bone-eating cells.

It raised the go signal for bone eaters and lowered its decoy blocker, tilting the ratio sharply toward breakdown. Bone cells pre-treated with it then drove roughly seven-fold more bone resorption by added blood cells, an effect erased by replacing the decoy. It did not kill the bone cells, ruling out a distress artefact. Bone loss in ageing may thus be double-edged from one protein.
europmc-pmc3188800:
Daniel Aird and colleagues traced and tamed a bias that starves some DNA regions in sequencing in a 2011 paper in Genome Biology. On the dominant sequencing platform, stretches with extremely skewed letter composition often come back thin or missing, wasting depth and hiding medically important genes. The team followed test sequences spanning nearly the whole composition range through library preparation step by step.

The copying step used to multiply fragments before sequencing proved the chief culprit, favouring middle-composition fragments. Retuning that step cut the bias substantially and shrank the previously strong effects of machine model and heating speed. Their improved protocol promises fuller coverage of stubborn regions, from composition-rich gene starts to the skewed genomes of major parasites.
europmc-pmc3216000:
Jie Zhao, Tracy O'Connor, and Robert Vassar examined whether activated astrocytes help produce the amyloid behind Alzheimer's disease, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Neurons are usually blamed for making beta-amyloid, but astrocytes outnumber them at least five to one in the brain. Even modest production by astrocytes could add up.

Treating mouse astrocytes with inflammatory signals, especially two cytokines together, sharply raised their levels of BACE1, the enzyme that starts amyloid production, and of amyloid itself. Amyloid applied to the cells had the same effect. Blocking certain signaling enzymes did not stop the cytokine effect. The authors propose a feed-forward loop: inflammation and amyloid each push astrocytes to make more amyloid, feeding the disease during brain inflammation.
europmc-pmc3309600:
Hoffmann and a large team identified a brand new cattle virus in Europe, reporting in 2012. In 2011, dairy farmers in Germany and the Netherlands saw cows fall briefly ill with fever, diarrhea, and a sharp drop in milk. Tests ruled out every known cattle virus, so the team turned to broad genetic screening of blood from sick animals on a farm near Schmallenberg.

The screening turned up a previously unknown member of the orthobunyavirus group, which the team then grew in the lab. Officials began checking malformed newborn calves and lambs in the region for the same virus. The report is the first description of what soon became widely known as Schmallenberg virus, and it shows how open ended genetic searches can name an entirely new disease agent.
europmc-pmc3311200:
Mansuy and co-authors tested blood donors in southwestern France for past hepatitis E infection, reporting in 2011. Hepatitis E is a liver virus better known from outbreaks in poorer countries, and its presence in Europe was thought to be low. Using a validated sensitive blood test, the team looked for antibodies showing past infection in people giving blood.

More than half of the donors carried the antibodies, a strikingly high share. That finding suggests the virus circulates widely and quietly in the region. The authors point to local food habits as a likely explanation, especially eating pork and game products that are raw or lightly cooked. Their short report helped recast hepatitis E as a homegrown European infection rather than only a traveler's disease.
europmc-pmc3321500:
Blesa, Phani, Jackson-Lewis, and Przedborski reviewed the animal models researchers use to study Parkinson disease, in a 2012 article. Parkinson is the second most common nerve degenerating disease of aging, yet much of its process stays mysterious. Animal models cannot capture everything, but they have reproduced nearly all the disease's hallmarks and remain the main testing ground for protective treatments.

The classic models use toxins that kill the same dopamine neurons lost in patients. Newer models carry the gene changes found in inherited cases, involving proteins such as alpha synuclein, PINK1, Parkin, and LRRK2. For each model the authors weigh strengths and weaknesses, and note recent gains in modeling features beyond movement problems. The review aims to help researchers pick the right model for the question at hand.
europmc-pmc3340400:
Bertram and colleagues mapped where two virus activating enzymes sit in human airways and gut, in a 2012 study. Flu viruses and the SARS coronavirus enter cells through surface proteins that must first be cut by a host enzyme to become active. Two such cutting enzymes, named TMPRSS2 and HAT, can do the job in lab cells, but their presence in real human tissue was uncharted.

Both enzymes appeared alongside flu's preferred docking sugars throughout the breathing passages. The SARS receptor and TMPRSS2 also frequently appeared together along the airway and digestive tract, with a few gaps such as the vocal folds and windpipe. The enzyme from birds and pigs activated flu just as the human version did. The authors say these enzymes stand in the right places to abet infection, making them plausible drug targets.
europmc-pmc3459100:
Brookes, Woolrich, and Barnes presented a method in 2012 for measuring true connections between brain areas in magnetoencephalography data without being fooled by signal leakage. The technique promises a window on the brain's network traffic, but signals smear between nearby reconstructed spots, faking connections. Their approach is multivariate and looks for interactions where one area's rhythm genuinely lags another's.

The method ignores the zero-lag leakage that contaminates other measures and stays spatially unbiased, with a modest false-alarm rate. Simulations and real recordings both behaved as hoped. Once an interaction is found, standard tests can rank which features of the signals drive it. The authors pitch it as a way to capture the richness of these recordings in a single trustworthy statistic.
europmc-pmc3463800:
Bradley and a huge international team described the work of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium in Mammalian Genome in 2012. The consortium set out in 2007 to create a mutation in nearly every protein-coding gene in the mouse. Five years on, this paper reports how far that shared effort had come and what it had built.

By then the groups had made well over seventeen thousand mutant stem cell lines and more than seventeen hundred mouse strains. Most mutations were conditional, meaning a gene can be switched off in one tissue or at one time. A shared web portal lets any lab order the materials. Bradley's team argues the resource will speed up work on gene function across medicine.
europmc-pmc3481400:
Mancini and co-authors tested a wearable balance test called ISway in the Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation in 2012. Clinicians need a quick, objective way to measure standing balance that can catch mild disease. ISway uses a small motion sensor worn on the body while a person stands still, replacing costly lab force plates and biased rating scales.

In two studies with Parkinson's patients and matched controls, sensor measures separated the groups as well as force plates did. flammarion-the-unknown-1900:
Camille Flammarion, a French astronomer known for popular books on the stars, published The Unknown in English in 1900. The French work, L'Inconnu, turned from astronomy to strange mental events. Flammarion collected reports of dreams, warnings, and sightings that seemed to come true.

Flammarion sorted cases of telepathy, apparitions, and dreams that matched later deaths or dangers. He argued that science should not mock such reports but study them, even when no known force could explain them. The book shows a respected scientist asking, in public, whether the mind has powers that the science of his day had missed.
fletcher-indian-story-and-song-from-nort:
Alice Cunningham Fletcher worked among the Omaha and became one of the first women to build a career in American ethnology. Her 1900 book pairs tribal songs with the stories behind them, arguing that music held a people's ritual life.

Songs from the Omaha, Pawnee, and other tribes appear with their music and words, each tied to a rite, a society, or a moment in tribal history. Fletcher explains when a song was sung, who owned it, and what it meant to the singers. She wrote for general readers, not only scholars. The book preserves performances that were already passing away.
flournoy-india-planet-mars-1900:
Theodore Flournoy took a seer to the lab of the mind in From India to the Planet Mars, his study of 1900. Flournoy taught the science of the mind in Geneva. His case, Helene Smith, spoke in trance of past lives in India and trips to Mars. She writ in Mars script and told rich tales of both far worlds.

Flournoy traces each tale to scraps of her youth, read and heard then lost to mind. He claims no fraud, just a rich hid self at play. The book founds the study of seers by mind science.
frere-hoxne-1800:
John Frere, an English country gent, sent this short letter on flint tools to a learned group in 1800. Work men had dug sharp flints from a pit at Hoxne in Suffolk, deep in old ground. Frere saw what the depth of the finds must mean for the age of man.

He wrote that the tools were made and used by a folk who had no use of metals. That plain line claims a deep, stone age past for man, the first such claim in print. No one heeded it for some sixty years, till the French finds forced the point.
frus-1861-d100:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 October 1861. The letter is document 100 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Lyons had a keen sense of American politics and reported it home in detail. His formal notes to Seward were the public half of that work. This one lets readers hear the British case stated by the man charged to make it in Washington. His private letters home, not printed here, show the same cool head at work. The cool head in private matched the firm hand in public, page for page.
frus-1861-d200:
Writing on 9 July 1861, William H. Seward sent Cassius Clay a second letter in two days. The letter is document 200 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters to Clay in two days close Seward's July round to Russia. The second takes up its own point, in the Secretary's usual way. Together they show even the friendliest post worked into the same tight system as London and Paris. Even friendly posts were kept to the same tight system of orders and reports. A tight system, fairly run, asked no post to bear the war alone.
frus-1861-d300:
Guidance for Mr. Dickinson left Washington on 5 June 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 300 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d100:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 12 July 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 100 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d200:
A second Seward note to Lord Lyons dated 7 January 1862 appears as Document 200 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Sending two notes in a day was routine when separate matters each needed their own paper.

With the Trent crisis ending, the two men faced a pile of lesser frictions left by a year of war. Stopped ships, detained men, and hard words in the press. Notes like these handled that residue one case at a time. They show diplomacy returning to its ordinary pace after a brush with war. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d300:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed William L. Dayton in Paris on 4 August 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 300 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The date also carries two Dayton reports, so the mails crossed.

Crossing traffic was heavy that summer because events outran the steamers: Bull Run was three weeks away, and Antietam six. Seward wrote to Paris in the dark about the fall campaign, as Dayton wrote to him. The same-date papers in the file show two governments reasoning from different facts toward the same questions. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d400:
An instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Horace J. Perry in Madrid under the date 22 February 1862. It stands as Document 400 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, which accompanied the President's annual message to Congress.

By February 1862 Union armies were winning in the West, and Seward wanted foreign courts to hear of it from his own men first. Spain, holding Cuba just off the Confederate coast, could help or harm the Union cause. Orders of this kind told the Madrid legation what facts to stress and what claims to answer. They did so week by week, as the war's news reached Europe.
frus-1862-d500:
On 10 May 1862, the day after his previous order, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The note is Document 500 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

A next-day follow-up usually carried a correction, an enclosure, or a point that could not wait for the weekly pouch. In May 1862 the points that could not wait often concerned ships. They might be a raider fitting out, or a blockade runner in a Dutch colonial port. They might be a ruling to be sought. Seward's habit of writing twice in two days to a minor post shows how seriously the Department took the maritime war. The note is small; the system it reveals is not.
frus-1862-d600:
On 25 December 1861 Spain's minister of state wrote again to the Spanish representatives in Paris and London. The letter is Document 600 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in the Spanish appendix on Mexico.

A second circular within five days suggests fast-moving allied business that Christmas week, as the expedition's landings in Mexico began. Madrid's envoys in Paris and London were its channels to the two senior partners in the venture, and they had to speak with one voice. For the modern reader, these internal Spanish papers are the volume's most unusual feature. They are the other side's orders. The State Department printed them so Congress could judge the Mexican affair from the actors' own instructions.
frus-1862-d700: Dated 29 July 1862, this paper came from the Secretaryship of Foreign Relations of Salvador, tied in its title with Nicaragua. It is document 700 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, among the Central America papers. The record names the sending office and the date, but no signer and no subject, so it is described at that level only.
frus-1863p1-d100:
This letter of 2 March 1863, from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, carries the round number 100 in the volume's count. It is the fourth of twelve Seward letters to Adams dated that day. Adams was the American minister in London; the letter is in part one of the 1863 volume.

Milestone numbers mean little, but the batch behind this one means much. On a single day Seward laid out the London brief head by head, in a dozen short sheets. Adams could then take each point to the British in its turn. This letter is a mid-batch piece, valued as part of the most packed day in the whole printed exchange.
frus-1863p1-d200:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 18 May 1863. The letter is document 200 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d300:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 28 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 300 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d400:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 23 February 1863. The note is document 400 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d500:
The letter printed as document 500 was written on 8 May 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d600:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington received a letter dated 3 August 1863 from Secretary William H. Seward. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d100: Ambassador Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on November 7, 1943, and his dispatch is Document 100 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The round number is a fitting mark for the volume's middle, with Cairo a fortnight away. Harriman's reports from the Soviet capital helped the president judge what Tehran might yield. The record gives the date and the two men. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d200:
Paul Alling, chief of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs, wrote to three senior officials on 9 November 1943. His secret memorandum relays the British Embassy's account of Anthony Eden's talks in Cairo with Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu, held on 5 and 6 November.

Eden pressed for Allied use of Turkish air bases and raised full entry into the war. Numan answered that the two were the same thing, since Germany would strike back, and he voiced deep suspicion of Soviet aims in the Balkans. Eden warned that Allied supplies might stop if Turkey refused, and recalled no promise of a free choice, though Numan cited the earlier Adana meeting with Churchill on that point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d300:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 406/1 at Cairo on 24 November 1943, answering the American proposal for a United Chiefs of Staff. Their study concludes that no change at all should be made to the standing machinery of the Combined Chiefs of Staff.

Anglo-American forces, they argue, are fully merged worldwide, while Russian and Chinese forces look mainly to their own fronts, so the combined body must stay American-British. A standing United Chiefs of Staff would have tangled relations with it, might claim higher rank, and its members could not take big decisions anyway. The better course is better liaison in the four capitals, and inviting the Russians and Chinese to big conferences, as at Sextant, when their own problems are discussed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d400:
Arthur Millspaugh, administrator general of finances of Iran, wrote President Roosevelt a personal letter at Tehran on 1 December 1943. A conversation that day had given him leave to write. It makes the case for a long American administrative mission in Iran.

Millspaugh recalls three waves of American help: the Shuster mission of 1911, dismissed under a Russian ultimatum, his own first mission of 1922 to 1927, and his second, begun in 1943. Each came in crisis, to balance British and Russian ambitions and to set Iran's finances in order. Iran today, he warns, is in a state of disorganization, demoralization, and corruption beyond belief. A lasting job needs fifteen or twenty years, not four, under a three-power understanding that keeps the American effort exclusive, free of commercial interest, and neutral between Britain and Russia.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d500:
Lord Louis Mountbatten, Supreme Allied Commander in Southeast Asia, addressed the Combined Chiefs of Staff on December 6, 1943. Mountbatten had come to the Cairo conferences to press the claims of his new command, which faced the Japanese in Burma. The State Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Theater commanders at a summit were supplicants as well as advisers, competing for troops, planes, and landing craft against the demands of Europe. Mountbatten's message shows the Southeast Asia command making its case at the highest level. For readers, it widens the Cairo story beyond the Atlantic alliance's heartland to the war against Japan, which every global plan had to fit in.
frus-1944-quebec-d100:
On August 26, 1944, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill. The State Department printed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume. It came the day after Paris was liberated. The two leaders were preparing to meet in Canada.

Presidential letters set the tone for a coming conference. Roosevelt wrote as host, ally, and commander in chief. The Quebec meeting would open on September 12. Its agenda covered Germany's defeat and the Pacific war. For readers, the message shows the President framing that work. He put American views in writing before Churchill crossed the Atlantic. Churchill then crossed the Atlantic to meet him there.
frus-1944-quebec-d200:
Mackenzie King came to the Citadel, the editors explain, to ask Roosevelt and Churchill to accept honorary degrees from McGill University. His notes preserve the rest of the conversation. Churchill raised Canada's wish to serve in the northern Pacific and to have Canadian chiefs confer with the American chiefs. Roosevelt said he and King had settled that the previous night.

The president mentioned the Kuriles needing patrolling and Japanese still to be driven from northern China. His divisions would leave from Seattle, Canadian forces from Vancouver. King made clear Canada was prepared to operate in the central Pacific too, even as far south as Burma. Churchill objected that Canadians should not fight in the tropics.
frus-1944-quebec-d300: From Quebec's aftermath came this 19 September 1944 instruction, sent by President Roosevelt to his secretary of state. It is document 300 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the 1944 conference, published by the Department of State. Presidential messages of this kind set the department in motion, turning conference talk in Quebec into orders carried out in Washington.
frus-1945-50-intel-d100:
Minutes of the 171st meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee appear again in the volume under the date 29 November 1945. The volume prints some records twice where two of its files overlap. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Readers who meet the same minutes in two threads should not be surprised. The State Department's intelligence business crossed its own files. The editors chose completeness over tidiness. The 171st meeting belongs to the committee's late-November run, when the department was fixing its position for the January settlement. Its second printing serves the SSU and State threads alike. The overlap is a small lesson in how archives work: one meeting, many files, no single home.
frus-1945-50-intel-d200:
Dated 21 August 1946, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) to the National Intelligence Authority. It survives in print as document 200 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d300:
"Central Intelligence Agency General Order No. 10" bears the date 27 August 1948. It is document 300 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

Directives were the rule books of the new system. A short one could fix the duties of a whole office. It could settle a fight over who owned a task, or set the steps staff had to follow each day. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d400:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to Sidney Souers, executive secretary of the National Security Council, on 7 October 1949. The memo is document 400 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Souers ran the Council's staff work and had been the first head of the CIA itself. Papers sent to him fed the meetings where President Truman and his top aides set security policy. The memo shows the CIA chief feeding his views into that central channel in the early Cold War. The Council staff kept such memos on file, where they built the case for later choices.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d100:
The Secretary of State sent the President a formal proposal on 18 January 1945: raise a new four-power body at the Big Three meeting. His memorandum, with a draft declaration and protocol attached, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It concerns the freed countries of Europe.

The body is the Emergency High Commission for Liberated Europe. Its first members would be the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and the French Provisional Government. Acting jointly, they would help set up popular governments and ease urgent want in the former occupied and satellite states. The commission would have no part in running the war or in the control of Germany, which stayed with the European Advisory Commission.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d200:
Stalin asked Roosevelt's advice before de Gaulle arrived in Moscow. His strictly confidential message of 2 December 1944 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It lays out the two questions the French general and his friends were expected to raise.

The first is a Franco-Soviet pact of mutual assistance, modeled on the Anglo-Soviet pact. It is hard to object, Stalin writes, but he wants the President's opinion and asks his advice. The second question is France's eastern frontier, which de Gaulle may seek to push to the left bank of the Rhine. That scheme competes with a rival project. A Rhine-Westphalian region might instead sit under international control, with France sharing in it. A similar message went to Churchill.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d300:
Word-level edits to earlier minutes open the American chiefs' sitting of 1 February 1945 at Floriana. These Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, show staff work at its most exact. Two amendments are agreed before the day's real business begins.

General Kuter asks that a remark on bombing U-boat yards be set right in the record. General Marshall then corrects his own reported words about Eisenhower's deadline for choosing between Bradley's advance and operation Grenade. Both changes go in. The chiefs next take up strategy in the Mediterranean, on paper C. C. S. 773. The secretaries have a draft of the directive to the Mediterranean commander ready, drawn from the British proposal.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d400:
Points to take up with the President: the heading of this delegation paper of February 8, 1945, is blunt. First came the place of the United Nations conference. Second came consulting France before invitations went out. France stood listed among the five permanent members "in due course," a phrase from Dumbarton Oaks.

France's sway among small powers, the paper argues, would help sell the organization. To save time, America could consult France for Britain and Russia too. China, a full Dumbarton Oaks partner, must also be consulted as a sponsoring power. The paper ends with Secretary Stimson's stand against territorial trusteeships. It is the conference's to-do list, typed for one reader.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d500:
Report of the Crimea Conference: the communiqué issued at the end, printed here, is the document the world read. For eight days, it announces, Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin met in the Crimea with their foreign secretaries, chiefs of staff, and other advisers. The American party is then named man by man, from Stettinius and Leahy to Hopkins and Byrnes.

Marshall and King head the military names. The full text goes on to the conference's decisions: Germany's defeat and occupation, reparations, Poland, the world organization, and unity in peace as in war. As a piece of prose it was edited by the leaders themselves. It remains the canonical public account of Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d100:
Air Chief Marshal Douglas Colyer, acting head of the British Joint Staff Mission, wrote to Admiral Leahy on June 25, 1945. The letter is document 100 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Leahy's note of June 15, in which the U.S. chiefs had declined a Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting in London before the summit.

London has dropped the London idea, Colyer reports. Instead, with the Prime Minister's approval, the British chiefs propose that the Combined Chiefs of Staff meet during the Terminal conference itself. They plan to arrive on July 15 and hope the American chiefs will do the same. Colyer asks whether the plan suits the U.S. chiefs. The letter settled where the Anglo-American military talks would happen: alongside the leaders at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d200:
Economic affairs chief Thomas Blaisdell advised telling Moscow about the coal question in a telegram from London on July 8, 1945. The message to Assistant Secretary Clayton is document 200 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Blaisdell had weighed the matter with Ambassador Winant.

They believe the Soviet government should be informed that the United States intends to raise, at Berlin, the organization of German coal production and distribution on open account. German coal was Europe's most urgent need for the coming winter, and most of it lay in the Western zones while the East needed food. Blaisdell argues the notice would land better coming from Washington, where the conference agenda was drawn up, than through embassies in London.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d300:
In a second top secret message from Bucharest on June 28, 1945, General Schuyler laid out the aims American policy in Rumania should follow. His first message that day had warned against an early peace treaty. This one turned from warning to program, addressed to the War Department.

His first goal was to fix, once and for all, the total value of what Rumania owed under the armistice, above all under articles 10, 11, and 12. Open-ended Soviet demands, he implied, kept the country under constant strain. The message shows an American commander trying to turn vague armistice terms into firm numbers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d400:
Basic data on the Ruhr fill a briefing book paper of June 30, 1945, which repeats the recommendation against separating the region from Germany. The Ruhr industrial area covers parts of Prussia's Rhenish and Westphalian provinces, centered on the Ruhr river basin. It reaches somewhat west of the Rhine.

The greater Ruhr zone covers about 3,000 square miles and holds 6,800,000 people. The main industrial zone alone covers about 1,000 square miles, with 5,300,000 people. It is the most thickly urbanized area in Europe, with twelve cities over 100,000 people. Its coal, plant capacity, transport, and skilled labor made the Ruhr a prize no settlement could ignore.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d500:
London's relief at the delay is reported in Winant's cable from London of July 4, 1945. Warner of the Foreign Office expressed deep appreciation of the agreement to postpone recognition of the new Polish government temporarily. The delay gives the Foreign Office some much needed additional time, Warner said, to complete arrangements for the problems arising from withdrawing recognition from the London Poles.

He mentioned specifically the servicing of Polish troops and refugees. Until now that work has been done by Polish government agencies in London, with our money, and it can be only partially liquidated. Working out a plan to carry on the remainder, under proper safeguards, is a complicated matter, Warner added.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d600:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff proposed three changes to a U.S. strategy paper on June 30, 1945. Their top secret memo is document 600 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper under debate set basic objectives and policies for the war.

First, the British want the words British Isles changed to British Commonwealth in one clause. The old wording, they say, would not guard imperial needs in places like India and Australia. Second, they still want the words or delay cut from a later clause. Third, they note that a cargo shipping review is now complete. They ask for a new clause to shield approved military operations from fresh civil demands. The memo is a small, precise piece of Allied staff bargaining on paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d700:
Ambassador Winant sent a short secret read of Soviet troop reports from London on July 5, 1945. It is document 700 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Foreign Office there took a cooler view than the men on the ground in the Balkans.

London believed the reports of a large increase of Soviet troops in Bulgaria were part of a war of nerves on Turkey. The moves also fit a simpler story, in the Office's view. Russian forces had filtered into Rumania and Bulgaria in part because the men had to be fed and rested before their return home. The Office did not think Moscow would make further diplomatic moves against Turkey before the Big Three meeting. The wire was repeated to Moscow and Ankara as well as Washington.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1000:
The United States delegation laid this proposal on German external assets before the Potsdam foreign ministers on July 30, 1945. It urges prompt action to take control and power of disposal over such assets, above all in neutral countries. The stated aims are Allied security and keeping the assets intact for Allied purposes.

The United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union should issue a declaration claiming jurisdiction, with France joining if possible. Two forms of the declaration are attached, one for three powers and one for four. After the declaration, the Control Council should issue a decree vesting the assets. Their diplomats would then act to enforce control abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1100:
Dated 24 July 1945, this report came from the Economic Subcommittee that served the Potsdam Conference. Staff experts from the three teams worked on the money side of the German settlement and sent their findings up to the foreign ministers. The State Department later printed the report as Document 1100 in its Potsdam record.

Subcommittee reports did the detailed work that leaders had no time to do in person. This one dealt with the state of Germany's economy and the terms to be set for it. Findings of this sort fed into the final protocol, the signed list of choices that closed the summit. Readers can see how expert staff turned broad aims into terms that could be signed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1200:
Clement Attlee sent this message to President Truman on 22 July 1945. The date holds a wrinkle: Attlee was not yet prime minister. He led the Labour Party and served as deputy premier, while the election count that would raise him was still four days off.

The volume keeps the paper under the title he would soon hold. Read with that in mind, the message shows the incoming leader entering the summit's circle before he took the chair. Attlee sat at Potsdam as an observer with the British team. This note is a glimpse of him on the edge of power, days before the chair was his.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1300:
Solborg, the American military attache in Portugal, wrote to the War Department on 22 July 1945. An attache was the army's eyes inside an embassy. In Lisbon, that meant watching a neutral capital where both sides kept agents and bought goods.

His report carried the military side of the Portuguese scene to Washington. Shipping, air fields, and the mood of the Portuguese forces all fell in his brief. This dispatch shows the attache's channel at work during the summit. It is a small military window on the war's quietest front, kept open while the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1400:
The sixth Caffery letter to Bidault in this run is also dated 1 August 1945. Six letters in two days between an ambassador and a foreign minister is a heavy traffic by any standard. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Runs like this one reward being read whole. Each letter alone is a fragment; together they trace a negotiation across forty-eight hours, with replies and counter-points in sequence. The subject binding them is France's place in the order the Potsdam powers were fixing that same week. Readers who take the six letters together get one of the volume's best lessons in how diplomacy actually fills its days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-100: This short note, printed without a number after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume, was written by the series editors. The Foreign Relations of the United States volumes rely on such notes to bridge gaps between documents. They tell readers where a paper came from and what it connects to. In a volume built from cables, minutes, and drafts, that guidance keeps the story straight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d800:
Maynard Barnes, the American representative in Bulgaria, reported to the Acting Secretary on July 17, 1945. Document 800 opens the volume's Bulgaria thread. Barnes held a tense post in Sofia, where a Soviet-led commission ran the armistice. His report was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Bulgaria's file at Potsdam was among the thorniest in the Balkans. Barnes wrote from inside that difficulty. Readers get the view of a man outnumbered in his own commission. The document shows why the eastern posts mattered: their reports were the alliance's eyes in lands slipping from its grasp. Barnes's letters give that loss a human voice.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d900:
Edwin Pauley wrote again to the Secretary of State on July 18, 1945, with an improved memorandum on reparations and ceded German territory. The letter revises his proposal of July 16. Pauley says its aim is simple fairness. Nations that gain German land should share both the burdens and the benefits of reparations.

Surpluses from ceded land would go first to sustain minimum life inside Germany. Next they would pay for imports Germany needs. Any remaining value would enter the general reparation fund. The worth of equipment and natural resources in ceded land would count as reparations delivered to the nation receiving it.
gao-gaoreports-b-298300: The Ideal Solution took its July 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299000: Quimba Software took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Software deals get the same full hearing as the steel ones.
gao-gaoreports-b-310100: A 2007 GAO ruling on a contract fight from VRC, Inc. The company said the agency's bid process was flawed; the ruling sifts each charge and delivers the verdict. For firms in the federal market, the published call is both closure and lesson — a window into how GAO reads the rules of a fair contest.
gao-gaoreports-b-311200: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Joint Venture Penauille/BMAR & Associates, LLC. Decided May 12, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-300: The young homeland shop's planning needed polish in 2005, and GAO's report says the plans could be more useful. The review writes the fix list. The young department deserved the better plans. The plans had to be better. The prescription was written.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-700: The homeland shop's cyber plan stayed half-done in 2005, and GAO's report says the rollout had to be finished fast. The findings demand the completion. The report warns that the shop's data deserved protection. The shop's data deserved protection. The rollout had to finish.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-100: IRS and USCIS data sharing faced challenges in 2005, and GAO's report says options existed to enable sharing, though each presented hurdles. The findings map the options. The report warns that the taxpayer data deserved careful handling. The challenges had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-200: Drug interdiction assets were likely to decline in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies needed to plan for the drops and develop better measures. The findings demand the planning. The report warns that the smugglers' hunters needed staying power. The planning had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-300: Medicare's error rate math was adequate in 2006, and GAO's report says the CMS methodology could estimate the national error rate. The findings give the nod. The report shows the payment errors were being counted. The methodology had to be adequate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-100: Teaching America about money was floundering in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the financial-literacy commission needed to get serious about a national strategy. The testimony grades the effort. The findings warn of good intentions and thin results. The nation stayed bad at budgets.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1000: The government's landlord was sloppy with its sublets in 2007 — GAO's report says the General Services Administration needed a tighter grip on agencies it let manage their own buildings. The findings target the delegated-property maze: who watches the watchers when everyone holds keys?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-300: Katrina and Rita relief money was still being looted in 2007, and GAO's report keeps finding fraud, waste, and abuse in the disaster aid. The findings document the ongoing bleed. The report's fury is plain: the storms passed, but the stealing did not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-900: Homeland Security's buying watch needed muscle in 2007 — GAO's report tracks the department's acquisition oversight, progress and potholes both. The findings grade the watchdog-within on its own watch. The report's theme: the buyer's referee needs a whistle that actually works.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-100: GAO published its findings on bankruptcy and Child Support Enforcement: Improved Information Sharing Possible without Routine Data Matching in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-200: The Government Accountability Office dug into hedge Funds: Regulators and Market Participants Are Taking Steps to Strengthen Market Discipline, but Continued Attention Is Needed in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-400: GAO published its findings on surface Transportation: Restructured Federal Approach Needed for More Focused, Performance-Based, and Sustainable Programs in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gierke-political-theories-maitland-1900:
Otto von Gierke's Political Theories of the Middle Age appears in F. W. Maitland's translation of 1900. Gierke was a German legal historian of corporations and groups. This short book distills his vast work on fellowship and association. Medieval thinkers, he shows, saw society as a web of real group bodies.

Maitland's translation made German medieval thought available in English. His introduction is itself a classic essay. Ideas of the state, the church, and the guild receive sharp summary. The book influenced political pluralism in Britain and America. It asks whether groups are mere fictions or real persons in law. That question still matters in law and politics today.
govdocs-archive_org-nikolateslascolorado:
In 1899 Nikola Tesla moved his experiments to Colorado Springs, where the thin air and open space let him work with very high voltages. His Colorado Springs Notes are the lab records of that year, kept day by day as the work went on.

The notes record his tests with the magnifying transmitter and his giant coil, and his claims to have received signals he believed came from beyond the earth. They mix careful measurements with bold guesses, in Tesla's own voice. For readers of electrical history, the notes are the primary record of the most dramatic experiments of his career.
grand-albert-1800:
Le Grand Albert, the Great Albert, is the senior companion to the Petit Albert in the French grimoire family. This Paris edition of 1800 carries the book of marvels that tradition hung on the name of Albertus Magnus. The medieval scholar's fame made him the supposed author of many books of secrets.

Wonders, secrets, and recipes fill its pages, aimed at household and farm. The Grand Albert covers the virtues of herbs, stones, and animals in the old manner. Its matter descends from medieval books of secrets reshaped for French buyers. Beside the Petit, it served readers who wanted the larger store. The pair together dominated the cheap magic trade of France for two centuries.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol3-1900:
Volume Three of Hastings's Bible dictionary, from 1900, runs from Kir to Pleiades. James Hastings edited the set to give the church a complete modern guide to scripture. Each volume was built to stand heavy daily use.

The entries here include major articles on the Law, the Messiah, miracles, and the lands of the Bible. Scholars set out the evidence for rival views rather than hiding the disputes. Illustrations and maps keep the ancient world visible. By this third volume the dictionary's plan is clear: sound learning, plainly written, for readers who take the Bible seriously.
herder-outlines-philosophy-history-man-1:
Johann Gottfried Herder published his Ideen, Ideas toward a Philosophy of the History of Man, in parts from 1784. T Churchill's English translation of 1800 gives the work as Outlines of a Philosophy of the History of Man. All four parts stand here, Books One through Twenty, from the earth itself to the fate of nations.

Herder begins with the planet, its plants and animals, and man's place among them. He then traces how climate, language, and tradition shape each people into its own form of humanity. Against cold universal schemes, he insists every culture carries its own center of worth. The Ideen founded the philosophy of history as a humane study.
hertz-electric-waves-jones-1900:
D E Jones published his translation of Heinrich Hertz's Electric Waves in 1900. Hertz, a German physicist, had died young in 1894, after proving by experiment that electromagnetic waves exist. Jones gathered Hertz's papers on those waves for English readers.

Hertz generated waves with sparks and detected them across his laboratory with a wire loop, showing they reflect, refract, and travel at light's speed. The experiments confirmed Maxwell's theory and opened the road to radio. Marconi and others built wireless telegraphy on this ground within a few years. Jones's volume, with Hertz's own introduction on his methods, is the founding record of radio science in the discoverer's words.
hobson-economics-of-distribution-1900:
Hobson's Economics of Distribution, published in 1900, sets out his challenge to orthodox economics in full. Hobson was a maverick thinker whom the universities kept at arm's length for his heresies. The question at the center of the book is how the product of industry gets divided among rent, wages, interest, and profit.

Hobson argues that bargaining power, not natural law, fixes the shares, and that some income is surplus taken without service. From there he builds toward his famous claim that oversaving can choke demand and cause slumps. The profession laughed at that doctrine then and honored it later, after Keynes made similar ideas famous. The book shows the path economics refused to take for thirty years, laid out by the man who saw it first.
hollandus-opera-mineralia-1600:
