Isaac Hollandus was a Dutch alchemist whose Opera Mineralia, published in 1600, collects his mineral works on the philosophers' stone. Latin readers across Europe prized Hollandus for plain, practical teaching. His books claim the experience of a working adept rather than a scholar's theory.

He describes the preparation of the stone from mineral matter step by step, with furnaces, times, and signs of success. His instructions on the great work influenced English and German practitioners for the next century. The Opera Mineralia preserves the Dutch practical alchemy of the late sixteenth century at its most confident.
hopkins-contending-forces-1900:
Pauline Elizabeth Hopkins published Contending Forces in 1900, a novel about Black life in Boston and the South. Sappho Clark is a singer with a painful past she keeps hidden. Grace and Ma are among the friends and family whose lives cross hers. The story links love plots with debates in Black parlors and churches.

Hopkins writes openly about lynching, sexual violence, and the color line. She also shows Black women leading clubs, papers, and reform work. The novel argues for justice through both story and speech. Hopkins was a pioneer of Black American fiction. Her book still reads as bold and urgent.
jami-lawaih-whinfield-kazvini-1900:
Jami, the last great classical poet of Persia, wrote the Lawa'ih, Flashes of Light, as a short treatise on Sufi truth in the fifteenth century. E. H. Whinfield and Mirza Muhammad Kazvini translated it for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1900. The edition pairs the Persian text with their English version. Whinfield's preface treats the mark of Greek thought on Sufism.

Flash by flash, Jami states the unity of being: God as the one real existence, and the world as His showing. The prose is spare, bright, and hard, a creed in epigrams. Scholars used the Lawa'ih as the clearest short statement of the school of Ibn Arabi. This copy keeps the English matter complete.
jastrow-fact-and-fable-in-psychology-190:
Joseph Jastrow was a US mind man of the new school of tests. His Fact and Fable in Psychology came out in 1900. The book takes a hard, cool look at the craze for the occult. Jastrow wrote as a friend of fact in a field full of fog.

Spirit men, mind sight, and the sway of crowds all come up for review. He shows how hope, habit, and slight flaws of sense breed false faith. Tales from the lab stand by tales from the seance room. The book is the great cool foil to the occult books of its age.
jenner-continuation-variolae-1800:
Edward Jenner's third vaccination tract, A Continuation of Facts and Observations, appeared in London in 1800. Two years of practice had passed since his first Inquiry of 1798. Jenner gathers the growing record in one place. Reports from other doctors now joined his own cases.

Page by page, the evidence firms up: cowpox protects against smallpox. Jenner answers errors, warns against false cowpox, and gives fresh instances. The tract consolidates a claim that was still being fought over. Readers watch a medical revolution gather proof in real time. Together the three tracts form one long argument. The last word here is confidence, earned slowly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luz-10200:
Luz is taken up in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as a name with three separate meanings. First, it was the older name of the city of Beth-el in the Bible. Second, it named a city in the land of the Hittites, founded by a man spared by Israelite invaders. Luz is the Hebrew word for an almond tree, which may explain the name.

The article gathers the legends that grew around the hidden city. Tradition said no conqueror could harm it and the angel of death had no power there. Entry came through a hole in an almond tree into a cave. The third meaning is a small bone at the base of the spine. Jewish belief held that this bone, being unbreakable, would seed the resurrection of the body. The entry traces that belief through the Talmud and into Christian and Muslim writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maimon-moisei-l:
Moisei Leibovich Maimon, a Russian painter, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Wilkowiszk in Russian Poland on February 4, 1860, he trained at Warsaw and Wilna. In 1880 he entered the Academy of Fine Arts at St. Petersburg. Silver medals followed in 1881, and he graduated in 1883.

The article catalogs a busy exhibition career. In 1886 the academy gave him a gold medal for Saint Irene curing Saint Sebastian. A painting of Ivan the Terrible won him the title Artist of the First Degree. He painted portraits of the czar and czarina and of Professor Chwolson. Many canvases show Russian peasant life, market wagons, kitchens, and cheap restaurants. His best-known Jewish work, The Maranos of 1893, shows a secret Passover broken in upon by the Inquisition. The old man at the table reads on calmly through the terror.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marczali-heinri:
Heinrich Marczali, a Hungarian historian, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Marczali on April 3, 1856, he studied at Raab, Papa, Budapest, Berlin, and Paris. In 1878 he became a gymnasium professor in his native town. The Hungarian Academy elected him in 1893.

The article follows his rise to the university. In 1895 he became professor of Hungarian history at the University of Budapest. His books, mostly in Hungarian, cover the sources of Hungarian history and the age of Joseph II. A life of Maria Theresa appeared in 1891. His study of the Arpads and Dalmatia was translated into French for Paris readers. He also wrote three volumes of Szilagyi's great history of Hungary, the first, second, and eighth. The entry records a historian who gave Hungary its scholarly past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mauthner-fritz-:
Fritz Mauthner was an Austrian poet, novelist, and satirist. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Horitz, in Bohemia, on November 22, 1849, attended the gymnasium at Prague, and nominally studied law. In truth philosophy and the history of art took his real attention. A book of sonnets, “Die Grosse Revolution,” came out in 1871 and nearly brought him an indictment for treason.

After early comedies were staged with success, he gave himself wholly to writing and moved to Berlin in 1876. From 1895 he wrote the dramatic articles for the Berliner Tageblatt. The entry lists his books at length. They run from parodies, the romance “Der Neue Ahasver,” and the literary satire “Schmock” to novels of Berlin life. Turning serious at the end, he wrote his 1901 “Contributions Toward a Critique of Language.”
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melchior-moritz:
Moritz Gerson Melchior was a Danish merchant who headed the commerce of Copenhagen. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Copenhagen on June 22, 1816, and at twenty-four entered the firm of his grandfather, Moses & Son G. Melchior. After the deaths of his father and a brother he ran it alone until his brother Moses joined him in 1850. They enlarged the business and planted a branch in Melbourne, Australia, to open a market for Danish goods.

His public life matched his counting-house. He was alderman for eighteen years. He sat on the Maritime and Commercial Court and on the Landsthing, Denmark's upper house. He co-founded the free-trade society and the Privatbanken and led the Chamber of Commerce from 1873. The entry ends on a note: Hans Christian Andersen was a guest in his house and spent his last days there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merodach-balada:
Merodach-Baladan was king of Babylon. He enters the Bible in one courteous embassy. Solomon Schechter, Louis Ginzberg, and A. Peiginsky retell it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He heard that Hezekiah had recovered from sickness. He sent letters and a present. The delighted king showed the messengers all his treasures, withholding nothing. Isaiah came in reproof and foretold the loss of everything: the kingdom destroyed, its wealth and children carried to Babylon.

The entry adds the spelling variant from Second Kings, where he is Berodach-baladan, and then a Talmudic curiosity. Baladan's face, the rabbis said, was changed to a dog's. That change forced his abdication in favor of his son Merodach. Out of reverence, the son kept adding his father's name to his own in every edict. He reigned, in effect, only as the old king's deputy. History and legend stand in two neat paragraphs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-middot-10800:
Middot is a treatise of the Mishnah, tenth in the order Kodashim, that measures and maps the Temple in Jerusalem. Solomon Schechter and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It has five chapters and thirty-four paragraphs, and its subject is the building itself: its dimensions, gates, courts, and chambers.

The first chapter, as summarized here, covers the night watches, priests guarding three posts and Levites twenty-one, under a captain who could strike a sleeping guard or burn his coat. It pictures Susa, the Persian capital, carved on the eastern gate and notes the cell where the Hasmoneans stored old altar-stones. Later chapters continue the survey room by room.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ju:
Mordecai ben Judah ha-Levi was chief rabbi of Cairo in the seventeenth century. He was a preacher and commentator who ended his life at Jerusalem. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn record him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His printed legacy is one book of responsa, Darke No'am. His son Abraham edited it, and it was issued at Venice in 1698.

The responsa run across all four parts of the Shulḥan Aruk. They lean toward marriage law and civil law. Sixty-eight fall on Eben ha-'Ezer and fifty-seven on Ḥoshen Mishpaṭ. That was the working docket of a chief rabbi. Four more works stayed unpublished. They are a Pentateuch commentary, holy-day sermons, sermons for life's ceremonies, and funeral orations. Azulai's Shem ha-Gedolim heads the entry's sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-jacob:
Moses ben Jacob of Coucy, known by his book's short name SeMaG, was a French tosafist and codifier of the thirteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Paris under Judah Sir Leon and became a famous preacher. In 1240 he was one of four rabbis made to defend the Talmud at Paris.

Moses traveled through France and Spain urging Jews to keep the commandments, and also to deal justly with everyone. His Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, finished in 1250, works through all the commandments and prohibitions one by one. It quotes many earlier rabbis and was printed again and again for centuries. The entry also notes his clear, brief comments on the tractate Yoma.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naioth-11300:
Naioth was the place where David and Samuel took refuge from Saul's pursuit. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn discuss it in the Jewish Encyclopedia. The name is always joined with Ramah, and the Septuagint supplies 'in Ramah' even where the Hebrew lacks it. So Naioth was no city of its own.

The word may be a plural meaning habitations. The Targum of Jonathan renders it house of instruction. On that reading Naioth was a kind of community house with several rooms, where Samuel's company of prophets lived. The article ends there: a name, a refuge, and an old guess at what stood behind it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neander-johann-:
Johann August Wilhelm Neander was a German church historian. Crawford Howell Toy and Max Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Göttingen on Jan. 17, 1789. His birth name was David Mendel. His mother was kin to Moses Mendelssohn, the philosopher.

At seventeen Neander embraced Christianity and studied theology. He taught at Heidelberg, then became Berlin's church history professor in 1813. His great history of the Christian church ran to eleven volumes. It appeared between 1825 and 1852, and reached English readers too. He is called the father of modern church history. Asked to ban Strauss's book, he refused state force. In 1846 he denounced the Damascus blood accusation as a lie.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-year-for-tr:
The New-Year for Trees falls on the fifteenth of Shebat. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Judah David Eisenstein for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew name means simply the fifteenth. The day is a semiholy one, kept by custom. No code makes its observance a strict duty.

At first the day settled tithes on fruit crops. Bet Shammai had picked the first of Shebat instead. Jerusalem once planted a tree for each newborn child. Cedar marked a boy, cypress a girl there. At marriage those trees became the wedding canopy's posts. Sixteenth-century cabalists revived the day by eating fruits. Seventeen courses of fruit mark their reading service. Children in Russia eat carobs from Palestine that day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nossig-alfred-1:
Alfred Nossig was an Austrian author and sculptor. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lemberg on April 18, 1864. Law, philosophy, and science filled his student years. Medicine at Vienna claimed several years more.

Paris held him a while before Berlin did. Polish verse and drama began his writing life. The King of Zion reached Lemberg's stage in 1887. German dramas and an opera libretto followed later. Social hygiene and socialism drew his learned pen. Art criticism made his name in two capitals. His sculpture showed at Paris and at Berlin. The Wandering Jew stands among his chief works. Jewish statistics and Zionism's balance sheet claimed him too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oholiab-a-v-aho: Oholiab was a skilled workman in the days of Moses. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. God chose him to work with Bezaleel of Judah. The two men built the Tabernacle, the tent shrine of Israel. Oholiab cut stone and wood, and wove cloth in blue, purple, and scarlet thread.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-othniel-11800:
Othniel was a son of Kenaz and a judge of Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the younger brother of Caleb, a chief. Caleb took his share of the land of Canaan. One town, Kirjath-sepher, still held out against him.

Caleb gave his daughter Achsah as the prize for that town. Whoever took the town would wed the girl at once. Othniel took the town and won the bride that day. His great deed came later, as a judge of men. A king from Mesopotamia held Israel in his grip. For eight years the tribes paid him in fear. Then they cried out for aid to God above. The spirit of God came on Othniel at that hour. He beat the foe and gave the land rest for forty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paradise-hebrew:
Paradise is a word for a garden, a park, and Eden. The board, George A. Barton, Judah David Eisenstein, and Mary W. Montgomery wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word is most likely of Persian birth. It stands just three times in the Old Testament texts.

In the Song of Songs the word means a garden in bloom. In two more books it means a park of trees. In later books it names the Garden of Eden itself. It names the heaven form of that garden as well. From that use, it came to name the home of the blest. The New Testament uses the word in that last sense. Genesis tells of the earthly garden in its first books. God set a garden eastward in Eden for Adam there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-penaforte-raymu:
Raymund de Peñaforte was a Dominican leader in Spain. He served as confessor to King James the First of Aragon. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His chief aim was to convert Jews and Muslims.

Peñaforte had Hebrew and Arabic taught in Dominican schools. Then he pushed the king to stage a public debate. In 1263 Moses ben Nahman faced Pablo Christiani at Barcelona. The rabbi spoke freely and held his ground. Afterward Jews were forced to hear mission sermons. Their books were censored on Raymund's orders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philippe-edouar:
Édouard Sylvain Philippe was a French playwright and music journalist. He was born at Paris on April 18, 1840. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He spent twelve years in business first. The Legion of Honor came to him in 1886.

In 1869 Philippe left trade for the world of music. He fought as a volunteer in the Franco-Prussian War. From 1872 he edited the Revue et Gazette Musicale. He wrote seventy-five pieces for the stage in all. Boussigneul, his best known play, crossed Europe in translation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-placzek-abraham: Abraham Placzek was a Moravian rabbi of high standing. Isidore Singer and S. Funk wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Prerau in 1799. He died at Boskowitz in 1884. He served his native town, then Weisskirchen, then Boskowitz. In 1851 he succeeded Hirsch as acting chief rabbi of Moravia. He defended Jewish rights through the years of reaction. His letters enrich many printed responsa collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-portugalov-benj:
Benjamin Portugalov was a Russian doctor and author born at Poltava in 1835. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at Kharkov and at Kiev. For a time he served as an army surgeon. He died at Samara in 1896.

Portugalov settled in the government of Perm after the army. There he was barred from work as a doctor. So he turned to writing for his living. His first piece ran in a journal of legal medicine. He wrote most often on health and clean living. His pieces ran in papers such as Dyelo and Nedyelya. In time he won a post as a city doctor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-proverbs-book-o:
The Book of Proverbs is one of the wisdom books of the Bible. Crawford Howell Toy wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands among the Ketubim, the third part of the Hebrew Bible. Its group is called Hokmah, or Wisdom. The Hebrew head line calls it Proverbs of Solomon. That line stands over the first and twenty-fifth chapters.

In Greek and later use, the book is just Proverbs. Its Hebrew name is Mishle, a short form of the long title. That long title fit one core set of sayings at first. The core runs from chapter ten to chapter twenty-two. A second set runs from chapter twenty-five on. The article sorts the book's parts and their ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbinovicz-rap:
Raphael Nathan Rabbinovicz was a Talmud scholar and a hunter of old books. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in the Kovno government in 1835. He died at Kiev in 1888. At twenty-eight he left Russia for the west. He passed through Lemberg, Presburg, and Eisenstadt on the way.

Rabbinovicz settled at Munich at the end of his travels. In its royal library he found a buried treasure. It was the famed Codex Hebraicus of the Talmud. That hand-written book dates from the year 1342. It is a full copy of the Babylonian Talmud. His find gave scholars a new base for the text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rawicz-victor-m:
Victor Meyer Rawicz was a German rabbi born at Breslau on August 19, 1846. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the seminary and university of his native city. He took his doctorate there in 1873.

The article lists his rabbinates in order. He served at Kempen from 1874. He then served at Schmieheim from 1876 to 1893. After that he moved to Offenburg in Baden. His published work was mainly translation. He translated four tractates of the Talmud into German. Megillah came in 1883 and Rosh ha-Shanah in 1886. Sanhedrin followed in 1892 and Ketubot in 1900. The entry records a rabbi who made Talmud texts reach German readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuben-12700:
Reuben was Jacob's eldest son by his wife Leah. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis tells how he brought mandrakes home at harvest. That small act set family events moving.

The article recounts his fault with Bilhah, his father's concubine. For that wrong he lost his firstborn rights. Those rights passed to Joseph's children instead. When brothers planned to kill Joseph, Reuben intervened. He urged a pit instead of death, hoping to rescue him. He returned to find the pit empty and grieved. Later he offered his own sons as pledge for Benjamin. A rabbinical part then expands his story. The entry shows a firstborn who lost rank but kept mercy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodriguez-12800:
Rodriguez is a surname borne by many secret Jews under the Inquisition. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries many were condemned. Charges called them Judaizantes, or secret confessors of Judaism.

The article lists case after case from Inquisition records. Miguel Rodriguez and his wife kept a secret Madrid synagogue. They were publicly burned on July 4, 1632. Catalina Rodriguez was burned in effigy in 1680. She had died in an Inquisition prison at age seventy. Maria Rodriguez, aged ninety, went to the stake in 1721. Her daughter went with her at Granada. A whole Cuenca family received lifelong imprisonment in 1722. More named cases follow from Cuenca, Madrid, and Valladolid. The entry is a grim roll of one name's persecution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saint-gall-st-g:
Saint Gall, or St. Gallen, is the chief town of its Swiss canton in the northeast. Gotthard Deutsch and Emil Schlesinger wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its first Jewish record is a grim one, from 1349.

That year the town's Jews were accused of poisoning the wells. Like other Lake Constance towns, St. Gall jailed, burned, or expelled them. For long afterward no Jews lived there at all, the entry says. Settlement stayed barred or dearly bought well into modern times. Only Swiss emancipation in 1863 lifted the harsh Jews' Law of 1818.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-harry-si:
Goodman Lipkind joined Joseph Jacobs to write this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Harry Simon Samuel. He was an English politician, born on August 31, 1853. His mother was Henrietta Montefiore. He studied at Eastbourne College and at St. John's College, Cambridge. He took his bachelor's degree there in 1875.

Samuel became a freeman of the city of London. He also joined the Coopers' Company. He served as a captain in the First Middlesex Volunteer Royal Engineers. In 1892 he ran for Parliament in the Limehouse division of Tower Hamlets. He lost that race. In 1895 he ran again and won. He sat for Limehouse as a Conservative. The entry records the start of his career in national politics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sardinia-13200:
Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sardinia. The Mediterranean island lies about 140 miles off Italy's west coast. Jewish settlement there reaches back to the year 19. That year the emperor Tiberius banished 4,000 Jewish youths from Rome to the island. They were punished for the frauds of four Jewish swindlers.

Under pagan Rome, Sardinian Jews held full citizenship rights. As Christianity gained power, those rights shrank. Vandals and Goths ruled the island from the fifth to the seventh century. Jewish life then fared fairly well. Communities stood at Oristano, Sulcis, Alghero, and Cagliari, the capital. At Cagliari a converted Jew placed saints' images inside the synagogue. Pope Gregory the Great ordered Bishop Januarius to remove them at once. The article follows the island's Jews into the native-rule period.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schonfeld-baruc:
Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Baruch Schönfeld. He was a Hungarian Hebraist. Schönfeld was born at Szenicz in 1778. He died at Budapest on December 29, 1852. He taught in several towns of Hungary and Moravia. His books mix prose, verse, and moral teaching.

His Ẓeror Peraḥim, printed at Vienna in 1814, holds essays in prose and poetry. His Mussar Haskel, from Prague in 1831, is an ethics manual for Jewish youth. He adapted it from Campe's Theophron. His Shalme Todah, from 1840, is an ode honoring Gabriel Riesser. His 'Anaf 'Eẓ Abot puts midrashic legends into meter. His Minḥah Belulah, from 1850, gathers more prose and verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seleucia-talmud:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Seleucia. The article treats three cities of that name. The first was a Greek colony on Lake Merom. Grätz inferred that Pharisees spared by Alexander Jannæus took refuge there. Seleucia joined the revolt against Agrippa in 66 of the common era.

The second Seleucia stood on the Tigris in Parthian lands. Babylonian Jews fled there when their neighbors pressed them hard. The city's Greeks and Syrians, though rivals, united in hatred of the refugees. About 41 B.C. they killed 5,000 of the fugitives. The third Seleucia, on Schürer's view, is Abila. Abila lay twelve Roman miles east of Gadara. Its people called themselves the Seleucians of Abila.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shobach-written:
Shobach captained the army of Hadarezer, king of Aram, against King David. Emil G. Hirsch and Kaufmann Kohler wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. David defeated and killed him at the battle of Helam. Chronicles spells his name Shophach in the same account.

Rabbinic lore made Shobach as famed for strength as Goliath. The Ammonites, Aram's allies, counted on him for victory. His defeat dragged their hopes down with him. Two rabbis explained his double name in rival ways. One tied it to a dove-cot shape, the other to terror. Foes melted at the sight of him, that view claimed. Samaritan legend later made him a Persian king's son. The entry shows a brief Bible foe grown large in legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-juda:
Simeon ben Judah ha-Nasi was a teacher between the tannaitic and amoraic ages. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was the younger son of Judah the Prince. Though far more learned than his brother Gamaliel, he ranked lower.

His father meant Gamaliel to succeed him as nasi, or president. Simeon was to be hakam, the scholar, only. He was close friends with Hiyya and Bar Kappara. Both had studied alongside him in their youth. Simeon surpassed both in legal and homiletic reading. Hiyya learned psalm exposition from him directly. Bar Kappara learned parts of the Leviticus midrash from him. Yet both men refused to honor him properly, which annoyed him. His father called him the light of Israel. Kindness and candor marked his character, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sloman-charles-: Charles Sloman was an English composer and singer of comic songs. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was born about 1808. He died in London on July 21, 1870. His works included Sacred Strains and Hymns, published in 1860. His songs included Charming Sue, Daughter of Israel, and Maid of Judah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ibn-zak:
Solomon ibn Zakbel was a Spanish poet of the twelfth century. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a relative of Abu Omar Joseph ibn Sahl. He wrote a satirical romance in Arabic maqamat form. That form was later imitated in Hebrew by Judah al-Harizi.

The hero of the romance is named Asher ben Judah. In rhymed prose he tells of his love adventures. Those adventures were marked by setbacks and turns of fortune. Small poems in strict rhythm are set through the prose. Al-Harizi may have borrowed both title and style from it. He praised Solomon's poetic talent highly in his Tahkemoni.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stein-abraham-1:
Abraham Stein was a German rabbi born at Wanfried, Prussia, in 1818. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on January 13 of that year. He studied at Cassel and at the University of Berlin. He took his doctor's degree at Berlin in 1844.

He led the seminary of Cassel from 1845 to 1847. He served as rabbi at Filehne and then at Danzig. In 1864 Prague called him as preacher to its modern temple. That temple had a choir, organ, and sermon in German. He served there until his death in 1884. His works include a history of the Jews in Danzig.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sufism-arabic-t:
Sufism is the mystic path within Islam, called Tasawwuf in Arabic. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The name comes from the Arabic word for wool. Sufis wore plain wool cloth as a sign of simplicity. Their ideas shaped Jewish ethical and mystic writing too.

Sufis read the words of Mohammed for a hidden, spiritual sense. Early Sufism stressed simple living and moral discipline. Later thought added Neoplatonic and Hindu Vedanta elements. The system taught that God alone truly exists. The material world only reflects his attributes and perfections. Loving beauty or goodness means loving God himself. The entry explains why Jewish scholars study this Muslim movement. Its influence ran through the Judeo-Arabic writings of the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tahash-14200:
Tahash is a Hebrew word the old versions render as badger. Morris Jastrow, Jr., and Gerson B. Levi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Tahash skins covered the tent of meeting outside. They also wrapped the Ark and other holy vessels. Ezekiel mentions tahash leather in fine sandals.

Ancient translators split on what tahash means. The Targum reads the word as brilliant. The Septuagint gives a hyacinth color instead. Rashi and Ibn Ezra took it as an animal's name. Modern scholars have guessed dolphin from Arabic kinship. Delitzsch compared an Assyrian word meaning wether. Assyrians covered boats with such wether skins. His match fits the Hebrew phrase exactly. The entry shows one small word testing every translator.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teman-14300:
Teman was first a tribe, then a district, of Edom. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Genesis makes Teman the eldest son of Eliphaz. Eliphaz was the first-born son of Esau. Teman ranks among the dukes of Edom there.

The genealogy proves Teman a leading Edomite tribe. Prophets use Teman as a synonym for Edom itself. Amos, Obadiah, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk all do so. The Temanites were famed for their wisdom in tradition. Jeremiah asks if wisdom is no more in Teman. Eliphaz, Job's oldest and wisest friend, was a Temanite. Obadiah places Teman on the mount of Esau. Eusebius sets a Thaiman region near Petra. The entry traces a tribe's name becoming a nation's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-timnath-serah-i:
Timnath-Serah was a town in Mount Ephraim tied to Joshua's last years. Immanuel Benzinger wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Joshua received the town as his inheritance. He fortified it and was buried there. Judges calls the place Timnath-heres.

Eusebius counted Timnath an important city near Lydda. Travelers were shown Joshua's grave among its ruins. The modern town of Tibna likely marks the site. One huge tomb there may be the grave he meant. Samaritan tradition instead places the tomb at Kafr Haris. The city may also be the Thamnatha of First Maccabees. Josephus calls that town capital of a Jewish district.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-urbino-14600:
Urbino was an Italian family named for the city of Urbino. Gotthard Deutsch and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Solomon d'Urbino heads the list in the early 1300s. He enjoyed Duke Frederick's favor at Urbino. His small work bore the title Yefeh Nof.

His descendant Solomon completed Ohel Mo'ed in 1500. That book treats Hebrew synonyms in detail. Venice printed it in 1548, and Vienna reprinted it in 1881. Joseph Baruch d'Urbino published poems at Mantua in 1659. He also translated an Italian astronomy work into Hebrew. That translation never reached print, the entry notes. Later members lived at Pesaro and Ancona. Responsa and letters preserve their names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vienne-14700:
Vienne is a town in the old French province of Dauphiné. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there as early as the tenth century. They had their own quarter, still called the Jewry in 1905. In the thirteen hundreds they built a fine synagogue.

The entry names the town's leading scholars. Tobiah ben Elijah wrote on the Pentateuch and composed liturgical poems. His pupil Abraham ben Ephraim wrote on legal cases. Yakar of Vienne issued legal decisions, and fragments survive. The short article preserves a small town's learned past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfsohn-wilhel:
Wilhelm Wolfsohn (1820-1865) was a German poet and essay writer from Odessa. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He read medicine and thought at Leipsic. He began his work with verse turned from Latin into German.

In 1843 he toured Russia to speak on German books. His talks won such praise that a chair was held out to him. The price was that he take the Christian faith. He said no and went back to Germany. There he helped run two big reviews of books. In 1852 he settled at Dresden to write. His plays and poems fill the rest of the entry. One play on the blood charge shows his Jewish pride in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-bar-juda:
Yizhak bar Judah was a Babylonian scholar of the fourth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a young peer of the famed Ulla. He was schooled at the home of his father in Pumbedita.

Ulla once came to that home on a visit north. He showed his ire that Yizhak was not yet wed. His father sent him to see how Ulla blessed the Sabbath close. Yizhak sent Abaye in his place on that errand. His father rebuked him with sharp words for that slight. He heard the talks of Rabbah in his youth first. He then sat with Rami bar Hama for a time. He left that man to study with Sheshet in the end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-ben-a:
Zechariah ben Abkilus was a sage and a Zealot chief at Jerusalem. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, M. Seligsohn, and Kaufmann Kohler wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the days when the Second Temple fell. The Talmud lays the fall of the town at his door.

He sat at the feast of the Kamza tale of old lore. His clout could have saved a man from shame that night. He did not use that clout at the feast at all. Next the king sent a flawed calf as a gift to the shrine. One school would have taken the gift to balk a foe. Zechariah cast the vote that made the gift be refused. The folk wished to slay the foe ere he could tell the king. Zechariah held them back from that deed as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuph-15300: Zuph is a name tied to the prophet Samuel and his country in the Bible. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One Zuph was a Levite among Samuel's ancestors; a parallel passage calls him Zophai. A district also bore the name, perhaps from his family. That country lay near Ramathaim-zophim and Mount Ephraim, where Samuel's story opens.
joh-andreae-stisseri-de-variis-erroribus: Johann Andreas Stisser's Latin dissertation, printed in 1700, takes the form of a letter to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Stisser was professor of chemistry and botany at the Julia academy, as his title page states. The letter treats errors committed in medicine through ignorance of chemistry, as its title declares. The scanned sample is badly garbled, so its argument cannot be followed in detail here. The title page alone fixes the author, the subject, and the famous man addressed.
kent-lectures-homoeopathic-philosophy-19:
American homeopathy found its clearest voice in James Tyler Kent, whose Lectures on Homoeopathic Philosophy appeared in 1900. Kent taught that good prescribing rests on ideas, not just lists of drugs. His lectures set out the thinking behind his famous Repertory, the tool his students used at the bedside.

A vital force in the body runs through the talks as the first key idea. Kent adds how a person becomes open to illness, and the rule of one remedy at a time. He also explains potentization, the step-by-step dilution said to free a drug's power. Doctors trained in his school shaped homeopathic practice for decades.
king-henry-vi-part-1-pg1500:
This edition of Shakespeare's Henry the Sixth, Part One prints a full cast and a scene plan for the five acts. Henry the Sixth heads the list, with the dukes of Gloucester, Bedford, and Exeter among his uncles. The French side names King Charles, his bastard son, and Joan la Pucelle. Talbot, England's captain, stands among the soldiers.

The contents move from Westminster Abbey and London streets to Orleans and the Tower. Rouen, Paris, and Bordeaux carry the French war to its close. The plan shows two stories at once: England losing France town by town, and English lords quarreling at home. The Temple Garden rose-plucking scene sits in act two, planting the civil war to come.
knopf-aspects-of-birth-control-1900:
S. Adolphus Knopf wrote Aspects of Birth Control, issued as a cheap ten-cent pamphlet. The sample shows his paper on the moral aspects of birth control. He wrote while war in Europe was killing many young men.

Knopf says birth control does not have to mean race suicide, as critics claimed. He argues it should raise the health and vigor of the next generation. His plea aims at fewer children born with serious weakness. The pamphlet preserves an early medical voice in a heated public debate. Knopf frames his case as a moral duty, not a scandal. That framing shows how reformers argued inside a hostile climate.
kuyper-work-of-holy-spirit-1900:
Abraham Kuyper was a Dutch theologian who also served as prime minister of the Netherlands. His Work of the Holy Spirit, in this 1900 English edition, is his Reformed pneumatology, the doctrine of the Spirit's work. Kuyper writes as statesman and churchman at once.

He traces the Spirit's work in creation, in the church's common life, and in the individual heart's rebirth and growth. Against both cold orthodoxy and shallow revivalism, he stresses the Spirit's quiet, sovereign, and thorough action. Reformed readers still treat the book as the fullest classic treatment of its theme. English readers met in Kuyper a mind at home in pulpit, press, and parliament.
l-initiation-alchimique-treize-lettres-i:
Albert Poisson wrote L'Initiation Alchimique, printed in Paris in 1900. Its subtitle promises thirteen unpublished letters. Those letters concern the practice of the Great Work, the central aim of alchemy.

The book appeared under the imprint of Édition de l'Initiation. It even carries a portrait of its author. Poisson wrote for readers drawn to France's occult revival. larmor-aether-and-matter-1900:
Joseph Larmor, an Irish sage who worked at Cambridge, built his most deep ether scheme in this book of 1900. It came out just five years before Einstein changed the field for good. Larmor sought a scheme in which the ether could bear all the new finds.

At its heart stand electrons, tiny charged parts that strain the ether round them. From their moves he draws light, magnetism, and the drag of fast bodies through space. The book is the most fine spun ether scheme ever made, and a peak of the old physics.
le-petit-rosaire-extract-on-alchemy-from: Le Petit Rosaire is an extract on alchemy drawn from the Roman de la Rose. Its record dates it to 1600. london-son-of-the-wolf-1900:
Jack London published The Son of the Wolf in 1900, his first book, after struggling through years of rejections. London had rushed to the Klondike gold fields in 1897 and come home sick and empty-handed, but rich in material. These stories were the first Klondike tales to reach a wide public.

The tales follow miners, prospectors, and Native people through a frozen world ruled by what London called the White Silence. Malemute Kid, his recurring hero, settles disputes and saves lives with rough frontier justice. Greed, cold, and dog teams drive the plots. London's terse, muscular style made the far North vivid to readers who would never see snow like it. The book made his name.
love-and-life-an-old-story-in-eighteenth:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Love and Life retells a very old fable in eighteenth-century costume. In her preface Yonge traces the tale back to Apuleius, the early novelist. Forms of it live in folk tales from India to Scandinavia. English readers know it best as Beauty and the Beast.

Yonge moves that story into the England of powdered hair and country houses. A young woman is sent to live in a strange, grand house. There, love must grow through trust, absence, and a broken promise. The manners are of the 1700s, but the feelings are timeless. Yonge's version is tender, moral, and quietly romantic.
majmu-al-sanai-1800: Majmu al-sanai, 1800. The Arabic collection. This book preserves that manuscript. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
malebranche-search-after-truth-taylor-17:
Nicolas Malebranche, a French priest and philosopher, published his Search After Truth in the 1670s, and Thomas Taylor's English translation of about 1700 is the text here. The Treatise of Nature and Grace accompanies the Search in this volume. Malebranche asked why the mind errs so often, and how it may find truth under God's light.

His answer blames the senses and the imagination, those loud servants who drown the intellect's quiet voice. His bold doctrine holds that we see all things in God, who alone truly acts in the world. The Search made Malebranche the leading Cartesian of France. Its long, luminous argument shaped French thought until Hume and the next age arose.
mandeville-travels-pollard-1900:
Mandeville's Travels claims to be the work of Sir John Mandeville, an English knight who journeyed through the East. A. W. Pollard produced this modernized edition in 1900. No medieval book of travel was read more widely, and much of it is invention.

Part pilgrim guide and part wonder book, it leads readers to the Holy Land and far beyond. Its pages parade the monster races of the East, men with heads in their chests and feet like umbrellas. Readers believed it for centuries. Pollard's edition makes the old bestseller easy to read today, marvels, lies, and all.

mark-twain-a-biography-volume-ii-part-1-:
This part of Paine's biography opens with Mark Twain at forty. John Hay tells him a man reaches his zenith at forty. Paine answers that both Hay and Twain refute the rule. Each gained in strength and honor to the very end.

At forty, Twain's name was on every lip in two hemispheres. Every talk was pointed with some saying of his, true or not. The chapters cover his Hartford prime and growing empire of books. Fortune, family, and famous friendships fill these full years. Paine knew many of the people and places himself. His account of Twain's great decade is rich and intimate. It sets the height from which sorrow later fell.
mark-twain-a-biography-volume-ii-part-2-:
Volume two, part two of Paine's biography covers 1886 to 1900. It opens with Twain's Browning readings in the winter of 1886. He studied each poem line by line before reading it aloud. A club of friends, including the Saturday Morning Club, gathered to listen.

His rich voice gave those obscure verses marvelous clarity, Paine says. The Hartford house stood at the height of its splendor then. Yet the same years brought the publishing crash and deep debt. Twain set out on a world tour to pay every creditor. Paine tells the fall and the fight with full sympathy. The part closes on honor recovered at great cost.
mark-twain-s-letters-volume-4-1886-1900:
Volume four of Mark Twain's Letters runs from 1886 to 1900. Paine opens with the Clemens family's home theatricals at Hartford. The household staged The Prince and the Pauper again and again. A sculptor friend built their scenery and little stage.

A letter of January 1886 fixes the date of one performance. Other letters touch his mother's romance and letters never mailed. Splendor fills the early part of this volume. Then the publishing house fails, and debt closes in. Twain's world lecture tour answers the crash with honor. The letters darken, harden, and keep their humor through it all.
maspero-passing-of-empires-1900:
Gaston Maspero ends his grand tale in The Passing of the Empires, in English from 1900. The tome spans from 850 years ere Christ to 330, the age of Alexander. One realm past the next takes the lead of the old East, then fades: Assyria, Babylon, Persia, and at last the Greeks at the gate.

Maspero writes the long fall with grace and calm. He knew the soil and texts of Egypt as few did. The three tomes as one are his crown work. This last one has a sad, grave glow. Readers meet each realm at its peak ere its fall.
mermaid-wonderful-prophecy-whitehaven-18:
A cheap chapbook of 1800, printed at Whitehaven, tells this strange tale of a mermaid and a lost sailor. No author's name stands on the small book, as was the way with such prints. John Robinson is the sailor at the heart of the tale.

Robinson spent six days adrift at sea and met a mermaid who spoke words of fate to him. The words came true in the minds of the folk: he died five days after he came home. The small book shows how sea lore lived in cheap print for port town folk.
morris-man-and-his-ancestor-1900:
Charles Morris, an American popular writer on science, published Man and His Ancestor in 1900. He set out to explain human evolution in plain language. The subtitle promises a study in evolution for general readers.

Morris traces human descent through the primates, step by step. Chapters weigh the antiquity of man and the fossil evidence then known. He writes clearly and confidently, without technical clutter. Later bones have filled in much that he could only guess at. The book shows how Darwin's ideas reached ordinary readers by 1900. Morris had already won readers with popular works on animals and nature.
mother-shipton-prophecies-1700:
Mother Shipton was a famed English folk seer, said to have lived in Yorkshire in the days of Henry VIII. This set of her life and forecasts came out as a cheap chapbook in 1700. Chapbooks were small, cheap books sold by men who walked from town to town.

The book tells of her birth, her strange looks, her life, and her death. Then come her forecasts, in verse and prose, on kings, wars, fire, and flood. It shows Mother Shipton as the common folk of England knew her and passed her name on.
nasa-tm-19700020649-experimental-perform:

The controls used all static parts, with no moving switches, the authors note. They were designed to work in a vacuum, as space hardware must. Test results show how the alternator and its control package behaved together. Such gear turns engine power into steady electricity that a spacecraft can use.
novalis-hymns-to-the-night-1800:
Novalis wrote his Hymns to the Night after the death of his young fiancee, Sophie von Kühn. The six hymns appeared in 1800, and George MacDonald printed them complete in his Rampolli in 1897. Night, usually feared, becomes in these pages the doorway to love, death, and God.

Verse and prose alternate as the speaker turns from daylight's bustle to the dark. The dead beloved appears as guide toward a higher world beyond the grave. Novalis wrote with a miner's training and a poet's faith in symbols. The hymns became the summit of German Romantic poetry. MacDonald's love for German mysticism made him a fit carrier of them into English.

plos-pone-0000100:
Justin A. Harris, Ehsan Arabzadeh, Adrienne L. Fairhall, and their team studied the sense of touch in PLOS ONE in 2006. People can tell apart vibrations of different frequencies through the skin of the fingers. The team tested what limits that skill, such as how strong the vibration feels versus how often it repeats.

Their results bear on how the cortex codes touch: whether by the rate of firing, its timing, or both. That code is what a prosthetic hand would need to speak to feel natural. Careful measures of what people can and cannot tell apart set the spec for such devices. The paper links a lab measure of perception to real neural code questions.
plos-pone-0000200:
Milena Raffi and Ralph M. Siegel published this vision neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Optic flow is the streaming pattern of light across the eyes when we move through the world. The authors map how the inferior parietal lobule of a behaving monkey's brain organizes responses to that flow.

Optic flow tells an animal its heading, speed, and the layout around it. A functional architecture for flow in this brain region shows how the cortex divides that job. The work helps explain how primates, including humans, steer through space using vision alone.
plos-pone-0000300:
Xiao Xiao Jenny Gu, Feng Yun Yue, Colin M. Kovacs, and colleagues published this HIV immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many cytokines, immune signal proteins, share one receptor part, the common gamma chain. The authors study the role of those cytokines in reversing T cell anergy. Anergy is the switched-off state of HIV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells in infected patients.

Anergic T cells are present but useless against the virus. If cytokine signals can wake them, that is a therapeutic opening. The paper tests which signals do the waking, informing immune-based strategies meant to restore the body's own control of HIV.
plos-pone-0000400:
Roser Pinyol and colleagues described a control circuit for nerve cell shape in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The circuit involves N-WASP and the Arp2/3 complex, proteins that build branching scaffolds of actin, the cell's structural fiber. A third protein, Abp1, helps regulate them, and the team placed it in the pathway that shapes neurons.

A neuron's shape, its trunk of dendrites and its long axon, decides what it can connect to. Actin scaffolds push the membrane into those forms. Showing that Abp1 helps control the N-WASP and Arp2/3 machinery adds a link to the chain of command. That chain sculpts nerve cells as the brain wires itself.
plos-pone-0000500:
Dana Sumilo and colleagues challenged a popular explanation for a disease surge in the Baltic states, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Tick-borne encephalitis, a viral brain infection spread by ticks, rose sharply in the Baltics in the 1990s. Climate change was often blamed, since warmer weather favors ticks. The team's title states their finding: climate change cannot explain the upsurge.

Ruling out the easy explanation redirects attention to social and land-use changes after the Soviet era, which altered farming, forests, and human contact with ticks. The paper is a caution against attributing every disease shift to climate without checking the numbers, and it models how to test such claims.
plos-pone-0000600:
Cristina A. Faria and colleagues found a weakness in a flagship farm technology, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bt maize is engineered to poison caterpillar pests. The team found a chain of effects. Bt maize is highly open to aphid attack, so aphids thrive on it. The wasps that attack caterpillar pests feed on the aphids' honeydew. With more food, the wasps perform better against the pests.

The chain is indirect: a pest the plant cannot stop ends up feeding the allies that kill the pests it can. Such side effects decide whether engineered crops help or hinder biological control in real fields. The study is a reminder that fields are food webs, not single-trait demonstrations.
plos-pone-0000700:
Julio Echegoyen, Axel Neu, Kevin D. Graber and colleagues studied how brain circuits steady their state after activity is blocked. Their 2007 PLOS ONE work concerns homeostatic plasticity, the adjustments that keep circuits from becoming hyperactive or falling silent. Little was known about this process after activity changes in vivo, inside a living animal.

Blocking activity in the hippocampus, they studied synaptic scaling, where synapses strengthen or weaken all at once, and intrinsic plasticity of the neurons. Age-dependence was part of the question too. Brains that cannot regain balance in activity are prone to disorders like epilepsy. Knowing how the balance is restored, and how it changes with age, guides that research.
plos-pone-0000800:
Stephen B. Beres and James M. Musser catalogued the borrowed genes in the group A Streptococcus metagenome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Strains of one bacterial species differ in gene content, and those differences drive medically relevant traits such as virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Group A Streptococcus causes a diverse array of human infections and after-effects, and shows complex population structure.

Exogenous genetic elements, DNA arrived from outside, are their focus: genes picked up from viruses and other bacteria. Such imports can turn a mild strain dangerous in one step. Tallying their contribution to the species' total gene pool explains how one species produces so many disease patterns.
plos-pone-0000900:
Gang Li, Jinhong Wang, Stephen Rossiter and colleagues found fast change in the FoxP2 gene in echolocating bats, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. FoxP2 helps control the face and mouth movements behind speech and calls. Across backboned animals it barely changes, yet humans and chimps differ at two building blocks.

Bats that hunt by sound place huge demands on mouth and voice control. The team compared FoxP2 across bat species and report sped up evolution in the echolocating lines. The result links a speech related gene to another group that lives by precise vocal skill. It widens the story of how vocal control evolves.
plos-pone-0001000:
Logan Walsh, Deanna Carere, Colin Cooper and colleagues tracked two tissue remodeling partners through frog metamorphosis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Matrix metalloproteinases cut up the material around cells, and their inhibitors, TIMPs, keep them in check. Together they rebuild tissue, and TIMPs also help switch some enzymes on.

In the frog Xenopus laevis, metamorphosis rebuilds nearly everything, from tail to gut. The team found RNA levels of one enzyme, MT1-MMP, and its inhibitor TIMP-2 mimic each other across that change. Matched timing suggests the pair are managed as a unit. The frog gives a whole body view of remodeling that cell cultures cannot.
plos-pone-0001100:
Ruvandhi Nathavitharana, Jorge Coronel and David Moore tested sunlight for making TB culture waste safe, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disposing of TB culture material is a real problem in poor settings. Cultures multiply the infectious load of patient samples greatly before they are thrown away.

Solar cookers had already shown they can kill conventional bacteria. The team examine solar disinfection of MODS mycobacterial cultures, a low cost TB culture method. Sunlight is the one resource many poor clinics have in surplus. If a solar cooker can sterilize culture waste, a safety step that rich labs automate becomes possible where it is needed most.
plos-pone-0001200:
In a complex system, it is often unclear which parts to adjust to improve performance. Di Wu, Elizabeth Townsley, and Alan Tartakoff present a selection strategy for that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their test bed is the cell, where the components that most affect a trait are rarely obvious.

The authors describe covert genetic selections to optimize phenotypes, ways of letting a population of cells reveal which molecular targets matter most. The method identifies and prioritizes targets rather than testing guesses one by one. The same logic, they note, applies to other high-complexity systems, from institutions to economies.
plos-pone-0001300:
Interleukin-24, also known as mda-7, is a signaling protein said to kill tumor cells while sparing normal ones. Stephanie Kreis and colleagues tested a lab-made version against melanoma cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. IL-24 belongs to the IL-10 family of cytokines and is produced by certain immune cells.

The authors report that recombinant interleukin-24 lacks apoptosis-inducing traits in melanoma cells. A result like this matters: it tests a hopeful claim in the cancer literature and warns against building therapy plans on it without care. Their study used the purified protein itself, rather than gene delivery.
plos-pone-0001400:
Bernard Couvreur and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on tick proteins that blunt the host defense. Ticks feed on blood for a long time, so they must calm host blood clotting, swelling, and immune attack. They do so with a suite of spit proteins from large gene families. The team studied one family that blocks a key defense arm.

The authors describe how members of this family vary and how each one acts. Small shifts in form lead to shifts in target and strength. The work maps a key tool ticks use to stay attached and feed. It may also point to new ways to foil ticks and the ills they spread.
plos-pone-0001500:
Emily Manderson, Mohan Malleshaiah, and Stephen Michnick published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a yeast gene of unknown job. More than a thousand yeast genes still lack a clear role, despite vast data on gene use and protein links. The team built a screen that merges gene tests with protein link data. They used it to probe one such gene.

Their screen ties the gene, called Elm1, to shutting off a yeast growth factor. A new job for an old gene shows the screen works. The same tack can be run on the rest of the unknown list. That promises a faster close to the yeast gene map.
plos-pone-0001600:
Asako Shindo, Takamasa Yamamoto, and Naoto Ueno wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell polarity in frog embryos. Polarity, the built in top and bottom of a cell, shapes how embryos form. In frog gastrulation, gut layer cells line up and slide past each other. That slide stretches the embryo from head to tail. The team tracked how polarity is set in step across the sheet.

Their work maps the cues that align cells as the sheet moves. A shared alignment is what lets the whole tissue stretch in one course. Faults here cause grave birth defects. The frog model gives a clear view of a step all backboned embryos share.
plos-pone-0001700:
Denise M. Wolf, Lisa Fontaine-Bodin, Ilka Bischofs, and their co-authors measured memory in a bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Memory is usually credited to higher organisms. But many bacterial control networks show complex dynamics and multi-stable behavior. Those traits are linked to memory in other systems, and bacteria plainly respond to their own past states.

The team quantified history-dependent behavior: how a cell's response to a signal depends on what it met before. The full text gives the experiments, the time scales of the effect, and the model they built. A measured bacterial memory gives a concrete system for studying how single cells store information about their past. It also has uses in engineering microbes that remember exposures.
plos-pone-0001800:
Alfonso J. C. Soler Bistué, Daniel Birshan, Andrew P. Tomaras, and their co-authors sequenced a resistance plasmid in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The spread of antimicrobial resistance genes is an important public health and biodefense threat. Plasmids, small DNA circles that jump between bacteria, drive the rapid acquisition of resistance by pathogens.

The paper gives the nucleotide sequence of pMET1, a multiresistance plasmid from Klebsiella pneumoniae. It also gives its similarity to pCRY, a plasmid of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis, and to integrative conjugative elements. The full text gives the gene map and the shared segments. Shared parts across plasmids of very different pathogens show how resistance genes travel.
plos-pone-0001900:
John Lin and co-authors tested hunger-boosting drugs in monkeys in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The drugs switch on TrkB, a cell receptor tied to body weight. When this path fails, people and mice eat too much and gain great weight. When drugs in mice switch it on, food intake and weight drop.

The team gave TrkB-switching drugs through the body, not the brain, to non-human primates. As the title states, appetite rose and the animals gained weight, the reverse of the mouse results. That clash across species is a warning for drug work: a path that trims weight in mice may not do the same in primates.
plos-pone-0002000:
Anavaj Sakuntabhai and co-authors hunted host genes that shape malaria in Senegal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Attacks of falciparum malaria range from mild to deadly, even in the same region. Good evidence says genes of the person, not just the parasite, drive part of that range.

Most gene hunts had used a case and control design, which has limits. The team instead mapped traits tied to malaria to spots in the genome in Senegalese families, and tested how strongly each trait is inherited. Family maps of this kind can find protective genes that case studies miss.
plos-pone-0002100:
Judith Legrand and co-authors modeled tuberculosis control in crowded prisons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. TB in prisons is a major health problem in countries with high or middling rates, such as Brazil. For operational reasons, control strategies in prisons cannot be compared through population-based intervention studies, since prisons cannot be run as trial sites at will.

A mathematical model is proposed to compare strategies instead, in highly endemic, overcrowded prisons. Models can weigh screening, isolation, and treatment options before scarce funds are spent. Prison TB spills into the wider public, so gains inside walls count outside them too.
plos-pone-0002200:
Jason Bourke and co-authors built a 3D model of a dingo skull to test bite physics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Jaw models predict that bite force depends on how wide the jaw opens and on which tooth does the biting. Few studies had checked those predictions in a real mammal, and none had weighed the role of gape angle.

The team used a finite element approach, which breaks the skull into many small pieces in a computer. They computed bite force and skull stress across gapes and tooth positions. Their results test long-used jaw models against hard numbers from an iconic Australian predator.
plos-pone-0002300:
Darren Soanes, Intikhab Alam, Mike Cornell, and co-authors compared the genomes of fungi and their kin across many species, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fungi and oomycetes cause many of the most serious diseases of plants, from potato blight to tree diebacks. A shared genomic pattern might explain what makes them good pathogens.

The team analyzed genome sequences from thirty-six species, including seven plant pathogenic ones. They looked for gene families that had expanded in the pathogenic lines. Expanded families are candidate tool kits for infecting plants, and each one offers targets for crop protection that go beyond spraying single chemicals.
plos-pone-0002400:
Holt and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alison R. Holt, Zoe G. Davies, Claire Tyler, and others. Its subject is meta-Analysis of the Effects of Predation on Animal Prey Abundance: Evidence from UK Vertebrates. Controlling vertebrate predators is one of the most widespread forms of wildlife management and it continues to cause conflict between stakeholders worldwide.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002500:
Led by Haslam, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Niall J. Haslam, Nava E. Whiteford, Gerald Weber, and others. Its subject is optimal Probe Length Varies for Targets with High Sequence Variation. The title goes on to note implications for Probe Library Design for Resequencing Highly Variable Genes. Sequencing by hybridisation is an effective method for obtaining large amounts of DNA sequence information at low cost.

The efficiency of SBH depends on the design of the probe library to provide the maximum information for minimum cost. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002600:
Research by Wei and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Yan Wei, Mei-Hua Qu, Xing-Sheng Wang, and others. Its subject is binding to the Minor Groove of the Double-Strand, Tau Protein Prevents DNA from Damage by Peroxidation. Tau, an important microtubule linked protein, has been found to bind to DNA.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002700:
Work by David Caramelli and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a 28,000 years old Cro-Magnon mtDNA sequence differs from all potentially contaminating modern sequences. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David Caramelli, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. DNA sequences from ancient speciments may in fact result from undetected contamination of the ancient specimens by modern DNA. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002800:
Research from Shinobu Ueda and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers establishment of rat embryonic stem cells and making of chimera rats. The catalog record names Shinobu Ueda first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The rat is a reference animal model for physiological studies and for the analysis of multigenic human diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, neurological disorders. The authors add a further point. The rats have long been used in extensive chemical carcinogenesis studies. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002900:
Philip Monahan, Kevin de Souza and William Idsardi used brain imaging in 2008 to time how listeners restore a missing pitch. When the lowest tone of a complex sound is absent, hearers still sense it. When the brain rebuilds that missing fundamental was still unclear.

Their MEG recordings, which track fast magnetic signals from the brain, placed the recovery in auditory cortex within 100 milliseconds of the sound. That is a tight time bound from the study itself. Hearing scientists get a clearer timeline for one of the basic tricks that lets us judge pitch and voice.
plos-pone-0003000:
Etienne Morel, Stéphane Fouquet, Carine Strup-Perrot and co-authors studied the cellular prion protein in epithelial cells in 2008. The normal prion protein, PrPc, is found throughout the body, yet its everyday function was still debated. Most work had focused on the nervous system, leaving epithelia poorly investigated.

The team had earlier found PrPc targeted to cell-cell junctions in polarized epithelial cells. Their PLOS ONE study reports it is involved in epithelial cell proliferation and in placing junction proteins. That widens the prion protein's normal job beyond the brain, a useful baseline for disease work.
plos-pone-0003100:
Ildefonso De La Fuente, Luis Martínez, Alberto Pérez-Samartín and co-authors argued in 2008 that cell metabolism self-organizes globally. For many years enzymes were assumed to work either alone or in small catalytic groups. Studies using metabolic network models were helping to reveal the functional complexity of enzyme dynamics.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors present evidence for global self-organization of the cellular metabolic structure. That view treats metabolism as one coordinated system, not a bag of separate pathways. It changes how models of cell chemistry should be built and tested. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003200:
Paola Ferrante, Claudia Catalanotti, Giulia Bonente and colleagues build a regulated gene switch for an alga in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a model system for algal and cell biology and is used for biotechnology, such as molecular farming and biological hydrogen production. Its metal-responsive CYC6 promoter is repressed by copper and induced by nickel ions.

The team present an optimized, chemically regulated gene expression system for Chlamydomonas. Readers get a tighter on-off tool for a workhorse alga. Reliable switches matter when engineered algae must make a product only at the right stage of growth.
plos-pone-0003300:
Marilis Rodriguez and co-authors study a malaria parasite surface protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. To invade a red blood cell, Plasmodium falciparum must use many contacts between its own proteins and receptors on the cell. Finding those receptors is a major task in learning how invasion works, since each contact is a chance to block it.

The team describe PfRH5, a new member of a binding protein family, show it binds the red cell, and hunt for its receptor. Readers meet a parasite protein at the heart of cell entry. Entry proteins are top vaccine targets for blood-stage malaria.
plos-pone-0003400:
Sitao Wu and Yang Zhang built a prediction program called ANGLOR, presented in this 2008 paper. A protein's shape depends on the twist angles along its backbone. Those angles can be guessed from the order of its amino acid building blocks. ANGLOR mixes several learning methods to make that guess.

The program reads sequence profiles plus predicted shape and exposure features. It then outputs the backbone angles as real numbers, not rough classes. Tests on large sets showed the mixed method beat single methods. Good angle guesses bring scientists closer to a protein's full three-dimensional shape.
plos-pone-0003500:
Paolo Marinho de Andrade Zanotto and David C. Krakauer compared whole virus genomes in this 2008 paper. They covered four families of DNA viruses. Viruses swap genes with hosts and each other at high rates. That swapping raises doubt about what single genes say about virus history.

Their phylogenies suggested regulatory cores and accessory satellites evolve in concert. Core control genes and extra satellite genes move as a linked set. Concerted change hints at deep order in viral genomes. The claim reframes how virus family trees should be read. Virus trees guide vaccine strain choice for fast-changing germs like flu.
plos-pone-0003600:
Berna Atik and co-authors hunted gene variants tied to a blinding eye condition in this 2008 paper. Trachoma is the leading preventable cause of blindness worldwide. It follows infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, often again and again. A balanced immune response is critical for clearing that infection.

Trachomatous trichiasis is a late, sight-threatening stage of the disease. The team identified new single-letter variants in inflammatory genes as risk factors. Mass antibiotic programs have not stopped reinfection everywhere. Host genetics may explain who progresses to blindness. Most trachoma blindness falls on women and on the poorest rural areas. There surgery and clean water are hard to reach, and infection passes fast among small children at home.
plos-pone-0003700:
Arne Ø. Mooers, Daniel P. Faith, and Wayne P. Maddison published this conservation study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Groups like the IUCN Red List grade species by how imperiled they are. Those grades are often turned into extinction probabilities to rank species by the evolutionary history they carry.

The authors test how stable such ranked lists are when the conversion changes. Small shifts in the odds can reorder which species count as top priorities. The study gives conservation programs a sharper, more honest way to spend limited funds on saving evolutionary history.
plos-pone-0003800:
Daniel Lietha and Michael J. Eck published this structural study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Focal adhesion kinase, or FAK, helps cells move, multiply, and survive. It is overproduced in many human cancers and tied to poor outcomes. A new inhibitor, TAE226, had recently been reported against it.

The authors solved crystal structures of the FAK kinase bound to TAE226 and related inhibitors. The structures reveal an unusual helical shape in a key segment of the kinase. These atomic pictures guide the design of tighter, better FAK blockers for cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0003900:
John H. Malone and Brian E. Fontenot compared breeding barriers across toad species in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. How new species split apart remains a core question in evolution study. Crosses between species show where mating or offspring fail. The authors gathered a very large set of such crosses.

Their data cover more than 1,900 crosses between 92 toad species. With that spread, they could look for general patterns in how isolation builds. Wide comparisons reveal whether barriers arise early or late in splitting. The toad data set gives evolution researchers a rare, broad test bed.
plos-pone-0004000:
Margaret Kweku, Dongmei Liu, Martin Adjuik, and co-authors trialed seasonal malaria prevention in Ghanaian children in 2008. Malaria and anaemia are the top causes of illness and death for children there. Giving preventive drugs at intervals might cut both problems. The trial tested that idea under real conditions.

Children received either sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine or artesunate plus amodiaquine, or a placebo. Dosing followed the seasons when malaria spreads most. The randomized design gives a fair test of benefit. Results can guide national programs weighing seasonal treatment for children. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004100:
Jarukit Edward Long, Nicholas Renzette, Richard C. Centore, and co-authors studied DNA damage alarms in bacteria in 2008. Repair of DNA damage starts with detecting the harm. In E. coli, the RecA protein coats single-stranded DNA after damage. That filament triggers the SOS response, a broad repair program.

Their PLOS ONE article compares two recA mutants for SOS switching. The mutants differed in what they need to keep SOS on without damage. Such details map how the alarm is triggered and sustained. The work refines a classic model of bacterial stress response. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004200:
Sheng-zhi Wang and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Geneticists often want to switch a gene on in only a few scattered cells, but controlling the probability of activation has been hard. Existing tools tend to flip the gene in nearly all cells or in none.

The team presents STARS, a genetic strategy for stochastic gene activation with regulated sparseness. In plain terms, the method lets researchers dial in how sparse the labelled or altered cells should be. Such control is valuable for tracing single neurons and for mimicking the scattered mutations seen in disease.
plos-pone-0004300:
Michelle Wagner and colleagues published this yeast cell cycle study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Whi5 is a transcriptional repressor that holds back the G1 phase of the cell cycle in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It plays a role equivalent to the retinoblastoma tumour suppressor in mammals. In early G1, Whi5 binds and inhibits the SBF transcription factor, keeping growth genes off.

The team mapped how site-specific phosphorylation by CDK enzymes regulates Whi5. Adding phosphates at particular sites releases the brake at the right moment. The study details the switch that commits a yeast cell to divide.
plos-pone-0004400:
Four mountain massifs in the central Sahara hold pools with tropical fish. Those fish are relicts, leftovers from a wetter age. Sébastien Trape surveyed one such refuge in 2009. His PLOS ONE paper covers the Adrar mountains of Mauritania. Nearly all older records there came from surveys made before 1960. Those surveys reported five fish species.

Trape asks what climate change now means for these desert fish. Their pools are small, isolated, and hard to recolonize if lost. A drying climate threatens the water they depend on. The paper updates a record that had stood for about fifty years. It makes the case for guarding these mountain refuges before the fish vanish.
plos-pone-0004500:
Whether evolution repeats itself when given the same problem is tested by Scott William Roy in PLOS ONE in 2009. How organisms adapt is one of the most basic questions in evolutionary biology. Two recent studies had watched E. coli bacteria evolve in response to the antibiotic cefotaxime.

Those studies followed five mutations in one gene, for an enzyme called beta-lactamase, that together made the bacteria drug-resistant. Roy asks how predictable that path was: would neutral changes, and pairs of changes, lead down the same road again? Asking whether adaptation can be rerun is more than a curiosity. If evolution is partly predictable, scientists can better foresee how bacteria will defeat the next antibiotic.
plos-pone-0004600:
A signaling enzyme helps drive the leakiness of lungs injured by breathing machines, report Mahendra Damarla, Emile Hasan, Adel Boueiz, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mechanical ventilation is a fundamental therapy for acute lung injury. Yet the machine's mechanical stress on the respiratory system can worsen the leak of fluid into the lungs, causing ventilator-associated lung injury.

The team postulated that an enzyme called MK2, switched on through the p38 MAP kinase pathway, drives this harm. They show MK2 regulates actin polymerization, the building of cell skeleton fibers, and vascular leak in this injury. Blocking such a mediator could one day let ventilators support breathing with less collateral damage to the lungs they are saving.
plos-pone-0004700:
Harleen Kaur and colleagues showed that soil microbes can erase plant chemical warfare effects, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plants can release chemicals that slow the growth of rival plants nearby. Past tests often used one chemical on one species on clean paper, which is far from real soil.

In real soil, microbes break down or change those chemicals fast. The team showed that this soil life can wipe out the growth block seen in lab tests.
