The result warns against bold claims from simple lab assays. Field claims about plant warfare need soil included. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004800:
Nguyen Thi Hue and colleagues studied the TLR4 gene and typhoid fever in Vietnam, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Understanding host genetic susceptibility to typhoid may clarify pathogenesis and help develop new therapeutics and vaccines. TLR4 encodes the principal receptor for bacterial endotoxin, a key sensor that triggers immune defense against Salmonella, and Other Gram negative bacteria in the gut and blood.

The team determined genetic variation within TLR4 in Vietnamese populations. They tested links between variants and typhoid occurrence or course. Receptor genetics could explain why illness varies. It may also guide vaccine design for endemic regions.
plos-pone-0004900:
Mai Nguyen Chi and colleagues studied temporally regulated traffic of HuR and ARE mRNAs during mouse spermatogenesis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In mammals, temporal disconnection between copying and translation occurs during late germ cell cell change. During late spermatogenesis copying ceases while stored mRNAs must be translated on schedule. With HuR protein shuttling messages from the chromatoid body to polysomes at defined developmental stages.

Timed delivery ensures proteins appear when needed. Storage bodies organize delayed translation elegantly. Male fertility depends on this choreography. Defects could explain some infertility. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0005000:
Creatine kinase recycles the cell's energy currency, ATP. It is famous for powering muscle contraction. Yafeng Zhang and colleagues found it a second job in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied creatine kinase B in immune cells. Their focus was T cell development and activation.

The enzyme regulates both processes. Interfering with it weakens the T cell response. An energy enzyme is doubling as an immune signal. That dual role was unexpected. The finding connects metabolism to immunity at a basic level. It may matter for conditions where T cells fail or overreact.
plos-pone-0005100:
Fruit flies bolt when danger looms. That startle response is an innate escape reflex. Gregor Zimmermann and colleagues pinned it to specific neurons. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used photoexcitation, switching neurons on with light. The target was a set of brain cells called acj6 neurons.

Lighting up acj6 neurons induced the escape response. No threat was needed. The defined circuit alone fired the whole behavior. Drosophila genetics links genes to circuits to behavior. This study completes one such chain. It shows a reflex can be traced to named cells. Mapping instinct this way is a long-standing goal. Each pinned circuit teaches how brains turn sensation into action.
plos-pone-0005200:
Whether a common lung germ plays a role in multiple sclerosis has been debated for years. The germ, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, would need to be found in spinal fluid to support the claim. Tang and colleagues built a standardized test for that search in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their test detects the germ's DNA in cerebrospinal fluid and can also measure how much is present. They validated it in samples from MS patients and controls. A shared, trusted test lets different labs compare results fairly, which is what a long-running dispute like this one needs most.
plos-pone-0005300:
Obesity makes fat pile up in the heart, where it can poison heart muscle. The heart's fat pool was thought to reflect only uptake and burning of fatty acids. Bartels and colleagues found another route in PLOS ONE in 2009: fat can also be shipped out.

A protein called microsomal triglyceride transfer protein handles that export. Its activity in the heart rose in obesity and served to limit triglyceride accumulation. The heart, in other words, fights back against fat overload, and boosting that defense might protect obese hearts. Heart fat is not just stored fuel. too much of it can poison the heart wall itself, so a built-in way to ship the fat out is a real line of defense.
plos-pone-0005400:
Flight gets harder as animals grow, since muscle power and the power flight demands scale differently. The margin between the two should shrink with body mass, capping flying size. Sato and colleagues studied soaring seabirds in PLOS ONE in 2009 to test that scaling.

Measured seabird flight data anchor the scaling rules in real animals. Those rules can then be extended to giant extinct pterosaurs, whose flight abilities are debated. Seabirds thus serve as living stand-ins for judging whether the largest fliers could truly soar. The largest of those past fliers had wings as wide as a small plane, and whether such bulk could stay aloft has long been in doubt. Which is why hard data from live birds counts so much here.
plos-pone-0005500:
Long Yang and co-authors studied a faulty immune switch in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The IRF family of proteins helps run immune responses, blood cell growth, and cell growth in general. One member, IRF-5, when switched on, drives the making of signals that cause inflammation.

The team tested a mutant form that blocks the normal protein. Studying what the blocker stops shows which jobs truly need IRF-5. That kind of detail can guide drugs for diseases where inflammation runs too hot, such as lupus and other autoimmune conditions. Blocking IRF-5 too much could weaken defence against real infections, so the balance matters for any future drug.
plos-pone-0005600:
Catherine Lovelock and co-authors found that added nutrients can kill mangrove trees, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Extra nutrients washing off farms and towns put heavy pressure on coastal life. Earlier work showed that mangrove forests grow faster when nutrients rise.

But faster shoot growth came at the cost of roots, and the trees died at higher rates in the long run. A forest that looks greener at first may be on its way out. The warning matters for how coastal pollution is judged and managed. Coastal cities keep growing, so nutrient loads on mangrove shores are set to rise unless drainage is handled better.
plos-pone-0005700:
Prasanna Venkatraman and colleagues built a computer method in 2009 to guess what tasks a protease can do. Proteases are enzymes that cut other proteins at set spots. They keep cells in balance, but many newly found proteases have unknown jobs.

The method reads a protease's sequence and shape to predict what it cuts, what it does, and which networks it joins. Labs can then test the best guesses first, saving time and cost. As gene scans keep finding new proteases, such forecasts help turn raw lists into working biology. The paper offers the tool as a guide for that work.
plos-pone-0005800:
Manuel Irimia, Jakob Rukov, and Scott Roy tested in 2009 whether shifts in gene splicing across primates track with shifts in the splicing regulators themselves. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins, and it is tightly controlled in time and place. Regulator proteins bind tags in and around gene segments to set the pattern.

Changes in the tags found in exons did not line up with changes in splicing levels between primate species. That null result is informative: regulation must shift by other routes. The study cautions against simple stories in how splicing evolves.
plos-pone-0005900:
Darren Gray and co-authors ran a village-cluster trial in China in 2009 against a parasitic worm spread by water buffalo. Schistosoma japonicum infects people through water contact, and buffalo are thought to pass much of it to humans. An earlier drug-based pilot ran from the late nineteen-nineties.

The trial randomized whole clusters to intervention or control, treating both people and bovines with praziquantel. Its design tests whether cutting bovine transmission lowers human infection. If it does, control programs must fund animal treatment, not just human doses. The study is a model for tackling diseases shared with animals.
plos-pone-0006000:
The plague bacterium spread across the world from hearths in Central Asia. Yanjun Li, Yujun Cui, Yolande Hauck and colleagues traced that spread with gene typing in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses a method called MLVA, which reads repeating stretches of DNA, to sort Yersinia pestis strains and build their family tree.

The species is usually split into three classic groups, plus a less harmful one found in small mammals. Gene typing sharpens that picture and shows how Central Asian foci seeded plague across continents. Knowing the routes the germ took helps explain old pandemics and helps health teams read the source of any fresh outbreak.
plos-pone-0006100:
Some bacteria carry their own weapon and the scabbard in one protein. Jens Brockmeyer, Sabrina Spelten, Thorsten Kuczius and colleagues dissected such a weapon in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies EspP, a serine protease autotransporter from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, a proposed factor in the germ's virulence, across its four known subtypes.

The subtypes differ sharply in how well they transport themselves out of the cell and cut their targets. Linking those differences to structure shows which parts of the protein do which job. A virulence factor understood at that level is easier to block, and the work helps judge which subtype a patient isolate carries.
plos-pone-0006200:
Melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer, resists many treatments once it spreads. Peng Hou, Dingxie Liu, and Meiju Ji tested a clever switch in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Two growth pathways drive much of melanoma's growth, and blocking them might do more than slow the tumor.

Blocking those pathways turned on thyroid genes that handle iodine inside melanoma cells. The cells also began taking up radioactive iodine, a treatment long used for thyroid cancer. If the switch holds up, some melanomas could be made treatable with an existing therapy. The paper lays out the idea and its first supporting tests.
plos-pone-0006300:
The aquarium trade moves more exotic vertebrates than any other import route, and labels are often wrong. Dirk Steinke, Tyler Zemlak, and Paul Hebert applied DNA barcoding to ornamental fish in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Pressure is growing to ensure species are harvested sustainably and their origins reported honestly.

A short standard DNA tag identified the traded fish reliably in their tests. Regulators could use barcodes to verify species at borders. Honest identification protects wild populations from hidden over-harvest. The study shows a lab method ready for practical enforcement work.
plos-pone-0006400:
A small quail once spread all through New Zealand, then died out fast in the 1870s. Mark Seabrook-Davison and his team used DNA from old specimens in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Doubt had long hung over what the lost bird was and which quails are its kin.

The old DNA settles the lost quail's name and its place on the quail family tree. It clears up the ties of the living quails of the region at the same time. Such work shows the worth of museum skins as stores of past life. It also helps guards of the birds that are left to plan their care.
plos-pone-0006500:
Grégory Lacraz and colleagues studied how diabetic pancreatic cells protect themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Oxidative stress, from excess reactive oxygen species, mediates diabetes-related damage in many tissues. Pancreatic beta cells, which make insulin, are among the victims. The team examined how these cells respond when stressed.

Their title reports that diabetic beta cells can achieve self-protection against oxidative stress. They do so through an adaptive up-regulation of their defenses. A built-in rescue program is hopeful news for diabetes research. If it can be supported, beta cells might last longer. The work also shows that stressed cells are not merely passive victims.
plos-pone-0006600:
Anna Nolan, Hiroshi Kobayashi, Bushra Naveed, and colleagues studied costimulatory molecules in sepsis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inflammation in the early stages of sepsis is governed by the innate immune response. Costimulatory molecules are a receptor and ligand class capable of regulating that response. The team examined CD80 and CD86 in murine polymicrobial sepsis, sepsis from mixed microbes.

Their title highlights a differential role for CD80 and CD86 in regulating the innate response. Two similar molecules turn out to do different jobs. That distinction matters for drugs that target costimulation. Sepsis still lacks targeted treatments, so each regulatory detail counts.
plos-pone-0006700:
Leonid Teytelman and co-authors reported a hidden pitfall in genome experiments in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chromatin is the packed form DNA takes inside cells. Its structure affects repair, copying, and recombination of DNA. The team found it also affects routine laboratory handling of DNA. That influence can distort the results of widely used experiments.

They first noticed the problem in chromatin immunoprecipitation, known as ChIP. ChIP is meant to show where proteins bind along the genome. If chromatin structure skews the processing steps, binding maps can mislead. The authors traced how the distortion arises during analysis. Their warning helps genome researchers clean up a common source of error.
plos-pone-0006800:
Christiane Cuny and colleagues tested people's noses for a livestock-linked resistant bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, clone CC398. Studies in Europe and North America found it often colonizes farm animals. People working directly with colonized animals also carried it. Whether it spreads onward to others was open.

The study compared people with and without pig exposure. Nasal colonization was checked in both groups. Transmission beyond exposed workers would widen the public health concern. Contained carriage would limit it to an occupational issue. The results help draw that boundary for MRSA CC398 in humans.
plos-pone-0006900:
George Chahine and Bart Krekelberg studied how the brain dims vision during eye movements in PLOS ONE in 2009. Every rapid eye movement, or saccade, would blur the world. Saccadic suppression selectively reduces visual sensitivity during the movement. The neural mechanisms behind that reduction remain unknown. Early visual relays like the lateral geniculate nucleus were candidates.

The authors examined cortical contributions to the suppression. Cortex may actively quiet visual signals around each saccade. Knowing where suppression happens explains perceptual stability. It also informs how the brain edits its own input. The study moves the search from the eye's relay toward higher processing stages.
plos-pone-0007000:
Yaguang Si, Hai Shi, and Kyongbum Lee modelled energy burning in fat cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Raising energy use at the cell level is an appealing route against obesity. A protein called UCP1 uncouples mitochondria, wasting fuel as heat. Its presence tracks with lower white fat stores in animals.

The team ran a metabolic flux analysis on cultured 3T3-L1 adipocytes. Their model mapped how fuel flows change when mitochondria uncouple. Quantifying those flows helps judge uncoupling as an anti-obesity strategy. It also flags the costs, since wasted fuel must come from somewhere.
plos-pone-0007100:
Felicity Johnson and Michael Kaplitt searched for targets of a mitochondrial protease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protease Omi, also called HtrA2, is tied to Parkinson's disease. Mice with faults in it develop severe nerve pathology. Omi was thought to protect cells, partly by cutting harmful proteins.

The pair identified new mitochondrial proteins that Omi cuts. Fresh substrates point to a wider regulatory role in nerve cell survival. That role was not the one most researchers assumed. Their findings may redirect how Omi is viewed in neurodegeneration, from simple guard to active manager.
plos-pone-0007200:
Jason W. Bohland, Hemant Bokil, Cara B. Allen, and colleagues tackled a naming problem in brain science in 2009. Neuroscientists divide the brain into regions using atlases. Different atlases draw those borders differently, and no single standard is widely accepted for cortex or deeper structures.

Their PLOS ONE paper calls this the brain atlas concordance problem. They offer a quantitative way to compare anatomical parcellations from different atlases. Such comparisons help researchers judge whether two studies that name the same brain region actually mean the same patch of brain tissue. The comparison method is the paper's main tool for that judgment.
plos-pone-0007300:
Jean-Noël Arsac, Dominique Bétemps, Eric Morignat, and colleagues tested transmission of an unusual sheep prion disease in 2009. Atypical scrapie, also called Nor98, is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy. It is clearly distinct from classical scrapie and from BSE, the cattle disease often called mad cow disease.

The differences show in the biochemistry of the resistant prion protein. Genetic factors also differ between the diseases. The authors use transgenic mice that carry sheep prion genes. They report major effects of host prion protein levels and donor prion genotype on transmission. Their work guides surveillance of atypical scrapie.
plos-pone-0007400:
Holly E. Copeland, Kevin E. Doherty, David E. Naugle, and colleagues mapped energy development against wildlife in the American West in 2009. Many studies quantified indirect effects of hydrocarbon economies on climate and biodiversity. Few had measured the direct effect of new energy production on species where drilling actually occurs on the ground.

The authors map oil and gas development potential in the US Intermountain West. They estimate impacts to species from that footprint. Their PLOS ONE maps show where future development is likely and which habitats overlap. Land managers can use the overlap to plan protections before leasing decisions.
plos-pone-0007500:
Mélanie Bilodeau and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on cystatin genes and blood formation in mice. Cystatins are proteins that block enzymes which chew up other proteins. In mice, most cystatin genes sit in two clusters on one chromosome. The team studied mice missing a stretch of DNA covering two of those genes, Csta and Stfa2l1.

They measured blood stem cell activity in the mutant mice. They also tracked how the remaining cystatin genes behaved without their neighbors. The results connect this family of enzyme blockers to how blood cells are made. A deletion model like this shows what a gene cluster does as a unit. It also reveals how the surviving genes compensate, or fail to, when partners are lost.
plos-pone-0007600:
Nelli Salminen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the human brain locates sounds. Parts of the auditory cortex specialize in spatial hearing. How their neurons represent a sound's location was unknown. The team used magnetoencephalography, which records the brain's magnetic fields, while subjects heard sounds from different directions. They tested competing ideas about the underlying code.

The results favor a population rate code. Location is read from the combined firing rates of many neurons, not from dedicated place spots. Broad, overlapping responses carry the information together. Such codes are flexible and robust, since no single neuron holds the answer. The finding settles a basic question about hearing's spatial sense. It also aligns the auditory system with coding schemes found elsewhere in the brain.
plos-pone-0007700:
Ajoy Basak and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It presents a new compound designed to block an enzyme called furin. Furin helps activate many other proteins, and it has been linked to cancer growth. Viruses and bacteria also exploit it.

The compound is a peptide built around an enediyne unit. In tests it stopped furin from processing three target proteins, proPDGF-A, proPDGF-B and proVEGF-C. Blocking furin could slow signals that help tumors grow. The work adds a fresh chemical tool to the search for furin-based drugs.
plos-pone-0007800:
Man-Koumba Soumahoro and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It follows people after infection with chikungunya virus. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, causes fever and severe joint pain. Months later, many patients still report joint and muscle pain, and low mood.

Earlier reports had not compared patients with an unexposed group. This retrospective cohort study makes that comparison. It measures how often lasting symptoms occur after infection. It also measures their impact on health status and quality of life. The results show the burden patients carry long after the fever ends.
plos-pone-0007900:
Luca Giliberto and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It introduces mice engineered to model two inherited dementias. Familial British and Danish dementia share one cause: mutations in a membrane protein called BRI2. In both diseases, a short peptide fragment builds up in the brain.

The team created knock-in mice, where the mouse gene carries the human-style change. They report the generation and first characterization of these animals. A faithful mouse model lets researchers watch dementia develop step by step. It also gives drug developers a test bed that older models lacked.
plos-pone-0008000:
John McCarty and colleagues watched a migratory shorebird feed in farm fields for PLOS ONE in 2009. Buff-breasted sandpipers cross continents and pause to refuel on the way. More and more of those pauses happen in crop fields shaped by modern farming.

The watchers logged how the birds used the fields: where they fed, how they moved, and what they seemed to gain. Such detail is the first step in judging whether farm land helps or harms the birds. The answer shapes how farm practice and bird protection can be planned together.
plos-pone-0008100:
Urmi Sengupta and colleagues read type 2 diabetes as a network failure, not a single broken gene, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease tangles blood sugar control and insulin response, and its advanced form harms heart, kidneys, and nerves. Gene activity data hold clues about which control paths fail first.

By laying activity data over known networks, the team picked out the key paths that shift in diabetes and its hazards. Master regulators on those paths are the prizes. Hitting a master switch may do more good than chasing each small fault one by one.
plos-pone-0008200:
Cong E. Tan and colleagues studied birth outcomes after the Wenchuan earthquake in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Earthquakes strike without warning and can harm health far beyond direct injuries. Pregnant women face stress, loss, and broken care during such disasters. The team asked how the quake affected births in the region it hit.

They examined outcomes such as birth timing and infant health after the event. Comparing births before and after helps separate quake effects from normal patterns. The findings matter for planning care for mothers in disaster zones. They show why support for pregnant women belongs in relief plans.
plos-pone-0008300:
Thomas R. Hawn and colleagues studied genes and bladder infection in women in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Several studies suggest genes influence who gets urinary tract infections. Yet how DNA variation shapes early urine inflammation in the body was not fully examined. Some women carry bacteria in urine without symptoms, a state called asymptomatic bacteriuria. The team focused on that state.

They tested whether candidate gene variants relate to urine inflammatory responses. Genes of the innate immune system were prime candidates. Linking variants to responses could explain differing susceptibility among women. It may also guide care for recurrent infection.
plos-pone-0008400:
Takayoshi Ubuka and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a brake on sex hormones in man. For years, proof of a brain brake on these hormones was hard to pin down. A small protein with that job was found not long ago in the quail brain. It blocks the making and release of sex hormones at the pituitary gland. No match for it in man had been shown yet.

The team found two such matches in man, named RFRP-1 and RFRP-3. They also found the switch these proteins use, GPR147, in the brain-to-pituitary path. Man thus seems to have this brake too. That fact opens new paths in the study of birth and sex health.
plos-pone-0008500:
Johan Almenberg and co-authors run an experiment on prediction markets in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Prediction markets let people trade on future outcomes. Prices in such markets aggregate private information from many traders. They can create a shared consensus and reward those who seek facts. Science could use that power to forecast which results will replicate. The team test a market built for that purpose.

Traders bet on outcomes tied to scientific claims. The authors check how well market prices forecast the results. They also study what drives traders to gather information. The experiment shows if markets can serve as a tool for science itself.
plos-pone-0008600:
Monika Heiner and co-authors find the core of a low-oxygen network in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. New lab methods let scientists map complex networks in cells. But such networks tend to be huge. Their size makes math analysis hard, and data for each link are scarce. One key network helps cells survive when oxygen is low. It is called the hypoxia response network.

The team strip the network down to its core parts. Those parts drive the response to low oxygen. A small core is far easier to model than the full map. Models of the core can predict cell behavior and guide drugs for cancer and stroke.
plos-pone-0008700:
Zhemin Zhou, Xiaomin Li, Bin Liu, and colleagues traced the family history of a dangerous gut germ. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper studies Escherichia coli O157:H7, a cause of severe food poisoning. A milder relative, O55:H7, looks like its ancestor. Dozens of E. coli genomes existed, yet close kin had not been compared in detail.

The team lined up the genomes of the two kinds side by side. Step-by-step changes show how the harmful clone emerged. New DNA arrivals and small edits both played a part. Knowing that path helps scientists read outbreak strains and guess how germs gain harmful traits.
plos-pone-0008800:
Geoffroy Berthelot, Muriel Tafflet, Nour El Helou, and colleagues charted the rise and stall of elite sports records. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The data covered more than forty thousand top performers. Seventy track, field, and swimming events spanned the modern Olympic era. A growth model fitted the long climb of best marks. Human performance, the team found, stopped climbing after a late peak.

Performances stagnated following the final peak around 1988. The plateau appears across many unrelated events. Such a broad stall hints at a true physiological ceiling. The analysis frames debate about technology, doping controls, and human limits.
plos-pone-0008900:
Ting Guo, Lin-Chen Gong, and Sen-Fang Sui proposed that fusion proteins prefer a sideways stance. Their modeling study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells merge membranes using SNARE proteins that zip together. Fusion is basic to secretion and nerve signaling. The exact steps of SNARE-driven merging stayed poorly understood. Speed matters most at synapses, where release is nearly instant.

Electrostatic forces favored a lateral orientation of the SNARE complex. A sideways start suggests fresh mechanisms for pulling membranes together. New geometry can explain fusion steps that upright models miss. The proposal gives experimentalists concrete predictions to test.
plos-pone-0009000:
Anne Wanders, Ingeborg Brouwer, and Els Siebelink fed volunteers a dairy fat and watched their blood fats, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fat, conjugated linoleic acid, is a trans fat made in the stomachs of cows and sheep. Industrial trans fats raise bad cholesterol and lower the good kind. Whether natural trans fats from dairy act the same way was unclear.

Healthy subjects took a high intake of the fat during the trial. The team measured lipoproteins, the particles that carry cholesterol in blood. Comparing before and after showed how this natural trans fat shifts the balance. The answer helps separate dairy fats from factory-made trans fats in diet advice.
plos-pone-0009100:
Charmaine Uys, Michelle Hamer, and Rob Slotow laid out a step plan for counting forest creepy-crawlies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Invertebrates are so diverse that conservation work usually skips them. Yet earthworms, millipedes, ants, and snails run the forest floor. South Africa's Afrotemperate forests were the test case.

No team can census every invertebrate species in a forest. The process picks stand-in groups whose diversity mirrors the whole. Each step checks that the chosen surrogates really track the rest. Good stand-ins let limited conservation money protect far more species.
plos-pone-0009200:
Shaomei Wang and co-authors published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It addresses retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited disease that slowly destroys vision. Patients first lose night vision, then side vision, and often central vision last. No effective treatment existed, apart from gene therapy that helped only a few patients.

The team tested a gentler idea: stem cell therapy given without surgery on the eye itself. They used a rat model that copies both the retinal decay and the blood vessel problems of the disease. A non-invasive treatment that works in rats would be far easier to offer patients. The study checks whether that approach can protect the retina.
plos-pone-0009300:
Hitomi Suzuki and co-authors published this mouse embryo study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Germ cells, which become eggs or sperm, must be set apart from ordinary body cells early in life. The protein NANOS3 is essential for mouse germ cells. Its production is controlled partly by the tail end of its gene message, the 3-prime UTR.

The team showed that this tail is required for NANOS3 to appear only in germ cells. Without the tail's control, the protein's pattern goes wrong. Such message tails act as address labels, deciding where and when a protein is made. The finding shows how embryos keep the germ line distinct from the body.
plos-pone-0009400:
Guilherme Roberto Zammar and co-authors published this research methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Modern clinical studies need both doctors and data specialists. Neither side fully understands the other's field. Statistics and clinical practice are each complex enough alone, and their meeting point creates friction.

The team qualitatively analyzed how data analysis specialists and novice clinical researchers interact. They watched where knowledge exchange broke down in interdisciplinary teams. Naming those breakdowns is the first step to fixing them. The study offers lessons for any field where experts must think together across a knowledge gap.
plos-pone-0009500:
Lina Fassi Fehri and colleagues traced a trick used by a stomach germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicobacter pylori can live in the stomach for life. In some people it leads to ulcers or stomach cancer. Infected tissue holds many regulatory T cells, which damp immune attacks. The team studied how the germ shapes those T cells.

The germ raised levels of a small RNA, miR-155, in T cells. It did so through a path that uses cAMP and the protein Foxp3. That path helps explain how the germ calms the immune system to survive. Blocking the trick could one day help the body clear a germ tied to cancer.
plos-pone-0009600:
Jong Hyun Kim and co-authors filled a gap in sugar control wiring in PLOS ONE in 2010. Muscles draw sugar from the blood when energy runs low. A protein called AMPK senses that low energy state. It starts a chain that brings sugar transporters to the cell surface. The team showed that an enzyme, phospholipase D1, carries the signal forward in muscle cells.

Without that enzyme's action, the AMPK signal did not lead to normal sugar uptake. With it, glucose entered the cells as it should. The link matters for diabetes, where muscle sugar uptake fails. It names a step that future treatments might aim to support.
plos-pone-0009700:
Wolbachia is a bacterium that lives inside insects and rewrites their breeding rules. Pablo Tortosa and colleagues measured how its numbers vary by age and sex in the Asian tiger mosquito. Their counts appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The bacterium spreads by causing cytoplasmic incompatibility, which blocks some matings from producing young. Density patterns across age and sex may show how the mosquito host pushes back over generations. That push and pull matters because Wolbachia is used to fight mosquito-borne disease. Knowing where the bacterium thrives helps those control programs work.
plos-pone-0009900:
Lab cell cultures can hide mycoplasma, tiny bacteria that quietly change experiments. Ekaterina Zakharova and colleagues showed how these invaders blunt immune responses in a standard cell line. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycoplasma lack cell walls, which makes them hard to spot.

The cells were THP-1, a human immune cell line used worldwide. Mycoplasma suppressed their TLR responses, the alarms cells raise against germs. Treatment with antibiotics corrected the suppression and restored normal responses. The warning is plain: hidden contamination can fake or hide results. The fix was as plain as a dose of drugs.
plos-pone-0010000:
The authors were Susan Twine, Mireille Petit, Kelly Fulton, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE vaccine study covered tularemia. That disease is caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis. A weakened live vaccine strain had protected people, yet safety worries kept regulators from licensing it. The team worked with an improved form of that strain in mice.

Using immunoproteomics, a method that maps which bacterial proteins mouse antibodies target, they charted the antibody response after vaccination. That map shows which parts of the germ the immune system actually sees and answers. Such maps can guide safer vaccine design and better tests for protection against a dangerous germ.
plos-pone-0010200:
Tarek Elnaccash and Stephen Tonsor combined two classic genetics methods in a 2010 paper. Recombinant inbred lines are plant or animal lines bred to mix two parents' genes in fixed patterns. Line cross analysis sums the overall genetic effects that separate two parental lines. Each method alone describes only part of a trait's genetic architecture, or overall pattern.

Wedding the two, in their phrase, raises the power to describe gene interactions. Their PLOS ONE paper presents that combined approach for other researchers. Better tools for gene interaction matter wherever traits, from crop yield to disease risk, depend on many genes at once.
plos-pone-0010300:
The authors were Viivi Majava, Eugenia Polverini, Alberto Mazzini, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study characterized a myelin protein from the peripheral nerves. Myelin is a tightly packed, layered membrane that insulates selected nerve fibers. It wraps axons in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. It also carries a specific set of proteins suited to that wrapping job.

The team made and purified the human protein P2 in the laboratory. They then described its structure and function in detail. Knowing P2's shape helps explain myelin stability and diseases where peripheral myelin breaks down.
plos-pone-0010400:
Noelia Madroñal and co-workers tested a memory molecule in learning rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. Lasting memory is thought to need lasting strengthening of synapses in the hippocampus, a brain area vital for memory. A protein called PKMzeta is a leading candidate for holding that strength. The team trained animals in a task linking a sound to a blink response. Learning itself raised synapse strength in the hippocampus.

Blocking PKMzeta then undid both the extra strength and the memory. That reversal, after learning had finished, is the key evidence. It suggests the protein actively maintains memories rather than just forming them. A maintenance molecule could be a target in memory loss diseases. It also raises hard questions about erasing unwanted memories.
plos-pone-0010500:
James Balhoff and a large team presented Phenex, a tool for recording trait diversity in a structured way, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biologists have long described species' traits in plain sentences. Those sentences record how traits evolved, but computers cannot easily compare them. Phenex lets researchers annotate traits using shared vocabularies called ontologies. Trait data then become searchable and computable across species.

Structured trait records can feed evolutionary trees and genetic databases alike. They also preserve expert knowledge in a form that will not rot. Building such tools is slow, unglamorous, and field-changing. Phenex aimed to bridge old natural history and new data science. This paper is its formal introduction to the community.
plos-pone-0010600:
Yan Coulombe and colleagues mapped how one mouse gene is switched on, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, Hoxa5, helps lay out the body plan during early development. Genes in the Hox family must turn on at the right place and time.

Hoxa5 turned out to be controlled by several starting points, not just one. The gene's messages were also cut and rejoined in different ways, making multiple versions. Each version appeared at its own stage or place in the embryo. That layered control helps explain how one gene can serve several jobs during growth.
plos-pone-0010700:
Shi Wang and colleagues described a strange family of jumping DNA in corals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MITEs are tiny DNA bits that copy and paste themselves around a genome, riding on enzymes made by larger jumping elements. They are common in plants and animals but poorly charted in corals.

In two coral genomes the team found a MITE group with features not seen before. The elements were plentiful and oddly uniform. Their spread must have been driven by a partner element the corals still carry. Stowaway DNA shapes how genomes grow, so these records help explain why coral genomes differ so much in size and layout.
plos-pone-0010800:
Carolin Brandl and colleagues studied dendritic cells that teach tolerance, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dendritic cells can start immune attacks or calm them, depending on their state. Half-mature dendritic cells favor calm, protecting tissue from needless attack. A surface molecule called B7-H1, also known as PD-L1, helps set that balance.

Cells lacking B7-H1 proved stronger teachers of tolerance than normal cells. They worked by waking a class of natural killer T cells restricted by the molecule CD1d. Those cells then reinforced the calm state. Removing one brake thus strengthened tolerance overall, a counterintuitive result with clear value for autoimmune disease research.
plos-pone-0010900:
Adiba Isa, Jan Nehlin, Hardee Sabir and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HLA molecules display a cell's contents to the immune system, and stem cells keep them low, which helps transplants avoid rejection. Whether all three classical HLA types follow the same schedule during development was unknown.

Using sensitive flow methods, the team compared human stem cells from bone marrow and fat, muscle progenitor cells, and blood cells. HLA-A sat at high levels on every cell type, but HLA-B was missing or barely present on the stem and progenitor cells, sparing them from antibody-driven killing in tests. Only a strong immune signal switched HLA-B fully on. Isa and colleagues show transplant-friendly invisibility is selective, not total, a detail that matters for judging the safety of stem cell therapies.
plos-pone-0011000:
Itzhak Ohad, Hagai Raanan, Nir Keren and co-authors published this desert microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biological sand crusts in deserts are held together by filamentous cyanobacteria such as Microcoleus, which photosynthesize in brief morning wetting by dew, then face drying under harsh light. Excess light destroys the photosynthetic machinery of most organisms, yet this one survives.

Field plots, both drying naturally and kept wet, showed the organism dimming its light capture as intensity rose. In the lab its photosynthesis kept running at light levels several times higher than needed to saturate it, even while standard stress signals suggested most of its photosystem was down. Ohad and colleagues argue that rapid internal changes in photosystem II act as a safety valve. The trick helps explain how desert crusts fix carbon in one of Earth's harshest light regimes.
plos-pone-0011100:
Bower and Johnston studied farmed Atlantic salmon in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their focus was muscle growth in young fish, and the gene signals that drive it. Food proteins and growth factors both tell muscle genes when to switch on, and the team traced how those signals interact.

The team mapped which growth genes respond to amino acids and to insulin like growth factors during muscle building. That map helps explain how feed turns into fish flesh. Better knowledge of growth control could improve fish farming and cut waste. It also supports more sustainable ways to produce protein for people.
plos-pone-0011200:
Van Sluis, Nieuwdorp, Kamphuisen and colleagues tested a blood thinner in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. A low weight form of heparin is widely used to prevent clots. In mouse cancer tests, the team asked whether it also blocks metastasis, the spread of tumors to new sites.

The drug did inhibit spread in the experiments. The team also checked whether the effect ran through a sugar layer on vessel walls, and found it did not. If the anti spread effect holds in people, a familiar drug could gain a second use in oncology. The negative result on mechanism saves others from a false lead.
plos-pone-0011300:
Gigante, Bennet, Leander and colleagues examined heart attack genes in men for PLOS ONE in 2010. One gene affects a receptor tied to clotting, another shapes an inflammation signal. Separately each may add modest risk. The team tested whether carrying variants in both raises the risk of heart attack more together.

The interaction between the two gene sets did increase risk in men. Gene gene interactions like this hide from studies that test one variant at a time. Cardiology can use such pairs to refine risk screening. The result also fits biology: clotting and inflammation jointly drive the events behind heart attacks.
plos-pone-0011400:
Miriam Nörder and co-authors examined in 2010 how a vaccine carrier virus itself reshapes immunity in mice. Modified Vaccinia virus Ankara is a weakened relative of smallpox that cannot copy itself in humans, so it is widely used to ferry vaccine material into the body. Designers usually credit the cargo for the immune effect, not the carrier.

The team showed the carrier alone exerts strong effects on the mouse immune system, steering which defenses wake up and how strongly. Knowing the carrier's own influence helps designers predict the full response to a vaccine built on it. It also opens a chance to use that influence on purpose, tuning vaccines for diseases where a particular style of immunity protects best. Ignoring the carrier, the paper warns, means missing half the vaccine's action.
plos-pone-0011500:
Betsy Von Holle, Yun Wei, and David Nickerson analyzed long records in 2010 and found Florida plants flowering later as climate varies. Wildflowers open on a seasonal schedule set by temperature and rain, and pollinators time their lives to that schedule. The team asked whether year-to-year climatic variability, not just steady warming, shifts when Floridian plants bloom.

Their analysis links greater climatic variability to later seasonal flowering across the plants studied. A delayed bloom can uncouple flowers from the insects that pollinate them and the birds that eat their seeds. Most climate studies track steady warming, so showing that wobble itself matters widens the picture of climate harm. For Florida's ecosystems, the paper is a local fingerprint of global change, measured in missed appointments between plants and the animals that depend on them.
plos-pone-0011600:
Robert Pool and co-authors tackled a measurement problem in HIV prevention trials, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trials of microbicide gels depend on honest reports about gel use and sexual behaviour. No gold standard exists for such data, so researchers must rely heavily on what participants say.

After reviewing the options, the authors propose mixing methods and cross-checking them against each other. Interviews, diaries and other measures are combined so that errors in one source can be caught by another. Trials using this triangulation model should get truer adherence data, which in turn makes their verdicts on new products far more trustworthy.
plos-pone-0011700:
Pawan Kaler and co-authors showed how colon tumours recruit bodyguards, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The team had earlier found that colon cancer cells provoke macrophages, a type of immune cell, to release a signal that boosts tumour growth. That created a self-amplifying loop favouring the cancer.

Here they show macrophages also protect colon cancer cells from TRAIL, a molecule that can trigger cancer cell suicide. The protection works through the same signal stabilising a protein called Snail inside tumour cells. Blocking that shield could make an existing class of cancer drugs work better.
plos-pone-0011800:
Sachin Gupte and co-authors studied vessel damage in a rat model of non-obese diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in diabetics, with a complex cause operating at several levels. Endothelial dysfunction and increased production of reactive oxygen species are believed to underlie much of the vascular trouble.

In Goto-Kakizaki rats, the team pinned a family of enzymes, NADPH oxidases, as a source of superoxide driving endothelial dysfunction. Naming that source reveals a target for protecting diabetic blood vessels before heart disease takes hold.
plos-pone-0011900:
Tao Huang and colleagues built in 2010 a method to predict which single-letter DNA changes are likely to cause harm. The changes of interest alter one amino acid in a protein, and they account for much inherited disease. Older prediction tools relied mostly on the protein's own sequence and structure.

The new approach adds the protein's interaction network, who it partners with in the cell, together with mixed sequence and structural features. A protein's neighborhood carries clues about how damaging a change will be, since hubs have more to lose. Better sorting of harmful from harmless variants helps doctors read a patient's genome without testing every variant in the lab.
plos-pone-0012000:
Melanie Norgate and co-workers tested in 2010 whether warm nectar attracts Australian stingless bees more on some days than others. Flowers that warm their nectar above the surrounding air can gain an edge with pollinators. The bee studied, Trigona carbonaria, is a native social species and an important local pollinator.

The team found that ambient temperature changes the bees' preference for warm nectar: a warm drink is worth more when the day is cool. That sliding scale makes sense for a small insect that must manage its own body heat. It also means flower warming is a signal whose value rises and falls with the weather, a detail pollination studies should not average away.
plos-pone-0012100:
Jérôme Toussaint, Virginie Durbecq, Sevilay Altintas, and colleagues wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about an early, contained form of breast cancer. This stage, often found by screening, does not always turn invasive, yet many patients still get strong treatment because doctors cannot tell which cases are risky. The team studied a protein on the support cells that wrap each milk duct.

When those support cells die back, a tumor may break out of the duct. Tumors with low levels of the protein's gene message behaved like the high-risk kind. A marker like this could one day help doctors spare low-risk women harsh treatment while acting fast on the cases most likely to spread.
plos-pone-0012200:
Karen Joyce, Paul Laurienti, Jonathan Burdette, and co-authors proposed a new way to find key nodes in brain networks, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brain scans can now be read as webs of connected regions, and some regions matter far more than others for keeping the web working. Existing measures of that importance each capture only part of what central means in such a network.

Their measure aims to rank brain regions by their true role in holding the network together. Better rankings help researchers spot the hubs whose damage would ripple widest, in stroke or Alzheimer's disease. They also give network science, used from brains to power grids, a sharper general tool.
plos-pone-0012300:
Allen Katouli and Natalia Komarova modeled drug combinations for chronic myeloid leukemia in PLOS ONE in 2010. Three targeted drugs had transformed this leukemia's treatment, but one mutation, called T315I, resists all three, and patients who develop it run out of options. New compounds able to beat that mutation were on the way, raising a planning question: how should old and new drugs be combined?

Their mathematical model searches for combinations and schedules that suppress resistant mutants best. Working this out on paper first guides real trials toward the most promising arms. In a disease where each mutation buys the cancer time, planning combinations before resistance emerges is the strategic move.
plos-pone-0012400:
Jun-xiang Yin, Jiang-long Tu, Hao-jie Lin and co-workers tested pertussis toxin in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. The model, called EAE, mimics the immune attack on nerve insulation seen in MS. Pertussis toxin is often used to trigger the model, yet its direct actions inside the brain were debated.

Given into the central nervous system, the toxin stopped microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, from migrating to the spinal cord and kept disease from spreading. The result separates the toxin's brain effects from its body-wide ones. It clarifies how a standard lab tool shapes the very disease model scientists use to test MS drugs.
plos-pone-0012500:
Keiko Uchida, Megumi Aramaki, Maki Nakazawa and colleagues removed calcium channel genes in mice to watch the heart form, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The channels, IP3 receptors types 1 and 2, release calcium inside cells to control vital processes, from heartbeat to secretion. Each type alone seemed partly dispensable, raising the question of what happens without both.

Mice lacking both types showed disturbed heart development, revealing a joint job in cardiogenesis that single knockouts hid. Calcium signals thus help sculpt the early heart. The finding informs research on congenital heart defects, where signaling faults are suspected but hard to prove.
plos-pone-0012600:
Pulit, Voight and de Bakker wrote about a blind spot in gene hunting in 2010. Almost all large gene studies up to then had used people of European descent only. Their PLOS ONE paper asks what changes when studies include people from many ethnic backgrounds at once.

They show that mixed-ancestry studies can find gene locations that single-group studies miss. Different groups carry different patterns of gene variants, and those contrasts add power. The message matters for fairness as well as science, since findings from one group may not fit all. Their work helped push gene research toward wider samples.
plos-pone-0012700:
Campanella, Colvin and Luster reported that a messenger protein can slow blood vessel cell growth without its usual partner. The protein, CXCL10, is made under interferon signals and normally calls activated T cells to a site. It usually works through a receptor called CXCR3 on the cell surface.

Their 2010 work found CXCL10 still curbed the growth of vessel-lining cells when that receptor was absent. A second route must therefore exist for this effect. Splitting the protein's jobs apart matters for drugs that aim to block or mimic it in disease.
plos-pone-0012800:
Akhtar, Schneider, Chapman and co-authors counted a vessel inflammation marker in injured kidneys without surgery. VCAM-1 rises on blood vessel walls when kidneys suffer ischemia reperfusion injury, the damage done when blood returns after a cut-off. It stays raised after flow is restored, making it a lasting sign of injury.

Their 2010 study used magnetic resonance imaging with targeted particles to measure VCAM-1 in living animals. A scan that reads injury directly could spare patients repeated biopsies. It could also let doctors test kidney treatments by watching the marker fall.
plos-pone-0341400: Rastrygina and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a web of protein interactions. One side of the web is the tumor necrosis factor superfamily, signals that guide immune cells. The other side is a set of small proteins called S100. Mapping how these two families touch each other can reveal joint roles in inflammation and cancer that single-protein studies miss.
plos-pone-0344600:
Haresh Rengaraj Rajamohan and co-workers teach medical image models to predict a disease's future while keeping their skill at spotting it now. Prognosis data are scarce, but diagnostic scans pile up in archives. Their 2026 study pre-trains models on large sets of knee, brain, and breast images labeled for current disease, then adapts them to forecast worsening years ahead.

Pre-training lifted forecast accuracy across all three diseases compared with standard starts. Plain fine-tuning, though, made models forget diagnosis, a safety risk in live clinics. Their step-by-step method with replay of old cases kept both skills at once, matching specialist models on prognosis while holding diagnostic accuracy. Hospitals could reuse the same trusted tool instead of juggling two.
plos-pone-0345500:
José Douglas Bernardino Domingos and colleagues surveyed more than three thousand undergraduates at four Brazilian public universities about their cooking skills, a habit that shapes diet quality long after graduation. Students answered a validated Brazilian questionnaire between late 2020 and early 2021, and the 2026 analysis linked skill levels to social and learning backgrounds.

About sixty-eight percent showed high cooking skills, with women scoring higher than men. Learning through classes helped, but so did teaching oneself from the internet, books, and television. Knowing cooking terms and having fruit and vegetables within easy reach both protected against low skill. The authors advise universities to target male students and hands-on, independent learning.
plos-pone-0345700:
Aleahmad and colleagues, in a 2026 study, catalog the fungi that live quietly inside eucalyptus trees across Iran. These inner fungi, called endophytes, can protect or harm their host, and no one had mapped them for this tree in Iran. The team asked whether climate or the tree itself shapes the fungal community more.

More than seven hundred fungal samples were grown from leaves, branches, and fruit in five provinces, from dry to humid. The humid north held the richest, most even community, while the driest province held the poorest. Dry sites were ruled by tough generalist fungi, while the humid site hosted more specialists. Within every climate, leaves held the most kinds, then branches, then fruit. Climate, the authors conclude, does the coarse sorting, and tissue type fine-tunes the result. They warn that a warming climate could thin these hidden partnerships.
plos-pone-0345900:
Adeniyi Abiodun Adewunmi and co-authors surveyed pregnant women across Lagos, Nigeria, in 2026 about tokophobia, a severe fear of childbirth. The fear can drive requests for surgery and harm mental health, yet local figures were lacking.

More than eight hundred women at flagship primary care centres answered a standard fear questionnaire plus mood and anxiety scales. The team modelled which factors travel with strong fear, including past births, mental state, and social traits. Naming how common the fear is, and in whom, is the first step toward antenatal support that treats dread as a clinical issue, not weakness.
plos-pone-0347000:
Xia Li read sixty policy documents from Shanxi, a less-developed province in central China, to see where officials aim their attention when backing new strategic industries. Attention is scarce in any government, and where it lands shapes which industries grow. The study sorted the documents by who issued them, which tools they used, and which themes they stressed, over fifteen years of policy.

Coordination between policy actors was weak, and officials leaned heavily on supply-side and environment-shaping tools rather than demand-side ones. Themes formed a pyramid, with broad foundations laid first and narrower priorities stacked later, a pattern the author calls foundation-first and gradient in layout. Handy for an early takeoff, the pattern risks crowding out fresh innovation and locking the province into old paths.
plos-pone-0347500:
Jennifer Deal and colleagues report a side analysis of the ACHIEVE hearing trial. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The main trial split nearly one thousand older adults into two groups. One group got hearing care. The other got health classes. This analysis asked if better hearing slowed physical decline over three years.

Standard tests timed walking, standing, and chair rises. Grip strength was measured too. The hearing group did no better overall than the control group. Hints of gain showed in those whose thinking was fading fastest. Those hints were not firm, though. The flat headline result tempers hopes for hearing aids alone. A sharper question remains for future trials.
plos-pone-0348200:
Sarah Z. Wang and colleagues fed newborn mice formula pre-digested by an enzyme cartridge to test protection against necrotizing enterocolitis, a gut disease that kills premature babies. Undigested fat in formula is a suspect driver. The cartridge clips onto feeding lines and splits fats into absorbable pieces before feeding, and a new prototype allows the frequent feeds infants need.

Disease was triggered in mouse pups with bacterial toxin and low oxygen. Pups on cartridge-digested formula showed milder sickness, healthier-looking guts, and less tissue damage under blinded scoring than pups on placebo-processed formula. The authors argue the device deserves study as a gentle preventive therapy.
plos-pone-0348500:
Amr Ahmed WalyEldeen and colleagues searched the blood of obese women with breast cancer for tiny packages called small extracellular vesicles, bubble-like parcels that cells shed and that can carry tumour fingerprints. They compared seventy-six patients who had not yet received chemotherapy with thirty-six similar women without cancer, cataloguing the proteins inside these parcels with sensitive instruments.

Two proteins, fibronectin and von Willebrand factor, stood out, alongside a partner protein enriched especially in the aggressive triple-negative form of the disease. Vesicles from those tumours even pushed mild cancer cells toward more invasive behaviour in the lab. The authors propose the protein pattern as a blood-based aid for diagnosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0348600:
Hashim Hussain, Shailendra Mishra, and Reem Alshenaifi designed a security architecture for connected medical devices that must resist both today's hackers and tomorrow's quantum computers. Hospital gadgets are small and weak, yet quantum machines threaten to break the encryption they rely on. Their 2026 design pairs quantum-proof cryptography with a zero-trust engine that scores each device's behavior and grants, watches, denies, or quarantines access accordingly.

Trained on six intrusion datasets, the detection engine scored near the top of standard accuracy measures, especially on modern device traffic. The quantum-safe handshake takes a few seconds, acceptable for routine vital-sign reports, alerts, and updates rather than split-second care. Tests removing single parts showed the data balancing step and the adaptive engine each earn their keep.
plos-pone-0348700:
Felipe A. Toro-Cardona and a team of colleagues asked why the American tropics hold so many treefrog species. Their 2026 paper tests three ideas about climate niches, the range of temperature and rainfall each species can tolerate. They estimated niches for four hundred forty-one treefrog species and mapped how those niches line up with where species are most numerous.

Places rich in species tended to hold frogs with narrow niches, packed closely together, and niches close to those of their ancestors. One result ran against expectation: richness rose where today's temperatures sat farther from ancestral ones. The findings support the idea that frogs diversify by specialising, rather than by tolerating everything.
plos-pone-0348800:
Edmond Tchiakpe and colleagues mapped the genetic variety of HIV and its drug resistance in Benin, using samples from patients on treatment before the country switched to the drug dolutegravir in 2019. Patients had been on therapy for at least a year. The team measured virus levels nationwide and sequenced the virus in those whose treatment was failing.

Sequencing covered the parts of the virus targeted by older drugs, letting the researchers name viral subtypes and spot resistance mutations. A pre-switch baseline like this is valuable: it shows how much resistance the old regimens left behind and which viral families circulate in Benin. That record helps judge whether the newer first-line treatment starts from a strong or shaky position.
plos-pone-0349100:
Restoring a broken column base in a historic Chinese house demands guesses about its original look, and wrong guesses erase heritage. Binghua Zhang and Yuze Dan tested mixed reality glasses as a guide, in this 2026 PLOS One case study of Yanling House in Fujian Province.

Twelve participants used a headset system that overlays digital models onto the real hall while they worked on the column bases. Ratings and interviews followed. Participants said the overlay helped them match the original appearance through direct visual comparison, fine adjustment, and easier discussion with teammates. The authors present the method as practical support for preserving traditional dwellings where records are thin.
plos-pone-0349200:
Shiman Lin and colleagues built a light-based alarm for the electrical faults that brew inside gas-insulated switchgear, the sealed metal boxes at the heart of substations. Tiny discharges inside are early warnings of failure, but electrical sensors struggle with interference. The team first recorded the glow spectrum of discharges in the insulating gas under many conditions, then chose a silicon light sensor matched to that glow.

Installed on real one hundred and ten kilovolt equipment, their optical system beat the standard electrical sensor's clarity by a clear margin. It could detect discharges below the level many utilities treat as the reporting floor. Because the sensor choice now rests on measured spectra rather than habit, the authors present a template for optical fault watching across the power grid.
plos-pone-0349300:
Ayu Omiya and colleagues tested a therapy that pulses magnetic fields through the arm to wake up muscles after nervous system injury. The open question was how strong the pulses need to be. Twenty healthy adults received stimulation of the biceps at two levels: one strong enough to make the muscle contract, and one below that level.

Only the stronger level helped. After it, elbow bending force and muscle activity rose, and brain-evoked muscle responses grew larger, a sign of a more excitable pathway. The weaker level changed nothing. For clinics, the finding sets a floor: stimulation that never contracts the muscle is unlikely to retrain it.
plos-pone-0349400:
Baijia Song examined bias in computer systems used to screen job applicants in 2026. Such systems promise speed and fairness, yet they can learn and repeat the inequalities buried in past hiring records.

Song proposes a layered framework that checks a hiring system at every stage, from the training data to long term career effects. It breaks bias into parts, tests fairness across each hiring stage, and tries to keep useful information while removing unfair signals. Tested on made-up hiring data, the approach cut gaps between groups on key fairness measures. The work is a design proposal, offered as a route to hiring tools firms can audit.
plos-pone-0349500:
Lilia Cinti and colleagues measured levels of a harmless virus, torquetenovirus, that nearly everyone carries, using it as a gauge of immune strength in sixty-four patients with advanced lung cancer. Patients starting immune checkpoint therapy, a treatment that releases the immune system against tumours, gave blood before treatment and again after three months, while healthy donors gave a single comparison sample.

Before therapy, patients carried far more of the virus than healthy people, a sign of weakened immunity. After three months the viral load fell to healthy levels, and the drop ran deepest in patients whose cancers responded. The authors propose the virus count as a simple stand-in for immune recovery during treatment, while calling for larger studies to confirm its worth.
plos-pone-0349600:
Laura Svanekjær and colleagues measured what the heart drug amiodarone does to circulation in healthy anesthetized pigs. Doctors give the drug for dangerous heart rhythms, but it can drop blood pressure, and its direct effects during a normal rhythm are poorly mapped. Twenty-five pigs received a standard dose through a vein while sensors tracked the heart and blood flow in detail.

Within half an hour, blood pressure fell by about a tenth and the heart's output dropped by roughly a quarter, driven by a slower heartbeat and smaller strokes. A measure of heart muscle squeeze also weakened. The detailed pressure and volume traces show the drop is not just wider blood vessels; the heart itself pumps less strongly.
plos-pone-0349700:
Zachary Elwell and co-authors published the protocol for OtoSurg One in 2026, a worldwide study of tonsil removal. It is the commonest children's surgery on earth, yet how results differ across countries is almost unknown. No results are reported yet.

The study will prospectively record why tonsils are removed, how, and where, then track major complications over thirty days. Readmission after tonsil surgery is not rare in rich countries, and deaths in poorer countries are suspected far higher but uncounted. A shared global registry is the study's real product, built to make those comparisons possible at last.
plos-pone-0349900:
Hela Ghali and co-authors checked whether doctors' overall gut feeling about a training course matches a detailed, criterion-by-criterion grading of the same course. Their 2026 study evaluated continuing medical education run by a Tunisian medical faculty across 2021 and 2022, gathering two hundred sixty-eight structured evaluations covering the periods before, during, and after each course.

Average satisfaction landed at just under four on a five-point scale, with about sixty-nine percent of respondents classed as satisfied. Gut feeling and criterion scores moved together significantly across every criterion, suggesting a warm overall impression does not hide design flaws. Satisfaction also varied with age, experience, academic ties, specialty, and course format. The authors say planners can trust headline satisfaction while still mining criteria for improvements.
plos-pone-0350100:
Amsawrah M Mohammed, Khaled Lotfy, and co-authors built a math model of waves moving through semiconductor material when light, heat, and particles all interact. Such effects matter in tiny electronic and light-based devices, where laser pulses heat the material and set charge carriers moving. Their 2026 model adds two twists: quantum effects that appear at very small scales, and extra mass movement driven by heat-linked concentration changes.

Equations for motion, temperature, carrier density, and the new concentration field were solved together for a simplified one-dimensional case. The quantum transport and heat-driven diffusion changed how fast waves faded, how they shifted, and how deep they reached. The authors offer the model as a tool for designing small devices and managing heat in laser-driven systems.
plos-pone-0350300:
Katherine A Mankelow and co-authors published a review plan in 2026 on digital exercise programs for people with breast cancer. Survivors often live with pain, fatigue, swelling, and stiff shoulders, while physiotherapy services are hard to reach. No results are reported yet.

The scoping review will map online or app based programs, before or after treatment, that include exercise aimed at movement and daily function. Searches will cover four major databases for peer reviewed English studies. Charting what exists, and for whom, is the needed first step before anyone can say whether digital rehab fills the access gap or merely sounds modern.
plos-pone-0350400:
Xin Zhou and colleagues checked, in rats, whether a common blood pressure drug changes how the body handles three newer diabetes drugs, since patients often take both. All four drugs cross paths with the same cellular pumps that move medicines through gut, liver, and kidney. Twelve groups of rats received the drugs singly and in pairs, with blood levels tracked by sensitive instruments.

The blood pressure drug, telmisartan, raised blood levels of two of the diabetes drugs, empagliflozin and henagliflozin, while slowing their clearance. Run the pairing the other way, two diabetes drugs lowered telmisartan levels. The team also showed the interactions at the gene level, with pump expression turned down in several organs. Rat results do not set human doses, but they flag pairs worth watching when both prescriptions sit on one chart.
plos-pone-0350800:
Yanan Zhu and colleagues in China ran a trial in 2026 on a routine nursing step after prostate surgery: taping the urine catheter to the body. Two hundred patients were split at random between taping and no taping after their operation.

Rates of bleeding and catheter infection were much the same in both groups, and no catheter fell out in either. Skin pressure injury at the catheter opening, though, hit nine taped patients against one untaped, and taping cost more. The authors call the habit low value care: extra cost and harm with no gain, and a step wards can safely drop.
plos-pone-0351300:
Qiaoning Chang and seven colleagues report a 2026 laboratory and animal study of a gut bacterium that may protect the intestine from a common feed toxin. The toxin, zearalenone, contaminates grain and damages the gut lining. The team tested whether a probiotic strain of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum, named GUANKE, could limit that damage.

In pig intestinal cells and in mice, the bacterium improved cell survival, lowered signs of oxidative stress, and calmed inflammatory signals. Treated mice kept healthier gut structure, with taller villi and better measures of intestinal function. Gene activity data pointed to a key inflammation pathway. The toxin switched it on, and the probiotic quieted it. That suggests a route for protecting livestock, and possibly people.
plos-pone-0351400:
Faezeh Rastgoo and co-authors outline in 2026 a critical study plan on healthy living among women in city outskirts, where services and incomes often lag. The plan uses a critical ethnographic method that questions power structures and lifts marginalised voices, following a named multi stage approach. Preparation steps and five main stages structure the fieldwork and analysis.

Researchers will first build primary records, then test early readings through dialogue with participants, then map wider system links behind daily habits. The aim is practical solutions for women's health that address history, society, money, and culture together, rather than blaming personal choices alone. No results are reported yet.
plos-pone-0351500:
Fredrick Mutisya and seven colleagues measure how well a pneumonia vaccine works in Kenyan practice. Their 2026 study uses a national sentinel platform spanning thirteen sites. The ten-valent pneumococcal vaccine had already cut pneumococcal disease in children. The question here was narrower: does vaccination protect against dangerously low blood oxygen in suspected pneumonia? Over thirty-five hundred children under five with fever and breathing signs were included.

Ninety-four percent were up to date with their pneumococcal shots. Hypoxemia meant oxygen saturation at or below ninety percent. The team compared vaccinated and under-vaccinated children, adjusting for age, sex, and year. Children with proven non-pneumococcal causes were excluded, sharpening the test. Trial efficacy often fades in the real world of missed doses and cold-chain gaps. A surveillance platform answering such questions from routine data gives Kenyan policymakers evidence priced for their own system, not borrowed from abroad.
plos-pone-0351700:
Doreen Nayiga and colleagues built a risk score to flag Ugandan children with sickle cell anemia whose brain blood flow runs dangerously fast, a warning sign for stroke. An ultrasound test can measure that flow, but machines and trained staff are scarce, so most children are never screened. The team gathered routine clinic and blood data from three hundred eighty-five children and checked each child's flow with the ultrasound.

About one child in twelve had the high-risk flow speed. Twelve ordinary measures, including age, red cell counts, pulse, nerve symptoms, and faithfulness to a protective drug, combined into the prediction model. A score built from data any clinic already collects could decide who gets the scarce ultrasound first, aiming the test at the children most likely to need stroke prevention.
plos-pone-0352100:
Correction notice: PLOS One has fixed errors in an earlier study of birch pollen. The original paper asked how air pollution changes birch pollen chemistry. It also measured the pollen's main allergy protein. This short notice appeared in 2026. It replaces one figure. It also rewrites three passages word for word.

One passage compares pollution levels across Krakow and a smaller city. Another corrects a result about leaf photosynthesis. A third fixes a finding about carbon markers in the trees. The corrected figure is supplied with the notice. Readers should use these new versions. The originals should no longer be cited.
plos-pone-0352200:
Victoria A Bensel led a team of seven authors on this 2026 scoping review of artificial intelligence for diagnosing spine problems. Searching six databases for studies from 2019 to 2024, they mapped tools that read MRI and CT scans for disc wear, narrowed spinal canals, fractures, and inflammatory disease, plus newer symptom-based systems.

Most studies reported favorable accuracy, especially scan-based tools for degenerative and inflammatory conditions. Yet methods varied widely and quality scores exposed weak handling of missing data and feature choices. Bensel calls the evidence promising but preliminary and scattered.
plos-pone-0352400:
Hellen Phiri and five colleagues test two plants used in Zambian folk medicine for diabetes, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Leaves of Bidens pilosa, a common weed, and Cucurbita moschata, a pumpkin relative, were extracted with alcohol and tested separately and in mixtures. The team measured their plant chemicals and antioxidant power, checked safety in rats, and gave the extracts to mice made diabetic with a standard drug.

Even at very high doses the extracts caused no deaths or behaviour changes in rats. In diabetic mice, one mixture — one part Bidens to two parts pumpkin leaf — cut blood sugar dramatically. The authors caution that mouse success is not human proof, but the traditional remedy has earned a closer look.
plos-pone-0352500:
Qin and colleagues built light AI detectors for apple leaf disease that run on small farm devices in a 2026 study. Leaf spots are small and backgrounds messy, which strains tiny models. Their design adds modules that recover fine detail and blend features across sizes, then prunes the model further for speed.

Early spotting of leaf disease protects yield, but cloud computing is not always available in orchards. A detector that runs on the device itself gives instant answers among the trees. The pruned version trades a little size for speed while aiming to keep accuracy. Such tools fit precision farming for growers without big computing budgets.
plos-pone-0352900:
Stefan Müller led a team of six authors mining grant peer review for bias, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Grant decisions shape whole careers, and review reports may carry gender and disciplinary biases. The team analyzed the content and sentiment of a very large set of review reports, numbering in the tens of thousands.

Müller's massive sample exposes where bias creeps into funding decisions and how large it is. Sentiment differences are subtle but powerful: slightly cooler language can sink a borderline proposal. Funders can use such findings to train reviewers, structure forms, or audit outcomes. Few studies reach this scale, so the work gives the science-of-science field firm ground on a question usually argued from anecdotes.
plos-pone-0353000:
Zhuang Xiong and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study on why retinoblastoma, the commonest eye cancer of early childhood, resists the drug carboplatin. Their focus is ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat oxidation that cancers can evade. Database analysis flagged a gene regulator called SALL1 as overactive in these tumors, and experiments traced its target.

SALL1 switches on a protective gene, MGST1, which mops up the oxidized fats that would otherwise trigger ferroptosis. Silencing SALL1 made tumor cells stop growing and start dying by ferroptosis, and in a drug-resistant cell line it restored sensitivity to carboplatin. Restoring MGST1 reversed those effects. The authors identify this two-gene axis as a candidate target for overcoming resistance in this childhood cancer.
plos-pone-0353100:
Jingjing Song, Jiaying Li, and Dan Li published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies Chinese university students and exercise adherence, sticking with regular physical activity. Two ideas sit upstream: gameful experience, the feeling of play and challenge in exercise, and exercise identity, seeing oneself as an exerciser.

The authors test a moderated chain mediation model, a chain of influences whose strength depends on other factors. Chains matter because motivation rarely works through one simple link. Campus health promoters trying to keep students active past the first enthusiastic month are the readers for this layered account.
plos-pone-0353300:
Mazher, Masood, and Arai validated an Urdu version of a questionnaire on callous traits in young people in a 2026 study. The traits, such as low empathy and shallow feeling, flag severe behavior problems. No checked Urdu version existed for Pakistani youth.

Translation and cultural fitting came first, then stability checks with bilingual youth, then structure tests in three hundred young adults.
