A shortened twelve-item form with two parts, callousness and uncaring, fit best. Scores related sensibly to measures of criminal attitudes and self-control. Clinics, schools, and courts in Urdu-speaking settings now have a sound tool for early spotting of these traits.
plos-pone-0353400:
Gemechu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test the root of an Ethiopian medicinal shrub as a painkiller and inflammation fighter. Standard pain drugs carry side effects that push the search toward plants. The team made a root extract with alcohol and water, checked its safety in rodents, then ran standard pain and swelling tests.

In a pain test that makes mice writhe, the extract calmed the response in step with dose, nearly matching aspirin at the highest dose. On a hot surface, the top dose kept mice comfortable longer, a sign of action in the brain and spine, not only at the sore spot. In rats with a swollen paw, the extract cut swelling almost as much as a standard anti-inflammatory drug. One purified compound from the root also fought swelling on its own. The authors back the plant's traditional use, with caution that animal results come first.
plos-pone-0353500:
Elaine Boosalis Toaddy and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its subject is the lower dental arch, the row of bottom teeth. The authors ask how pressures from the resting tongue, the lips and cheeks, and forces between teeth affect that arch.

Two problems are at stake: the arch collapsing inward and molars drifting toward the front of the mouth. The study is a preliminary one using a 3D finite element model, a computer simulation that divides a structure into small parts to test stresses. Orthodontists planning long-term tooth stability are the readers for this kind of mechanical evidence.
plos-pone-0354200:
Qiuyang Wei, Yuanchuan He, and Shijiang Chen model where a prized caterpillar fungus can live on the Tibetan Plateau as the climate warms, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The fungus, harvested for traditional medicine, grows only in cold, high country and is already classed as vulnerable. Using just over two hundred verified sightings, they built a habitat model checked against past conditions.

Altitude and rainfall in the warmest quarter proved the strongest predictors of suitable ground. Under a mid-century warming scenario, suitable habitat shrank overall but persisted at the highest elevations. The authors warn that harvest pressure on the remaining refuges could grow as lowland sites disappear.
plos-pone-0354600:
Qasrawi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, map how diet, body function, and daily life connect to heart and metabolic risk in adults with disabilities in Palestine. This group faces higher risk, but the pathways are tangled: disability can limit movement and shopping, which shapes diet, which shapes the body. The team surveyed about one hundred twenty adults and modeled the links statistically.

Risk signs were common: well over half were overweight or obese, and half ate too little of key nutrients. More severe disability went with less muscle and poorer diet quality. Eating enough of the right foods predicted both better body makeup and better daily function. Being active and being able to function went with less body fat, while long sitting time bent the effect of diet on waist size. Mental illness hurt diet quality specifically. The authors argue support must treat food, movement, and mind together.
plos-pone-0354700:
Arthur James and six colleagues ask whether France's national hospital discharge database can stand in for the detailed clinical score used to predict trauma survival, in this 2026 modeling study. The database covers every hospital in the country but lacks the bedside measurements the Trauma and Injury Severity Score needs. The team linked discharge records with full medical records for more than two and a half thousand severely injured patients at an academic trauma center.

A machine learning model fed with individual billing-style codes reproduced the severity score well, explaining most of its variation. A physiology score available in both sources did most of the work, helped by codes for shock, coma, and anatomical injuries, though the two sources agreed poorly on shock and coma themselves. The authors say the method opens the door to nationwide trauma quality monitoring in France without new data collection.
plos-pone-0354800:
Charles Obeng and three colleagues survey residents of Bolgatanga Municipality in Ghana's Upper East Region about why they prefer one kind of primary care facility over another, reporting in 2026. Patients there can choose among facility types, including small community compounds close to home. Nearly four hundred residents answered structured questionnaires, and the team modeled which factors actually swayed their choices.

Perceived quality of care mattered, but convenience mattered at least as much. Distance and location, transport options, waiting time, and the chance of getting an appointment all shaped preferences, and higher costs pushed people away. Community compounds near home stayed essential for residents with little money. The authors advise managers to cut waits, ease transport and cost barriers, and lift quality if they want facilities used fairly.
plos-pone-0354900:
Sundarapandiyan S and Nandhini S model in 2026 a service queue where customers arrive in groups and may have to try again later if the server is busy. Some arrivals give up at once, others wait in a retry pool, and service happens in two stages with a chance of a repeat second stage. When the retry pool empties, the server slows down rather than stopping.

Using extra variable methods, the authors derive formulas for average line length and retry pool size. Worked examples show how giving up, slower vacation service, and two stage service change those averages. Managers of such systems can use the results to tune staffing.
plos-pone-0355100:
A A B D P Abewardhana, Rubasin Gamage Niluka Lakmali, and Paolo Vincenzo Genovese published this 2026 modeling study of ISIS-linked attacks between 2012 and 2019. Drawing on the Global Terrorism Database, they gridded past incidents and trained a random forest model to map where attack intensity had concentrated, rather than to forecast new attacks.

The model reproduced the historical pattern closely. The authors present a repeatable mapping routine for exploring how attacks cluster in space and for testing planning scenarios. They are explicit that the tool suits retrospective analysis, not real-time prediction of terrorism.
plos-pone-0355200:
Yu Yi and co-authors follow in 2026 older adults in China to see whether blood fat patterns predict diabetes combined with kidney disease. They used a national ageing survey and compared a single fat index with a version added up over time. Models accounted for many common health factors, and a separate look covered people who already had diabetes.

Both measures linked to new cases of the combined condition, with a steady rise as values climbed. The long term measure picked out risk somewhat better than the single reading. The authors suggest tracking fat patterns over years could help flag people who need closer checks and earlier care.
plos-pone-0355300:
Sobia Siddiq and colleagues review in 2026 hospital records for stroke patients under fifty in the United Arab Emirates, a group where local data were scarce. Charts came from one large hospital in Sharjah over several years and covered background, other illnesses, stroke type, treatment, and outcome. Most patients were men, and many came from South Asia.

Blocked artery strokes were most common, followed by bleeding types. High blood pressure and diabetes were the leading other illnesses, yet clot busting and clot removal treatments were rare. About one in eight patients died. The authors urge prevention aimed at changeable risks and more region specific study.
plos-pone-0355400:
Roy Ruddle presents in 2026 a visual method for exploring where data are missing and why the gaps may form patterns. Missing values can bias results if their shape is ignored, yet tangled gaps are hard to grasp from tables alone. His approach adds new purity scores for three basic gap shapes and pairs them with seven linked views.

Trials on a public dataset and on a huge hospital dataset showed the value. Tiny hidden flaws surfaced in the small set, and hundreds of thousands of gap mixes in the hospital data shrank to a short list of clear patterns. An explanation graph records each step for others to check.
plos-pone-0355600:
Negin Faraji and five colleagues map the non-coding RNA circuitry of HIV that drugs fail to control in this 2026 computer study. Using public gene expression datasets, single-cell data from infected people's immune cells, and checked interaction databases, they built networks linking circular RNAs, microRNAs, and ordinary genes involved in immunity. The goal was candidate biomarkers and drug targets for patients whose virus is not suppressed.

Single-cell analysis showed sweeping gene changes in both major T-cell types. Five hub genes sat off-kilter across them, two switched up and three down, all tied to infection-relevant pathways. The assembled network proposed specific three-part chains, with named circular RNAs sponging up microRNAs that would otherwise restrain key genes. The authors stress these are predictions for laboratory follow-up, offering a shortlist rather than proven mechanisms.
plos-pone-0356000:
John Martin Tumwebaza and colleagues counted bad drug effects in patients on antipsychotic drugs at a Ugandan referral hospital. Such effects drive costs, harm, and death, yet local rates were not well known. Their 2026 study spoke with more than four hundred clinic patients who had used the drugs for at least a month.

More than six in ten patients had at least one bad effect. Sleepiness and sedation were the most common, and most effects rated as mid-level in strength. Risk ran higher for patients split from a spouse. It also ran higher for those with bipolar illness, and for those who got both shots and pills. The team urges closer watch on these groups, plus drug experts on ward teams.
plos-pone-0356100:
Yonghong Li and colleagues used genes to ask if blood fats help cause a painful womb-linked illness. In endometriosis, tissue like the womb lining grows in the wrong places. Plain studies get tangled by lifestyle, so the team used inborn gene marks as a natural test.

Genes that push blood fats up also came with a small rise in illness risk. The team flagged seven genes that fat-lowering drugs act on. Three of them ran more hot in tissue from sick women. The genes cluster in fat transport, cell grip, and blood vessel growth. Two hormone-linked switches seem to run most of them. Li and colleagues say the paths need lab and clinic checks, not new care yet.
plos-pone-0356200:
Ming Guo and Yan Liu predict which online game players are about to quit, using the social fabric of the game itself, in this 2026 study. Most churn models look only at a player's own behavior, yet players are tied to each other in overlapping ways. The authors built two networks from a real game: declared friendships and the implicit ties between teammates who fight computer opponents together.

They compressed each network into numerical fingerprints that capture a player's position at several scales, then combined those with behavior data for classification. The combined model predicted churn with accuracy above ninety percent and clearly beat models using only one kind of relationship. Extra tests confirmed the two social layers reinforce each other. For game operators, the message is that a player's friendships and teammates signal their loyalty as loudly as their play habits.
plos-pone-0356800:
Yao Zhou led a team of eight authors who checked the real-world safety of a cancer drug called eribulin, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug is used for advanced breast cancer. Trials before approval enroll selected patients, so safety in everyday care can look different once many more people receive the drug.

Zhou's team mined a large database of adverse event reports from routine practice. The signals they found either support what trials showed or raise new points for doctors to watch. Oncologists weighing this drug for a frail patient gain a fuller picture of its risks. Real-world checks like this are now a standard part of judging any cancer drug.
plos-pone-0357000:
Pourya Mohammadipour, Hiwa Farughi, and Hasan Rasay build a decision model that runs factory maintenance and production together instead of apart. Modern sensors let managers watch machine wear in real time, yet upkeep delays and fixed demand complicate the best move each period. Their model treats each period as a choice point: fix early, repair after failure, or set the production pace, with costs counted over a fixed horizon.

Solving the model with a standard step-by-step method yields clear rules for when each action pays. A worked example and a case study compare the joint approach against fixed-pace production and simpler upkeep rules. Mohammadipour and colleagues argue that joining the two decisions trims total cost while keeping machines reliable.
plos-pone-0357100:
Jianjun Wang leads a team of eight using fractal geometry to read city soils for sponge city construction, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Sponge cities are designed to soak up stormwater like a sponge, and design depends on how local soil grains are sized and arranged, which governs infiltration and storage. The team measured particle sizes across a study area, summarized each sample with a fractal dimension, and mapped how that number varies with depth and place using geostatistics.

Silt dominated the soils, and the fractal values clustered in a moderate band with a clear spatial pattern that standard models fitted well. From the fractal measure the authors built curves predicting how soil holds and releases water, the key input for drainage design. Their three dimensional maps turn scattered borehole samples into a planning surface. The method offers other cities a shortcut from soil sampling to water aware design.
plos-pone-0357500:
Jing Wang, Yuxiao Yang, and Fei Chen use eye tracking to see how warning students about a coming test changes the way they watch subtitled video. The learners were Chinese students of English, split into a group told about the test ahead and a group not told. Cameras recorded where eyes rested on subtitles while vocabulary size and working memory were also measured.

Warned students looked at subtitles longer and more often, and then scored higher on questions about the video. Each glance, though, lasted about as long in both groups, so effort per glance barely moved. Among warned students only, stronger memory and vocabulary linked to less subtitle leaning. Wang and colleagues say a simple test warning is a cheap teaching lever for video lessons.
plos-pone-0357600: Yu and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on deep learning for heart scans in children born with heart defects. The software outlines heart parts in CT images, a task called segmentation. As a systematic review, the study gathers past work and judges how far the tools have come. Accurate outlines help surgeons plan repairs on small, complex hearts.
plos-pone-0357900:
Kaitlyn M Miller and four colleagues studied repeated pesticide exposure in rats, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Farmworkers meet the pesticide malathion again and again at low doses, and muscles and nerves may pay the price over time. The team gave rats repeated occupational-style exposures and tracked what changed.

Miller's group measured performance changes and alterations in the neuromuscular system. Their findings size up what chronic low-dose exposure does to strength and nerve function. Safety limits for pesticides often rest on single high-dose tests, which miss this pattern. Evidence from repeated exposure helps regulators judge real working conditions, and helps doctors know what to watch for in exposed workers.
plos-pone-0358600:
Mahbuba Begum led a team of eight authors who measured natural radioactivity at a gas field in Bangladesh, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Gas extraction can bring naturally radioactive material to the surface with the fuel. At the Fenchuganj field, the team assessed radiation levels and built the standard hazard indices from them.

Begum's group also set out management guidelines based on what they found. Those guidelines tell regulators and site workers where the real risks lie and how to limit exposure. Communities near gas fields deserve such checks, since the hazard is invisible. A measured local assessment replaces both complacency and panic with numbers that can guide action.
plos-pone-0358700:
Haoran Wu led a team of six authors reviewing how cars judge driver readiness, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In conditional self-driving, the car handles the road until it asks the human to take over. That handover is only safe if the driver is alert and ready at that moment.

Wu's group surveyed the methods cars use to read driver state, from eye tracking to steering patterns. Their review maps which tools best detect drowsiness and distraction, and where the gaps remain. Carmakers and regulators can use that map to set standards for handovers. As partly automated cars spread, this quiet technology may prevent many crashes.
plos-pone-0359100: Matsuoka and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on older patients after stomach cancer surgery. They asked what later problems after the operation mean for survival. Complications can hit older patients harder and slow their recovery. Knowing which complications most affect outlook helps surgical teams watch for them, act early, and talk honestly with families about risk.
plos-pone-0359300:
Sarra Ayouni, Maha Sliti, Abeer Alghanem, Fatimah Alhayan, and Mohamed Maddeh published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works on wearable activity monitoring, where wrist or body sensors record movement. The authors present a feature selection method, a way to choose which sensor signals matter, that is compact, target-aware, and stability-based.

The test is cross-dataset: a method tuned on one group of wearers must still work on another. Choosing fewer, steadier features can make activity recognition cheaper and more reliable on real devices. Engineers building fitness trackers and health monitors are the audience for selection methods that survive a change of dataset.
plos-pone-0359400: Huang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on finding flaws on factory surfaces with very few examples. Their network learns from a handful of defect photos by matching new images against stored prototypes. Attention at several scales helps it catch both tiny and large flaws. Inspectors often have few samples of rare defects, so methods that learn from little are valuable.
plos-pone-0360300:
Lei Wang and Xiaowei Zhang drew in 2026 on a big national survey of Chinese life, run in 2021, to study media habits and action against pollution. The survey lets them link what media people use with what those people do. Do they report pollution? Do they join efforts to stop it?

Their study asks which kinds of media use move people from knowing to acting, and in which groups the link is strong. The answer matters for public agencies. They spend large sums on campaigns that may inform the public without moving it to act. Sound survey evidence can show whether campaigns should spread facts, build social norms, or open clear paths for citizens to report and take part.
pmc-12418700:
Fettiplace and colleagues report a modified Delphi study on disclosing artificial intelligence use in scientific writing. The work was done for regional anesthesia and pain medicine publishing. AI tools can polish language and speed editing, the authors note, but they can also make things up, carry bias, and blur who is to blame.

A steering group ran two survey rounds with authors, reviewers, editors, and AI researchers. Focused talks followed. The group agreed on what AI means here, what must be reported, and where reports belong. It also agreed on authorship rules. Reviewers gained guidance too, including checklists and support for detection software. The aim is openness, with human duty for the work kept intact.
pmc-13241400:
Yen and colleagues at Brunel tested whether a simple Happy to Chat badge nudges strangers toward friendlier contact. A nationally representative online sample of one thousand seven hundred thirty-eight English adults took part. Respondents rated badge wearers for friendliness, trust, and openness. They also reported likely gestures like smiling and eye contact.

Badge wearers were judged significantly friendlier, more trustworthy, and more open to conversation. They attracted more smiles, nods, and eye contact in the scenarios. Yet stated intention to actually start a chat did not rise significantly. Older and female targets drew warmer responses overall.
pmc-13241700:
Davoudi-Monfared's team in Iran report granulomatous mastitis in a young woman defying every usual risk profile. The 26-year-old had autism and two decades of psychotropic medication behind her. She had never been pregnant and took no birth control. Her prolactin level sat well within the normal range.

Her right breast hardened and reddened; scans found organized fluid pockets. Core biopsy showed the trademark inflammation without any cancer. Antibiotics, steroids, and anti-swelling drugs cleared the breast fully within six months. The authors float long-term drug immune effects as a possible factor, though with care. The case had none of the usual triggers.

The self, he argues, is not a thing but a meaning: a life-plan interpreted within a larger consciousness. A Critical Exposition of the Philosophy of Leibniz, published in 1900, made Russell's name in philosophy. He read the German thinker through the new logic he was mastering, and found a system of surprising rigor beneath the metaphysics.

Russell argues that Leibniz's whole philosophy flows from his logic of subject and predicate and his theory of relations. The monads, the pre-established harmony, the best of possible worlds: all are traced to a few premises. The reading was contested, and it founded the analytic style of writing philosophy's history. Few first books in philosophy have carried this much consequence.

Interpretations of Poetry and Religion, published in 1900, was Santayana's first book, written while he taught at Harvard. Its essays argue one thesis from many sides: that poetry and religion are twin expressions of the imaginative life.

Religion, at its best, is poetry that has taken hold of conduct; poetry, at its deepest, is religion stilled into contemplation. Essays on Dante, Browning, and Emerson apply the idea with finesse. The young Santayana already writes in the serene manner of his maturity. The book announced a philosopher who would treat faith with an outsider's love and an insider's ear.

Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling published his System des transcendentalen Idealismus in 1800, at the age of twenty-five. The German first edition is the text here, since no public-domain English translation of the work exists. Schelling had been Fichte's brilliant young ally, and this book marks his step beyond the master.

The System traces how the self builds its world, stage by stage, from raw feeling to full awareness. Nature, in Schelling's hands, is mind made visible, and art becomes the highest proof of the whole scheme. His nature-philosophy and identity system form the bridge from Fichte to Hegel in German thought. The book's daring still draws readers who brave the German.

Mary Stuart, Schiller's tragedy of 1800, reached English in Joseph Mellish's translation of 1801. Mary, Queen of Scots, sits imprisoned in England while her cousin Elizabeth weighs her fate. Schiller imagines a meeting between the two queens that never took place in life.

In that meeting pride defeats mercy, and Mary's death is sealed. Around the queens, lovers, plotters, and counselors pull the state toward the scaffold. Mary walks to her death with a calm that rebukes her judges. Schiller gives both queens full humanity, which keeps the play from taking sides cheaply. It remains the classic drama of two women, one throne, and the price of power.

Shaftesbury wrote philosophy as a gentleman writes letters: polished, witty, and allergic to gloom. He defends free humor against religious panic, and a common sense of mankind against lone system builders. His Soliloquy teaches the writer to hold a dialogue with his own soul. Here the moral-sense doctrine stands complete: virtue is a natural harmony of the affections, known by an inner sense. Shaftesbury sets that doctrine in scenes of friendship, countryside, and dawn light that glow with feeling. Hutcheson took the teaching into the schools, but Shaftesbury gave it beauty first. Volume two is the heart of the Characteristics, and of his influence on the century.

Two pairs of young lovers flee Athens and get lost in the trees. Fairy king Oberon and his sprite Puck tangle their loves with a magic flower. Meanwhile workmen rehearse a crude play that turns to pure farce. Dawn sorts the loves aright, and a triple wedding ends the night. Dreams, desire, and theater itself are the play's glad themes.

Spirits of rice and river, charms, divination, and the craft of the pawang, the village magician, fill his classic study. Skeat gathered much of it at first hand, sitting with practitioners and recording their rites.

Birth, marriage, sickness, and harvest all pass under the pawang's art in these pages. Skeat writes as a scholar-adventurer, precise about what he saw and heard. His book remains the classic English account of Malay magic and the beliefs woven through Malay daily life.

Edgar, a retired captain, and Alice, a former actress, mark twenty-five years of marriage in a fortress tower. Isolated on their island, they tear at each other with memories, lies, and a practiced, intimate cruelty daily. Alice's cousin Kurt arrives and is drawn into their dance as witness, judge, and near victim himself. Edgar's heart scares, Alice's plots, and a dance to death's music bind the pair they cannot leave. Part Two turns to the young, who risk repeating the dance in the next generation.

What the record certifies is the work itself: creation hymns, wedding songs, and battle prayers that anchor Hindu worship to this day. No older scripture of a living faith survives in such bulk.
tolstoy-resurrection-maude-1900:
Louise and Aylmer Maude published their authorized translation of Leo Tolstoy's Resurrection in 1900. Resurrection was Tolstoy's last novel, written after his religious crisis had changed his view of art and society. The Maudes, friends of Tolstoy, worked with his approval on many of his books.

Prince Nekhludov serves on a jury and finds the accused is a woman he wronged in his youth. Guilt drives him to follow her into Siberian exile and to question land, courts, and church. Tolstoy used the plot to attack the systems he thought crushed the poor. The novel's force lies in that moral charge as much as in its story.
trevisanvs-de-chymico-miracvlo-qvod-lapi: Dionysius Zacharius wrote of the chemical miracle in this 1600 edition. The philosophers' stone treatise, reprinted. The Latin alchemy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This book preserves that work. Kept for readers. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
un-ga-res-1000:
Blueprint became command in Resolution 1000, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 5 November 1956. A day before, the Secretary-General had been told to draft a plan for an emergency force to halt the Suez fighting. His first report was now in hand. The Assembly acts on it at once, in the depths of the crisis over Egypt.

A United Nations Command is set up for the emergency force. Its task: secure and oversee the halt to fighting, on the terms of the cease-fire call of 2 November. Major-General E. L. M. Burns, chief of staff of the UN truce body in Palestine, takes command. He may draw officers at once from the truce observer corps, barring nationals of the five big powers.
un-ga-res-500:
Trade can be a weapon too, and Resolution 500, adopted by the General Assembly on 18 May 1951, turns it on the foes in Korea. A special team had weighed fresh steps to meet the attack in Korea, after the Assembly's vote of 1 February 1951. Some states had already acted to deny goods that fed the strength of the forces fighting the UN.

The team found that wider trade steps would back the fight and help end the attack. So the Assembly urges every state to place a ban on shipments to the areas held by the Beijing government and by North Korea. The ban covers arms, war goods, and the raw stock from which war strength is built. The vote was the trade arm of the Korean War.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1000 (ES-I) was adopted on 5 November 1956, during the Suez crisis. It set up a United Nations Command for an emergency international force. The force was to secure and watch over the end of fighting. It was to act on the terms the Assembly had laid down in resolution 997 (ES-I) two days before.

The Assembly named the Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization as the force's chief. He was named on an emergency basis. He could at once draw officers from that observer corps. With the Secretary-General, he could also recruit more officers. They would come from member states other than the permanent members of the Security Council.

General Assembly Resolution 500 (V), adopted on 18 May 1951, added economic pressure to the United Nations war effort in Korea. The Assembly acted on its Additional Measures Committee's report. It held that cutting off war goods to the forces fighting the United Nations would back the military action and help end the aggression.

Every state was urged to bar shipments to areas held by the Chinese and North Korean authorities. The ban covered arms, war gear, atomic energy materials, oil, and key transport goods. States were to police their own exports and stop cheating on others' controls. They were to work together and report their steps within thirty days. The drive for a peaceful settlement went on.
un-sc-res-100:
Works in a demilitarized zone between Israel and Jordan troubled the truce in 1953. Construction had begun on 2 September in the zone near the Jordan River. The truce chief of staff reported on the dispute in October. On 27 October 1953 the Council said the works should pause. A pause would let the Council study the question with care. It would not prejudice either side's rights or claims.

Israel's representative told the Council his government would suspend the works. The Council noted that pledge with satisfaction. It relied on the chief of staff to report whether the pledge held. The dispute concerned a planned hydroelectric project at Bnot Yaakov. Water, as often in the region, sat at the heart of the quarrel.
un-sc-res-1300:
The Golan observer force was renewed in May 2000 on standard terms. On 31 May 2000 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 30 November 2000. The Secretary-General had reported on the force eight days earlier. The Council noted United Nations work to protect peacekeepers from disease. The mission's shape stayed the same. Its observers manned the line set after the 1973 war.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. A closing report was due at the term's end. It would describe events and steps taken toward 338. The vote came as Israel completed its Lebanon withdrawal. Attention shifted, but the Syrian front stayed quiet under UNDOF's watch.
un-sc-res-1400:
UNAMSIL was extended through Sierra Leone's elections on 28 March 2002. The Mano River Union presidents had met in Rabat on 27 February. The state of emergency had been lifted, and disarmament stood complete. Refugee numbers across the region were swelling, and their plight caused concern. Election preparations by the government and the electoral commission were moving ahead.

The Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for six months from 30 March 2002. Troop-giving states won thanks for their service. The mission's 2002 concept of operations, set out in the Secretary-General's report of 14 March, was welcomed. The government and the Revolutionary United Front were urged to carry out the ceasefire and peace terms in full. They had to deepen dialogue and national reconciliation. The Council noted the funding gap in the trust fund for disarming and reintegrating fighters. Building the government's own capacity was named essential to lasting peace.
un-sc-res-1500:
The matter of Iraq was settled for the Council in Resolution 1500, adopted on 14 August 2003 by fourteen votes to none, with one abstention. Iraqis had formed a Governing Council on 13 July 2003. The United Nations needed staff on the ground to support the political path ahead. The Secretary-General had laid out a mission plan that July.

The Council welcomes the Governing Council as a step toward a recognized Iraqi government. It creates the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, called UNAMI. The mission starts with a twelve-month term. Its job is to back the Secretary-General's mandate under the post-war framework. That work spans aid, rebuilding, and help with the move to elected rule.
un-sc-res-1600: Resolution 1600 opens a new hundred in the Security Council's sequence, adopted in 2005. The text kept here follows the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Its structure rewards attention: concern stated, facts recalled, and then the decision itself, which is the part with legal force for the states it addresses.
un-sc-res-1700:
Iraq's United Nations assistance mission was renewed by the Security Council on 10 August 2006. Iraq's foreign minister had written on 3 August that the elected government still saw a vital role for the mission. The United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI, had been set up in August 2003. The Council stressed that national dialogue, which UNAMI should assist, is crucial to Iraq's stability and unity.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve months from the date of the resolution. It said it would review the mandate within twelve months, or sooner if Iraq's government asked. The Secretary-General had to update the Council regularly on progress in Iraq. The text welcomed the United Nations role as co-chair of the International Compact of Iraq, launched on 27 July 2006. The compact aimed to tie international support to Iraq's own programme for peace and prosperity.
un-sc-res-1900: Resolution 1900, adopted in 2010, opens the Council's 1900s run in this collection, preserved through English Wikisource. The act follows the long-settled form: a preamble weighing the situation, operative paragraphs settling the response. Its placement at a round number makes it an easy landmark in the sequence the collection preserves number by number.
un-sc-res-2000:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2000, adopted on 27 July 2011. The post-election crisis had ended, and the elected president had taken office on 21 May. Grave abuses during the crisis still needed investigation. Armed ex-guards, militias, and escaped prisoners kept the security picture shaky.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the peacekeeping mission, called UNOCI, until 31 July 2012. Its strength stays at 9,792 troops and 1,350 police, plus 205 added police advisers. The mission guards civilians, watches the arms embargo, and collects stray weapons. It backs a fresh disarmament program and deep reform of the security forces. Legislative polls, the first since 2000, must be certified as free and fair.
un-sc-res-300: An official UN record text, Resolution 300 is catalogued in this library with a 1971 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-400:
Security Council Resolution 400, adopted on December 7, 1976, recommended Kurt Waldheim for a second term as Secretary-General. Catalog copies dated 1978 are off by two years. Waldheim, a former Austrian foreign minister, had held the post since 1972. China had opposed his first term bid at first, but by 1976 the council settled on him with little open strife.

The Assembly confirmed him, and he served until the end of 1981. His decade at the top covered the end of the Vietnam War, Middle East crises, and Africa's wars of liberation. Later claims about his wartime past, raised after he left office, cast a long shadow over that record.
un-sc-res-800:
Security Council Resolution 800, adopted on January 8, 1993, recommended Slovakia for membership in the United Nations. Eight days earlier, Czechoslovakia had split by agreement into the Czech Republic and Slovakia, a parting so calm it gained the name Velvet Divorce. Neither half kept the old state's seat, so both applied as new members.

The Assembly seated Slovakia on January 19, the same day as the Czech Republic. The council's brief text records a rare event in the life of nations: a country dividing by talks rather than war, with both successors welcomed at once. For Slovakia, the vote marked its first seat of its own in the world body.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Digging in a no-go zone sparked a sharp clash in 1953. Work had begun on 2 September in the demilitarized strip between Israel and Syria. The strip sat by the Jordan River's headwaters. UN truce staff sent a report on 23 October. Resolution 100 passed with no dissent on 27 October 1953.

The Council said the works should pause. The pause would last while the case was probed with care. Israel's envoy told the room his state would halt the work. That pledge was noted with warmth. The truce staff's chief had to confirm the halt had in fact come. The text took care to guard each side's claims. No rights were judged; the diggers simply had to stop while the Council looked.

Spring of 2000 brought one more Golan renewal. The chief's report of 22 May set out a calm scene. UNDOF's term was near its end. The force had kept the Israel-Syria line still since 1974. Resolution 1300 passed on 31 May 2000.

The mandate grew by six months, to 30 November 2000. The Council called on both sides to act on the 1973 text at once. A report was due when the term closed. It would tell of events and steps toward a peace. A fresh clause in this text stands out. The UN's push to school its peace staff on health risks won a warm note. HIV and other ills were now a named care in each such file.

Sierra Leone's move from war toward elections fills Resolution 1400, adopted on 28 March 2002. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, had helped lift the state of emergency and finish disarmament. Peace talks in the wider Mano River region were moving ahead, though refugees were growing in number and the situation stayed fragile.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months from 30 March 2002, including help for the vote then being prepared. It welcomes the deal for a Special Court for Sierra Leone and backs UNAMSIL giving that court office support. It urges the government to restore its authority across the country, above all in diamond areas, and presses for funds for fighter reintegration and for the planned Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Iraq was under foreign occupation when Resolution 1500 passed on 14 August 2003. Fourteen members voted yes. Syria abstained. The invasion had toppled Saddam Hussein months earlier. A Governing Council of Iraqis had formed on 13 July 2003. The Council welcomed it as a step toward a sovereign, elected government.

The resolution created UNAMI, the UN Assistance Mission for Iraq. It would run for an initial twelve months. Its job was to support the Secretary-General's work in the country. That work followed the plan in his report of 15 July 2003. It covered aid, rebuilding, and help toward self-government.

Côte d'Ivoire's peace process gets one more month of cover on 4 May 2005. Ivorian parties had signed the Pretoria Agreement in April 2005, adding to the Linas-Marcoussis and Accra deals. The African Union, the regional bloc ECOWAS, and the United Nations were all working to get the agreements carried out.

All parties are called on to implement the Pretoria Agreement fully and to ensure a safe setting for the steps ahead, including elections. The mandate of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, and of the French forces supporting it is extended for one month, until 4 June 2005. That short bridge kept the operation lawful while the parties' compliance was tested.

Resolution 1700, adopted on 10 August 2006, renews the UN's political mission in Iraq for another year. UNAMI, the assistance mission created in 2003, advised Iraq on elections, a constitution, and rebuilding institutions. Iraq's foreign minister had written on 3 August saying the elected government still saw a vital role for the mission in building a stable, prosperous nation at peace with its neighbors.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve months. It stressed that Iraqi national dialogue, which the mission should support, was crucial to the country's political stability and unity. The renewal came as sectarian violence was climbing sharply, and the text thanks the UN for working in Iraq with international backing.

On 16 December 2009, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1900 about the war crimes court for the former Yugoslavia. The court, set up in 1993, was trying cases from the Balkan wars. Its judges reported that they could not finish all their work in 2010, as earlier decisions had asked.

The Council said it planned to keep the trial judges in their posts past the end of their terms. Appeals judges would stay until the end of 2012, or until their cases ended. Two temporary judges could also stay on to finish the Popović trial. For a short time the court could use thirteen temporary judges at once, one more than the normal limit. The aim was simple: trials should end with a proper judgment, not stop in the middle.

The Gambia is the subject of Resolution 200. The Council passed it by a full vote on 15 March 1965. The Gambia is a thin strip of land along a river, ringed by Senegal. It had won its freedom from Britain the month before, in February 1965.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit the Gambia as a member. The Assembly then gave it a seat. The text is one of the shortest kinds the Council writes. Yet it sealed the place of one of Africa's smallest states in the world. Some had doubted so small a land could stand on its own. Membership helped prove them wrong.

Côte d'Ivoire's mission is renewed for the post-crisis rebuilding year in Resolution 2000, adopted on 27 July 2011. The new president had been inaugurated on 21 May 2011 after a post-election crisis marked by atrocities. The International Criminal Court prosecutor was seeking to open an investigation into crimes since 28 November 2010, and legislative elections, the first since 2000, were due.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends UNOCI until 31 July 2012. It keeps its military component at 9,792 personnel, including the 2,400 surge troops, its police at 1,350, and adds 205 police advisers. The Special Representative must certify every stage of the legislative elections. UNOCI's mandate covers protecting civilians, watching the Liberia border with UNMIL, monitoring the arms embargo with no-notice inspections, collecting weapons, and building a new disarmament programme. It covers reviewing the security sector, whose forces were reorganized as the FRCI in March 2011.

Zambia complained that South Africa was violating its sovereignty, its airspace, and its territory. Forty-seven member states backed the complaint. The trouble lay near the Caprivi Strip, along the border with Namibia. South Africa's foreign minister gave his side as well. Resolution 300 was adopted unanimously on 12 October 1971.

The Council restated a basic rule of the Charter. Any violation of a member state's sovereignty and territory goes against the United Nations Charter. South Africa was called on to respect Zambia's sovereignty and territorial integrity in full. The Council also gave a clear warning. If South Africa violated them again, the Council would meet once more. It would then examine the situation under the relevant parts of the Charter.

Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim's first term was ending in 1976. The Austrian diplomat had led the UN since 1972. At a private meeting, the Council considered who should follow or continue. Resolution 400 records the outcome. No public debate or vote count appears in the text.

Members recommended Waldheim for a second term. The new stretch would run from 1 January 1977 to 31 December 1981. The General Assembly made the appointment. Waldheim's second term covered the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran-Iraq war's start. Years later, his wartime record in the German army drew scrutiny. The resolution itself is a single calm sentence of recommendation, preserved from a closed session.

A peaceful divorce brought this new applicant to the Council in 1993. On 8 January, it adopted Resolution 800 without a vote. The Slovak Republic had come into being a week before, on New Year's Day. Czechoslovakia had split into two states without a shot fired. The parting is often called the Velvet Divorce.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Slovak Republic. The Assembly did so on 19 January 1993. Its Czech twin entered on the same day. Swift seats for both halves showed how orderly the split had been. Yugoslavia's violent breakup made the contrast plain to all.
